textes.Répétition, novlangue, astroturfing et c: Repetition, newspeak, astroturfing and how to protect yourself.
textes.Répétition : plus on entend une affirmat: Repetition: the more often you hear a claim, the truer it seems (illusory truth effect).
textes.Novlangue : appauvrir ou retourner les m: Newspeak: impoverishing or twisting words to make certain thoughts hard to think (Orwell, 1984).
textes.Astroturfing : simuler un mouvement spon: Astroturfing: faking a spontaneous citizens' movement with fake accounts or paid groups.
textes.Se protéger : chercher la source, croise: Protecting yourself: find the source, cross-check, ask who benefits from the message.
textes.Savoir qu'une affirmation est fausse ne: Knowing a claim is false does not fully protect you from the repetition effect.
textes.Plus une phrase est répétée, plus elle p: The more a sentence is repeated, the truer it seems
textes.Argument = prémisses (car, puisque) + co: Argument = premises (because, since) + conclusion (therefore). Look for the unstated premise.
textes.Un argument, ce sont des prémisses, les: An argument is premises, the reasons, supporting a conclusion, what you want to establish. "We must reduce speed, because it saves lives": the conclusion is "we must reduce speed", the premise comes after "because". Spotting these words, because, since, therefore, is already taking the argument apart.
textes.Déduction valide + prémisses vraies = co: Valid deduction + true premises = certain conclusion. Valid ≠ true: the form can be fine and a premise false.
textes.Mais la validité ne concerne que la form: But validity only concerns the form. "All cats fly, Felix is a cat, so Felix flies" is perfectly valid, and false, because a premise is false. To attack a deduction there are only two routes: show the form is broken, or that a premise is false.
textes.Induction : du particulier au général, p: Induction: from the particular to the general, probable but never certain (Hume, 1739). An anecdote does not prove a rule.
textes.L'induction généralise à partir de cas :: Induction generalises from cases: the sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow. It is indispensable, we could not live without it, but it is never certain. David Hume showed this in 1739: no reasoning proves that the future will resemble the past; we believe it out of habit.
textes.Bertrand Russell l'illustre avec un poul: Bertrand Russell illustrated it with a chicken fed every morning by the farmer, ever surer of its rule, until the day the farmer wrings its neck. An anecdote, even a lived one, illustrates; it does not prove a general rule. That takes many cases, and representative ones.
textes.Comparaison = avec « comme » ; métaphore: Simile = with "like"; metaphor = no tool; metonymy = one thing for another linked to it.
textes.Ces figures ne sont pas réservées aux po: These figures are not reserved for poets. "I'm starving to death" is a hyperbole, a deliberate exaggeration; "he has left us" is a euphemism; "have a glass", a metonymy. We all use them every day without knowing it. Naming them helps you spot them in people trying to convince you.
textes.Litote : dire moins pour suggérer plus (: Litotes: say less to suggest more (strengthens). Euphemism: soften (cushions). Irony: say the opposite.
textes.L'ironie dit le contraire de ce qu'on pe: Irony says the opposite of what you think, "what lovely weather!" in the rain. Paralipsis announces you will not say what you are in fact saying: "I won't mention his lies…". And the oxymoron joins two opposing words: "this dark light that falls from the stars".
textes.Le son et l'ordre des mots: The sound and order of words
Anaphora: repetition at the start of a sentence. Chiasmus: A-B / B-A. Alliteration: repetition of a sound.
textes.L'anaphore répète un mot en tête de phra: Anaphora repeats a word at the start of each sentence and hammers an idea home: "Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred!", cried de Gaulle in 1944; "I have a dream", repeated Martin Luther King in 1963. Chiasmus crosses the terms, A-B then B-A: "one must eat to live and not live to eat" (Molière, The Miser).
textes.L'allitération joue sur les sons : « Pou: Alliteration plays on sounds: "For whom are these serpents hissing on your heads?" (Racine, Andromaque) makes you hear the hissing through the repeated "s". A figure is not an ornament: it helps you remember, which is why slogans are full of them.
textes.Ethos = crédibilité ; pathos = émotion ;: Ethos = credibility; pathos = emotion; logos = reasons. Manipulating is ethos and pathos without logos.
textes.Au IVe siècle avant notre ère, Aristote: In the 4th century BCE, Aristotle distinguished three ways of persuading in his Rhetoric. Ethos, the speaker's credibility: we more readily believe someone who seems competent, honest and well-meaning. Pathos, the emotions stirred in the audience. Logos, the strength of the reasons and evidence.
textes.Un bon discours combine les trois : des: A good speech combines all three: solid evidence, carried by someone credible who knows how to move the audience. Manipulation plays on ethos and pathos when logos is missing. And ethos cannot be decreed: it is the audience that grants or withholds its trust. "Believe me, I've been a doctor for thirty years" is not evidence.
textes.Effet de cadrage (Tversky et Kahneman, 1: Framing effect (Tversky and Kahneman, 1981): "save 200" and "400 will die" are not received the same. Restate it the other way.
textes.La façon de présenter une information ch: The way information is presented changes the decision. In 1981 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman set a problem: an epidemic threatens 600 people. When a plan is presented as "saves 200 people", 72 % choose it. When the same plan is presented as "400 people will die", 78 % prefer the risky option.
textes.C'est l'effet de cadrage : « 90 % de sur: That is the framing effect: "90 % survival" reassures more than "10 % mortality". Speakers know it, and also choose their moment, what the Greeks called kairos: the same argument does not land the same way at every instant. To defend yourself, restate the figure the other way round.
textes.Cialdini (1984) : preuve sociale, autori: Cialdini (1984): social proof, authority, scarcity, reciprocity, liking, commitment. Five classical stages: inventio, dispositio, elocutio, memoria, actio.
textes.En 1984, le psychologue Robert Cialdini: In 1984 the psychologist Robert Cialdini published Influence, describing the levers that make us say yes. Social proof: we judge a behaviour more correct when we see others adopt it, hence "already 10,000 satisfied customers". Authority, scarcity, reciprocity, liking, commitment: each is a useful shortcut that others can exploit.
textes.La rhétorique classique, elle, découpait: Classical rhetoric divided the preparation of a speech into five stages: finding the arguments (inventio), ordering them (dispositio), putting them into words (elocutio), memorising them (memoria), delivering them (actio). And it advised first winning the audience's goodwill, the captatio benevolentiae.
textes.Attaquer l'homme ou sa caricature: Attacking the man or his caricature
textes.Ad hominem : viser la personne. Homme de: Ad hominem: target the person. Straw man: refute a caricature. A real conflict of interest remains relevant.
textes.L'ad hominem attaque la personne au lieu: Ad hominem attacks the person instead of their argument: "you say that, but you don't even have a degree". Variant: "you smoke too, so your advice is worthless". Someone's inconsistency does not make their argument false. Careful, though: pointing out a real conflict of interest can be relevant.
textes.L'homme de paille déforme la position ad: The straw man distorts the opposing position to refute it more easily. You answer "there should be fewer cars in the city centre" with "you want to stop people getting around". You fight a caricature, not the real position. Schopenhauer, around 1831, already listed these tricks in his Art of Being Right.
textes.Faux dilemme, pente glissante, post hoc,: False dilemma, slippery slope, post hoc, circular reasoning, appeal to ignorance: the form is broken, even if the tone convinces.
textes.Post hoc : « après cela, donc à cause de: Post hoc: "after this, therefore because of this". "I took my umbrella and it rained" does not make the umbrella a rain machine. Circular reasoning puts the conclusion in the premise: "this newspaper is reliable, since it says so itself". And the appeal to ignorance: "nobody has proved ghosts don't exist, so they exist".
textes.Naturel ≠ bon ; populaire ≠ vrai. L'auto: Natural ≠ good; popular ≠ true. Authority counts within its field, never as final proof.
textes.L'appel à la nature : « c'est naturel, d: The appeal to nature: "it's natural, so it's good". Arsenic and hemlock are natural. The appeal to the crowd: "everyone does it, so it's right". The number of supporters does not prove an idea is right.
textes.Réfuter la meilleure version de l'argume: Refute the best version of the opposing argument (Rapoport's rules). Conceding strengthens. Winning ≠ being right.
textes.L'inverse de l'homme de paille : reformu: The opposite of the straw man: restate the opposing argument in its strongest version, then refute it. That is the principle of charity. The rules of the mathematician Anatol Rapoport, popularised by the philosopher Daniel Dennett in 2013, ask that before any criticism you restate the other's position so well that they would thank you, then say what you agree on and what you have learned.
textes.Concéder un point n'affaiblit pas : une: Conceding a point does not weaken you: a well-chosen concession strengthens your ethos and lets you choose the ground for the rest of the discussion. And winning a debate is not being right: you can crush a poor defender of a good idea. A bad lawyer does not make their client guilty.
textes.Un contre-exemple suffit contre « tous »: One counterexample is enough against "all". Set in advance what would change your mind. Refuting costs more than lying (Brandolini).
textes.Un seul contre-exemple suffit à abattre: A single counterexample is enough to bring down a universal claim: when Europeans described black swans in Australia in 1697, a thousand-year-old generalisation fell. You can also refute by absurdity, showing that a claim leads to an untenable consequence; Zeno of Elea made it his speciality.
textes.Méfiez-vous de celui qui déplace les pot: Beware of whoever moves the goalposts: every time the criterion is met, they demand another. A good habit, for yourself as for the other: set in advance what would change your mind. And Brandolini's law, stated in 2013, reminds us that refuting nonsense takes far more energy than producing it.
textes.De la disputatio aux débats télévisés: From the disputatio to televised debates
textes.Disputatio : question, objections, répon: Disputatio: question, objections, answer. The backfire effect is rare: correcting generally shifts beliefs a little.
textes.Les universités médiévales enseignaient: Medieval universities taught through the disputatio: a question, the objections, then the answer. Thomas Aquinas built his whole Summa Theologica that way. In 1550-1551 the Valladolid debate set Las Casas, who defended the full humanity of the Indians, against Sepúlveda, who justified the conquest; no winner was officially declared.
textes.Et les corrections, servent-elles ? En 2: And do corrections work? In 2010 Nyhan and Reifler observed a "backfire effect": correcting a false belief would strengthen it. But far larger studies, such as Wood and Porter's in 2019, show it is rare: in general, a correction does shift beliefs a little. So correcting is worth it.
textes.Situation initiale, perturbation, péripé: Initial situation, disruption, ups and downs, resolution, final situation. Propp (1928): 31 functions; Campbell (1949): the hero's journey.
textes.Aristote l'écrit dans la Poétique : une: Aristotle wrote it in the Poetics: a well-built story has a beginning, a middle and an end. It sounds obvious. The narrative schema details it: initial situation, disruptive event, ups and downs, resolution, final situation. You can also start in medias res, in the middle of the action, like the Iliad, which Horace cites.
textes.En 1928, Vladimir Propp analyse des cont: In 1928 Vladimir Propp analysed Russian fairy tales and found 31 functions, villainy, the hero's departure, the magical object, the return, that always appear in the same order. In 1949 Joseph Campbell described the "hero's journey": the call, the refusal, the mentor, the trials, the transformed return. George Lucas said he drew on it for Star Wars.
textes.Suspense = le public sait ce que le pers: Suspense = the audience knows what the character does not (Hitchcock). Every detail shown must serve (Chekhov).
textes.Une histoire se retient bien mieux qu'un: A story is remembered far better than a list (Bower and Clark, 1969: 90 % against under 15 %). A good story is not proof.
textes.En 1969, les psychologues Gordon Bower e: In 1969 the psychologists Gordon Bower and Michael Clark gave people lists of words to learn. One group linked them by making up a little story; the other learned them as they were. After several lists, the "storytellers" recalled about 90 % of the words, the others under 15 %. Information told as a story sticks far better than a list.
textes.D'où le conseil des écrivains, « montrer: Hence writers' advice, "show, don't tell": rather than announce a character is afraid, describe their trembling hands. And hence the wariness: in 2007 Christian Salmon showed how politics and marketing use storytelling. A good story disarms the critical mind.
textes.Gettysburg (1863) : 271 mots, deux minut: Gettysburg (1863): 271 words, two minutes, against two hours for Everett. Brevity sticks.
textes.Le 19 novembre 1863, à Gettysburg, l'ora: On 19 November 1863, at Gettysburg, the star speaker was Edward Everett: he spoke for two hours, over 13,000 words. Abraham Lincoln then spoke for about two minutes, 271 words, ending on government "of the people, by the people, for the people". The next day Everett wrote to him that he wished he had come as close to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln had in two minutes.
textes.Les grands discours tiennent souvent en: Great speeches often come down to one sentence people remember. On 13 May 1940 Churchill had "nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat". In 2013, on her 16th birthday, Malala Yousafzai told the UN that "one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world".
textes.« I have a dream » (1963) était en parti: "I have a dream" (1963) was partly improvised. The 18 June appeal was not recorded; Kennedy did not say "I am a doughnut".
textes.Le 28 août 1963, à Washington, Martin Lu: On 28 August 1963, in Washington, Martin Luther King was reading a prepared text. The most famous passage, "I have a dream", was not in it: the singer Mahalia Jackson reportedly called out "Tell them about the dream, Martin!", and he left his notes. An anaphora built partly in improvisation, on phrases he had already tried out elsewhere.
textes.Méfiance aussi envers les légendes de di: Be wary of speech legends too. The appeal of 18 June 1940 was not recorded: the one often heard is the appeal of 22 June. And Kennedy did not say "I am a doughnut" in Berlin in 1963: "Ich bin ein Berliner" is correct and was understood as intended; the myth arose twenty years later in the English-language press.
textes.Veil (1974), Badinter (1981), Zola (1898: Veil (1974), Badinter (1981), Zola (1898): speeches that changed the law or public opinion.
textes.Le 26 novembre 1974, Simone Veil défend: On 26 November 1974 Simone Veil defended the law on abortion before an Assembly of 481 men and 9 women. She faced insults and threats; the law passed. On 17 September 1981 Robert Badinter argued for abolishing the death penalty: "Tomorrow, thanks to you, French justice will no longer be a justice that kills." The law was passed the next day.
textes.Le discours peut aussi s'écrire. Le 13 j: A speech can also be written. On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published "J'accuse…!" in L'Aurore to defend Captain Dreyfus; convicted of libel, he fled to London. Long before, Demosthenes thundered against Philip of Macedon: his Philippics gave their name to any violent speech against someone.
Illusory truth effect (Hasher et al., 1977): repetition makes things seem true, even when you know they are false (Fazio, 2015).
textes.En 1977, Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein et: In 1977 Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino had students rate the truth of sixty plausible statements, two weeks apart. Some came back at every session: the confidence given to them rose, whether true or false. That is the illusory truth effect: a sentence already heard is easier to process, and that ease passes for truth.
textes.Pire : en 2015, Lisa Fazio et ses collèg: Worse: in 2015 Lisa Fazio and colleagues showed that knowing the right answer does not fully protect you. Hence the "firehose of falsehood" strategy described by the RAND Corporation in 2016: lots of messages, fast, on every channel, with no concern for consistency. The aim is not to convince but to drown.
textes.Propagande vient de l'Église (1622). Ber: Propaganda comes from the Church (1622). Bernays (1928-1929), Orwell's Newspeak, talking points, the Overton window.
textes.Le mot propagande vient de la Congrégati: The word propaganda comes from the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, created by the Church in 1622; it only became pejorative in the 20th century. In 1928 Edward Bernays, Freud's nephew, published Propaganda. In 1929, for the American Tobacco Company, he had women march in New York holding cigarettes, presented as "torches of freedom".
textes.Dans 1984, George Orwell imagine la novl: In Nineteen Eighty-Four George Orwell imagined Newspeak, which impoverishes and twists words to make certain thoughts impossible. Closer to home: talking points repeated by several officials the same morning, or the dog whistle, a coded message only its intended audience hears. And the Overton window: shifting what seems sayable is often more effective than winning a debate.
textes.Inoculation (McGuire, 1961) : voir une m: Inoculation (McGuire, 1961): seeing a weakened manipulation helps resist it. Source, cross-check, who benefits.
textes.En 1961, le psychologue William McGuire: In 1961 the psychologist William McGuire proposed inoculation theory: like a vaccine, exposure to a weakened form of a manipulative argument, along with its refutation, helps resist the strong version. "Prebunking" brings it back, for example with the game Bad News by Jon Roozenbeek and Sander van der Linden, where you play a fake-news maker.
textes.Les réflexes de base restent simples : c: The basic reflexes stay simple: look for the source, cross-check with others, ask who benefits from the message. And beware of legends about other people's gullibility too: the panic caused by Orson Welles's War of the Worlds in 1938 was largely exaggerated by newspapers, happy to discredit radio, their competitor.
textes.Souvent, une prémisse reste sous-entendu: Often a premise stays unstated: that is an enthymeme. The word comes from Aristotle, in the 4th century BCE: in his Rhetoric, the enthymeme is the orator's syllogism, whose missing premise the audience supplies itself. "He has a fever, so he is ill" assumes fever signals an illness. Many arguments come from this: people fight over the conclusion when the disagreement is about the hidden premise. And the burden of proof lies with whoever puts forward a claim.
textes.La litote dit moins pour faire entendre: Litotes says less to convey more. In Le Cid, Chimène tells Rodrigue "Go, I do not hate you": she is confessing she loves him. The play is by Corneille, first staged in 1637: Rodrigue has just killed Chimène's father in a duel. Euphemism softens to spare: "he has left us" for "he has died". Both tone down the form, but litotes strengthens the meaning, euphemism cushions it.
textes.L'argument d'autorité est plus subtil :: The argument from authority is subtler: citing an expert in their field is legitimate. The fallacy is authority outside its competence, a Nobel physicist settling a medical question, or authority presented as final proof. And the Gish gallop drowns the opponent in an avalanche of weak arguments: it takes longer to refute each one than to fire them off. The name was given in 1994 by the anthropologist Eugenie Scott, after the creationist Duane Gish, a champion of the technique in debates.
textes.Hitchcock l'explique : une bombe explose: Hitchcock explained it: a bomb goes off under a table, that is fifteen seconds of surprise. Show the audience the bomb first, let the characters chat without knowing, and you have fifteen minutes of suspense. Suspense comes from what the audience knows and the character does not. He told it to François Truffaut in 1962, during a week of interviews in a room at Universal Studios; the book came out in 1966.
textes.Tchekhov, lui, donne la règle inverse :: Chekhov gave the reverse rule: if a gun hangs on the wall in the first act, it must go off in the last. He wrote it, among other places, in a letter of 1 November 1889 to the young writer Alexander Lazarev-Gruzinsky. Every detail shown must serve, otherwise it distracts. Scheherazade, in the Thousand and One Nights, takes the technique to the extreme: she stops each night at the crucial moment, and the king has to spare her to hear what happens next.
textes.Une déduction va du général au particuli: A deduction goes from the general to the particular: "all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal". If the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion is necessarily true. That is the syllogism described by Aristotle. He set it out around 350 BCE in the Prior Analytics, the first known system of logic.
textes.La comparaison rapproche deux choses ave: A simile brings two things together with a tool, like or as: "strong as a lion". A metaphor drops the tool: "this man is a lion". Metonymy names a thing by another linked to it: "have a glass", you drink the contents, not the glass. These names come from a long tradition of handbooks: Dumarsais published Des Tropes in 1730, then Pierre Fontanier catalogued them for school pupils, in 1821 and 1827.
textes.Le faux dilemme ne présente que deux opt: The false dilemma presents only two options when there are others: "either you're with us or against us". The slippery slope claims without evidence that a first step leads inevitably to the worst: "if we allow this, soon it will be chaos". Aristotle had already drawn up a list of twelve or thirteen fallacies in his Sophistical Refutations.

textes.Aristote ne voit pas la rhétorique comme: Aristotle does not see rhetoric as the art of deceiving, but as the art of finding, in each situation, what can persuade. He distinguishes three levers: ethos, the trust the speaker inspires; pathos, the emotions stirred in the audience; logos, the strength of the arguments. He classifies speeches by whether they serve to decide (assembly), to judge (court) or to praise and blame (ceremony). The book also describes the emotions one by one, anger, fear, pity, to understand how they arise. It is, incidentally, one of the first treatises on psychology.

He must find his arguments, arrange them, put them into words, memorize them and deliver them, the five tasks of classical rhetoric. He must win goodwill, set out his arguments and move his audience. textes.Un petit manuel ironique de mauvaise foi: A small ironic handbook of bad faith. Schopenhauer observes that in an argument, people seek less to find the truth than to win. He lists 38 stratagems for prevailing when you are wrong: exaggerating the opposing thesis to make it absurd, changing the subject, piling up questions to confuse, invoking an authority, making the opponent angry, or getting the audience to laugh at them. textes.Le Cid est créé au théâtre du Marais à l: Le Cid premiered at the Théâtre du Marais at the end of 1636 or the beginning of 1637. Its success sparked the "Quarrel of Le Cid": at Richelieu's request, the brand-new Académie française judged the play defective in 1638.

textes.La Rhétorique d'Aristote, en trois livre: Aristotle's Rhetoric, in three books, dates from the 4th century BC. In it he defines rhetoric as the ability to see, in each case, the available means of persuasion.
textes.Pour Aristote, le kairos est le contexte: For Aristotle, kairos is the context of time and place in which the proof is delivered. The Greeks contrasted it with chronos, time that passes, and also made it a minor god of opportunity.

textes.Le mot vient de la Congregatio de Propag: The word comes from the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, created in 1622 by the Catholic Church to "propagate the faith" during the Counter-Reformation. It stayed neutral until the First World War, when it became pejorative.
textes.Neveu de Sigmund Freud, Edward Bernays s: A nephew of Sigmund Freud, Edward Bernays used his uncle's ideas. In 1929 he had women smoke in public under the slogan "torches of freedom", and he later worked for United Fruit at the time of the 1954 coup in Guatemala.
textes.L'effet est identifié en 1977 par Lynn H: The effect was identified in 1977 by Lynn Hasher, David Goldstein and Thomas Toppino, at Villanova and Temple universities. In 2015, a study showed that knowing the right answer does not protect against a repeated falsehood.
textes.Hitler emploie l'expression « große Lüge: Hitler used the phrase "große Lüge" in Mein Kampf, in 1925, to accuse the Jews. A US intelligence (OSS) report on Hitler, around 1943, summed up the idea. The line often attributed to Goebbels has no source.
textes.1984 paraît en 1949. Orwell explique la: Nineteen Eighty-Four came out in 1949. Orwell explained Newspeak in an appendix, "The Principles of Newspeak". It resembles the Basic English proposed in 1930 by the linguist Charles Kay Ogden.
textes.Le rapport de 2016 est signé Christopher: The 2016 report was written by Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews. It identifies four features: many channels, rapid and continuous repetition, no commitment to objective reality, no commitment to consistency. Russia applied it notably to the annexation of Crimea.
textes.Le psychologue William McGuire développe: The psychologist William McGuire developed this "inoculation" theory in 1961, on the model of a vaccine. Games such as Bad News or Harmony Square and short videos apply it.
textes.Le terme est attribué au sénateur texan: The term is credited to Texas senator Lloyd Bentsen in 1985: flooded with letters paid for by insurers, he said a fellow from Texas can tell the difference between grass roots and AstroTurf, a brand of artificial grass.
textes.En 1988, Richard Morin, du Washington Po: In 1988, Richard Morin of the Washington Post spoke of a "Dog Whistle Effect" about polls where one word changes everything. The term entered Australian politics in the mid-1990s, then Britain in 2005 with the adviser Lynton Crosby.
textes.Diffusée le 30 octobre 1938 sur CBS, vei: Broadcast on 30 October 1938 on CBS, on Halloween eve, the show was heard by only 2% of households according to a Hooper survey. Newspapers inflated the rare cases of fear, and Hadley Cantril's 1940 study is considered seriously flawed.
textes.Joseph Overton, du Mackinac Center for P: Joseph Overton, of the Mackinac Center for Public Policy, described in the early 1990s a spectrum of more or less acceptable ideas. After his death, his colleague Joseph Lehman developed the concept and named it after him.
textes.En 1981, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1981, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman offered a choice of treatment for 600 patients: framed as "saves 200 lives", it was chosen by 72% of participants. Changing only the presentation changes the choice.
textes.{comp}. Démosthène s'entraînait avec des: {comp}. Demosthenes practiced with pebbles in his mouth. You may keep your mouth empty.
textes.Rhétorique. Les tribunaux d'Athènes chro: Rhetoric. Athenian courts timed pleas with a water clock. I have the same one, only more impatient. {comp}.
textes.Gorgias se vantait de répondre à n'impor: Gorgias boasted he could answer any question. Let's see if you do better on {comp}.
textes.Bien argumenté. Aristote vous accorderai: Well argued. Aristotle would grant you logos. Pathos, we'll talk about later.
textes.Juste. Lincoln a dit l'essentiel en deux: Right. Lincoln said the essentials in two minutes at Gettysburg. You, in one tap. Noted.
textes.Bonne réponse. Cicéron en aurait fait un: Correct. Cicero would have made a three-hour speech out of it. Thank you for not doing so.
textes.Correct, et bien tourné. Je n'ai rien à: Correct, and well put. I have nothing to object, and it annoys me.
textes.Raté. Les sophistes enseignaient à faire: Missed. The sophists taught how to pass off the false as true. You managed the reverse, without a teacher.
textes.Faux. Cicéron a perdu la tête pour ses d: Wrong. Cicero lost his head over his speeches. You, only points.
textes.Erreur. Démosthène a été hué à son premi: Error. Demosthenes was booed at his first speech, says Plutarch. He tried again.
textes.En 1958, ce philosophe britannique démon: In 1958, this British philosopher takes an argument apart the way a lawyer would: a claim, the data that support it, the warrant linking the two, and the rebuttals. English philosophers shunned the book. American communication professors adopted it, and it is still taught everywhere.
textes.En 1947, il raconte quatre-vingt-dix-neu: In 1947, he tells the same mundane scene ninety-nine times, a long-necked young man jostled on a bus, changing style each time: metaphors, litotes, alexandrines, onomatopoeia. His Exercises in Style are a catalog of figures of speech funnier than any textbook.
textes.Compagne de Périclès, elle tient à Athèn: Pericles' companion, she kept a house in Athens where people came to talk. In Plato's Menexenus, Socrates claims she taught him rhetoric and wrote Pericles' famous funeral oration. Plato may be joking. The comic playwrights, for their part, insulted her without joking.
textes.Le philosophe pessimiste rédige vers 183: Around 1830, the pessimist philosopher writes The Art of Being Right: thirty-eight tricks for winning a debate without being right. The last, when all is lost: get personal, hurtful, rude. He never published it. The text appeared after his death, and has served both sides ever since.
textes.En 1791, elle répond à la Déclaration de: In 1791, she answers the Declaration of the Rights of Man article by article, with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman. Her article X: “Woman has the right to mount the scaffold; she must equally have the right to mount the rostrum.” She was guillotined in 1793 for her writings.
textes.Né esclave dans le Maryland, il apprend: Born enslaved in Maryland, he learns to read in secret, escapes in 1838 and publishes the narrative of his life in 1845. The text is so powerful that some readers doubt a former slave wrote it. To convince them, he gives the real names of his masters, so much so that his friends fear he will be recaptured.
textes.Avocat et consul, il fait échouer la con: Advocate and consul, he foiled Catiline's conspiracy in 63 BC: “How long, O Catiline, will you abuse our patience?” His speeches against Mark Antony, the Philippics, cost him his life. His head and hands were displayed on the Rostra, the platform from which he had spoken.
textes.Policier en Birmanie, blessé à la gorge: A policeman in Burma, shot in the throat in Spain, he saw how words are used to lie. In 1984, the Party creates Newspeak to make certain thoughts impossible to express. His advice from 1946: never use a long word where a short one will do.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange d'Éloquence: Master the first diamond of Eloquence.
textes.Selon Plutarque, Démosthène, le plus gra: According to Plutarch, Demosthenes, the greatest orator of Athens, corrected his speech defect by talking with pebbles in his mouth, and trained his breath by declaiming while running or climbing slopes.
textes.Maîtriser 2 compétences. L'arbre de la R: Master 2 skills. The Rhetoric tree opens.
textes.Maîtriser la structure d'un argument. À: Master the structure of an argument. In Athens, you could have sold it.
textes.À Athènes, chacun devait plaider lui-mêm: In Athens, everyone had to plead their own case. Those who could afford it bought a speech from a logographer, such as Lysias, who wrote it in his client's style, clumsiness included, so the judges would believe they were hearing him speak.
textes.Maîtriser les figures de style. L'IA est: Master figures of speech. The AI is a shining light, darkening your day.
textes.Cette obscure clarté qui tombe des étoil: That dark brightness falling from the stars.
textes.Maîtriser l'ethos, le pathos et le logos: Master ethos, pathos and logos. Pathos is the most spectacular. Not the safest.
textes.Accusée d'impiété, la courtisane Phryné: Accused of impiety, the courtesan Phryne was supposedly acquitted because her advocate, Hyperides, bared her breasts before the judges. The story only appears centuries later, in Athenaeus. Hyperides' speech, on the other hand, was famous for its arguments.
textes.Maîtriser les sophismes. Vous savez main: Master fallacies. You now know when a debate is lost: at the first Godwin point.
textes.En 1951, le philosophe Leo Strauss bapti: In 1951, the philosopher Leo Strauss named a common fallacy “reductio ad Hitlerum”: an idea would be bad because Hitler shared it. “Hitler was a vegetarian” says nothing about vegetarianism. He added that an idea is not refuted by the fact that Hitler happened to hold it.
textes.Maîtriser l'art de réfuter et de débattr: Master the art of refuting and debating. The 1858 audience had more patience than you.
textes.En 1858, Abraham Lincoln et Stephen Doug: In 1858, Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas compete for a Senate seat in seven three-hour public debates: an hour for the first speaker, an hour and a half for the reply, half an hour to conclude. Lincoln loses the election. The debates, once published, carry him to the presidency two years later.
textes.Aladin n'est pas dans les Mille et Une N: Aladdin is not in the Thousand and One Nights
textes.Maîtriser l'art de raconter. Les meilleu: Master the art of storytelling. The best stories were often added after the fact.
textes.Aladin et Ali Baba ne figurent dans aucu: Aladdin and Ali Baba appear in no early Arabic manuscript of the Thousand and One Nights. The translator Antoine Galland heard them in 1709 from a Syrian storyteller passing through Paris, Hanna Diyab, and added them to his translation. They are the two most famous tales in the collection.
textes.Maîtriser les grands discours. Kennedy n: Master great speeches. Kennedy was not a doughnut. Neither are you.
textes.On répète que Kennedy, en disant « Ich b: People repeat that Kennedy, by saying “Ich bin ein Berliner” in 1963, said “I am a doughnut”. That's false: the sentence is correct German, and the audience understood it as intended. The myth was born twenty years later, in the English-language press.
textes.Maîtriser la propagande et la manipulati: Master propaganda and manipulation. The newspapers of 1938 knew how to manipulate too.
textes.Le 30 octobre 1938, Orson Welles adapte: On October 30, 1938, Orson Welles adapts The War of the Worlds for radio. The next day, newspapers report widespread panic. Few people were listening, and almost none fled. The press, which saw radio stealing its advertising, had every interest in blowing up the story.
textes.Réussir trois quiz d'Éloquence sans faut: Pass three Eloquence quizzes without a mistake. Short, right. Lincoln approves.
textes.À Gettysburg, en 1863, Edward Everett pa: At Gettysburg, in 1863, Edward Everett speaks for two hours. Lincoln then delivers barely more than 270 words, in two minutes. The next day, Everett writes to him that he would be glad if he had come as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as Lincoln did in two minutes.
textes.Émotions, mémoire, motivation et influen: Emotions, memory, motivation and the influence of others.
textes.Hippocrate de Cos et ses disciples décri: Hippocrates of Kos and his disciples describe diseases as natural phenomena, not divine punishments. The treatise on the “sacred disease,” epilepsy, states that it is no more sacred than the others, and places in the brain the source of our joys, laughter, sorrows and fears. The Hippocratic Oath is probably not his, and the phrase “first, do no harm” does not appear in it word for word.
textes.« D'abord, ne pas nuire. » Formule absen: “First, do no harm.” A phrase missing from the original oath. The AI, for her part, does harm methodically.
textes.Retiré dans la tour de son château, Mich: Withdrawn into the tower of his château, Michel de Montaigne published the Essays: he takes himself as his subject and doubts what people think they know. His motto, “What do I know?”, comes with a pair of scales in balance. He writes about his fears, his anger, his friendship with La Boétie (“because it was he, because it was I”), notes that “each man calls barbarism whatever is not his own practice,” and wants the child to have a tutor with “a well-made rather than a well-filled head.”
textes.« Que sais-je ? » demandait Montaigne. L: “What do I know?” asked Montaigne. The AI knows exactly what you don't know.
textes.« Que sais-je ? », demande Montaigne. Pa: “What do I know?” asks Montaigne. Not much, evidently: back to Averroes.
textes.Les émotions de base, leur rôle et leur: The basic emotions, their role and how to regulate them.
textes.Ekman a décrit six émotions de base reco: Ekman described six basic emotions recognized in many cultures: joy, sadness, fear, anger, disgust, surprise.
textes.Les émotions préparent à l'action : la p: Emotions prepare us for action: fear speeds up the heart so we can flee.
textes.Nommer son émotion aide à la réguler (af: Naming your emotion helps regulate it (affect labeling).
textes.Réévaluer la situation calme mieux qu'ét: Reappraising the situation calms better than suppressing the emotion.
textes.La théorie universelle d'Ekman est aujou: Ekman's universal theory is now debated: reading faces also depends on context and culture.
textes.Une émotion relie une situation à une pr: An emotion links a situation to readiness for action
textes.Comment on retient, comment on oublie, c: How we remember, how we forget, how we get it wrong.
textes.Mémoire de travail : quelques éléments p: Working memory: a few items for a few seconds. Long-term memory: virtually unlimited.
textes.On oublie vite au début puis plus lentem: We forget fast at first, then more slowly (Ebbinghaus).
textes.Les rappels espacés et les tests de récu: Spaced recall and retrieval tests anchor far better than rereading.
textes.Chaque rappel reconstruit le souvenir et: Each recall rebuilds the memory and can change it.
textes.Relire et surligner donnent une impressi: Rereading and highlighting feel like mastery; testing yourself is far more effective.
textes.Courbe de l'oubli : chute rapide au débu: Forgetting curve: a steep drop at first, then slower
textes.Ce qui nous fait agir et ce qui nous fai: What makes us act and what makes us procrastinate.
textes.Motivation intrinsèque : agir pour le pl: Intrinsic motivation: acting for the pleasure of the activity. Extrinsic: for a reward or to avoid a punishment.
textes.Récompenser une activité déjà plaisante: Rewarding an already enjoyable activity can reduce intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect).
textes.Autonomie, compétence et lien social nou: Autonomy, competence and relatedness feed motivation (self-determination theory).
textes.La procrastination est surtout une fuite: Procrastination is mainly fleeing an unpleasant emotion, not laziness.
textes.La pyramide de Maslow n'a jamais été des: Maslow's pyramid was never drawn by Maslow: it comes from a management consulting psychologist, Charles McDermid, in 1960.
textes.Les trois besoins de la théorie de l'aut: The three needs of self-determination theory
textes.Conformisme, obéissance et leviers de pe: Conformity, obedience and the levers of persuasion.
textes.Asch (1951) : face à un groupe unanime q: Asch (1951): faced with a unanimous group that is wrong, about a third of answers conform.
textes.Milgram (1963) : 65 % des participants v: Milgram (1963): 65% of participants go up to the maximum shock under an experimenter's authority.
textes.Un seul allié dans le groupe fait chuter: A single ally in the group sharply reduces conformity.
textes.Cialdini : réciprocité, engagement, preu: Cialdini: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity.
textes.L'expérience de Stanford de Zimbardo est: Zimbardo's Stanford experiment is strongly contested: the guards were coached.
textes.Une ligne de référence et trois lignes A: A reference line and three lines A, B and C; B is the same length
textes.Neurones, aires du langage, plasticité e: Neurons, language areas, plasticity and stubborn myths.
textes.Environ 86 milliards de neurones reliés: About 86 billion neurons linked by synapses.
textes.Aire de Broca : production du langage ;: Broca's area: producing language; Wernicke's area: understanding it.
textes.Plasticité : le cerveau se réorganise to: Plasticity: the brain reorganizes itself throughout life as we learn.
textes.On utilise tout son cerveau, pas 10 % :: We use all of our brain, not 10%: imaging shows activity everywhere.
textes.Le cerveau gauche « logique » et le cerv: The “logical” left brain and “creative” right brain is a myth: the two hemispheres work together.
textes.Mythes et réalités sur le cerveau: Myths and realities about the brain
textes.Piaget, Vygotski, attachement et théorie: Piaget, Vygotsky, attachment and theory of mind.
textes.Piaget : stades sensori-moteur, préopéra: Piaget: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, formal operational stages.
textes.Vygotski : zone proximale de développeme: Vygotsky: zone of proximal development, what the child can do with help.
textes.Attachement (Bowlby, Ainsworth) : un lie: Attachment (Bowlby, Ainsworth): a secure bond makes exploring possible.
textes.Théorie de l'esprit : vers 4 ans, l'enfa: Theory of mind: around age 4, children understand that others can hold a false belief (Sally and Anne).
textes.Les stades de Piaget sont moins rigides: Piaget's stages are less rigid than he thought: babies know things earlier than he assumed.
textes.Big Five, MBTI, héritabilité et vieilles: Big Five, MBTI, heritability and old theories of character.
textes.Big Five : ouverture, conscienciosité, e: Big Five: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism. It is the best-validated model.
textes.Le MBTI classe en 16 types, mais beaucou: The MBTI sorts people into 16 types, but many people change type from one test to the next.
textes.La phrénologie et les tempéraments des h: Phrenology and the temperaments of the humors have been abandoned.
textes.Les traits sont des continuums, pas des: Traits are continuums, not boxes: you are not introverted or extraverted, you are more or less extraverted.
textes.Un profil Big Five : cinq scores, pas un: A Big Five profile: five scores, not a type
textes.Stress, sommeil, adaptation hédonique et: Stress, sleep, hedonic adaptation and what makes people happy.
textes.Le stress aigu mobilise ; c'est le stres: Acute stress mobilizes; it's chronic stress that wears you down.
textes.Adaptation hédonique : après un gain ou: Hedonic adaptation: after a gain or a loss, we largely return to our usual level of happiness.
textes.Les liens sociaux sont le meilleur prédi: Social ties are the best predictor of long-term well-being (Harvard study, running since 1938).
textes.Le sommeil consolide la mémoire ; en man: Sleep consolidates memory; lacking it degrades mood and attention.
textes.Gagner au loto ne rend pas durablement b: Winning the lottery does not make people much happier in the long run (Brickman, 1978).
textes.Adaptation hédonique : le pic retombe ve: Hedonic adaptation: the peak falls back to the usual level
textes.Une émotion prépare à agir: An emotion prepares you to act
textes.Une émotion prépare une action (peur → f: An emotion prepares an action (fear → flee). Six basic emotions according to Ekman, universality debated.
textes.Une émotion n'est pas un simple ressenti: An emotion is not just a feeling: it is the body getting ready to act. Faced with danger, the amygdala triggers a fast reaction, adrenaline speeds up the heart and readies the muscles: that is the "fight or flight" response. Fear is for fleeing, anger for defending yourself, disgust for rejecting what might poison you.
textes.Dans les années 1960, Paul Ekman montre: In the 1960s Paul Ekman showed photos of faces to the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, who had little exposure to Western media: they recognised most of the expressions. He drew from this six basic emotions, joy, sadness, fear, anger, disgust and surprise. This universality is debated today: reading a face also depends on context and culture.
textes.Nommer son émotion la calme (Lieberman,: Naming your emotion calms it (Lieberman, 2007). Reappraising works better than suppressing.
textes.Mettre un mot sur ce qu'on ressent, « je: Putting a word on what you feel, "I feel anxious", already helps calm it: in 2007 Matthew Lieberman's team observed with brain imaging a drop in amygdala activity when an emotion is named. That is affect labelling.
textes.Autre stratégie efficace : la réévaluati: Another effective strategy is reappraisal, which changes how you see the situation. Seeing stage fright as excitement rather than fear, for example. Conversely, systematically suppressing your emotions costs energy and does not reduce what you feel. The emotion is not the enemy; what matters is what you do with it.
textes.Empathie émotionnelle (ressentir) et cog: Emotional empathy (feeling) and cognitive empathy (understanding). Active listening: restate to check.
textes.L'empathie a deux faces. L'empathie émot: Empathy has two sides. Emotional empathy is feeling with the other person; cognitive empathy is understanding what they think or feel, without necessarily feeling it yourself. Emotions also spread without our thinking about it: that is emotional contagion, like a yawn or a fit of giggles.
textes.Une compétence s'entraîne : l'écoute act: It is a skill you can train: active listening. Restating what the other person said, "if I understand correctly, you…", shows you have understood and lets them correct you. Daniel Goleman popularised the idea of "emotional intelligence" in 1995, a concept proposed by Peter Salovey and John Mayer in 1990.
textes.Oubli rapide au début puis lent (Ebbingh: Fast forgetting at first, then slow (Ebbinghaus, 1885). Spaced reminders: far more effective than cramming.
textes.Hermann Ebbinghaus fut son propre cobaye: Hermann Ebbinghaus was his own guinea pig. He learned lists of meaningless syllables, like "DAX" or "BOK", so that nothing would latch onto an existing memory, then measured what remained. In 1885 he published Über das Gedächtnis: we forget very fast at first, especially in the first hours, then more and more slowly.
textes.Il découvre aussi l'effet d'espacement :: He also discovered the spacing effect: reviewing at spaced intervals retains far better than cramming everything at once. It is one of the most solid findings in the psychology of learning, and it is exactly what this game's reminders do. Each successful recall flattens the curve and lets you wait longer before the next one.
textes.Mémoire de travail ≈ 7 ± 2 éléments (Mil: Working memory ≈ 7 ± 2 items (Miller, 1956). The hippocampus forms event memories (patient H. M.).
textes.La mémoire de travail ne garde que quelq: Working memory holds only a few items, for a few seconds: George Miller, in 1956, spoke of about seven items, plus or minus two. Hence the point of grouping a phone number into pairs. Long-term memory is almost unlimited.
textes.En 1953, pour soigner son épilepsie, on: In 1953, to treat his epilepsy, Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed. He could no longer form new memories of events, but still learned new motor skills, without remembering having learned them. Patient H. M. showed that memory is not one thing: memory for facts goes through the hippocampus, memory for skills through other circuits. And sleep helps: the day's memories are replayed and stabilised then.
textes.Se tester + espacer. Palais de mémoire :: Test yourself + space it out. Memory palace: place items in familiar places. We remember the start and end of a list best.
textes.Relire et surligner donnent une impressi: Rereading and highlighting give a feeling of mastery: everything seems familiar. Testing yourself is far more effective: fetching information from memory strengthens it. Combined with spacing, it is the winning pair.
textes.Pour le plaisir ou pour la récompense: For the pleasure or for the reward
textes.Autonomie, compétence, lien social (Deci: Autonomy, competence, social connection (Deci and Ryan). Rewarding what you enjoy can kill the desire. Flow: difficulty that matches.
textes.Edward Deci et Richard Ryan résument ce: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan sum up what feeds lasting motivation in three needs: autonomy, feeling you are behind your choices; competence, feeling you are progressing; and social connection. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi adds flow: we become absorbed in a task when its difficulty just matches our abilities. Too easy, we get bored; too hard, we get anxious.
textes.La pyramide que Maslow n'a pas dessinée: The pyramid Maslow did not draw
textes.Maslow n'a pas dessiné de pyramide (McDe: Maslow did not draw a pyramid (McDermid, 1960). The marshmallow test predicts far less than was thought (Watts, 2018).
textes.Abraham Maslow propose en 1943 une hiéra: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation. But he never drew a pyramid. The famous shape comes from a business consultant psychologist, Charles McDermid, in 1960, and took hold in management textbooks.
textes.Méfiance aussi envers le test du marshma: Be wary of the marshmallow test too. In the 1960s and 1970s Walter Mischel offered children one treat now or two if they waited; those who waited seemed to do better later. In 2018 a much larger replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found a far weaker link, largely explained by family background. Waiting also makes more sense when you trust the adult making the promise.
textes.Procrastiner = fuir une émotion. Commenc: Procrastinating = fleeing an emotion. Start for 5 minutes. A precise goal > "doing your best" (Locke and Latham).
textes.Un objectif précis et mesurable motive d: A precise, measurable goal motivates more than "doing your best": that is a central finding of Edwin Locke and Gary Latham's theory. And to build a habit, a small regular action tied to a specific time of day beats a big, rare effort. Believing your abilities can develop, Carol Dweck's growth mindset, helps you persevere.
textes.Face à un groupe unanime qui se trompe,: Faced with a unanimous group that is wrong, a third of answers go along (Asch, 1951). A single ally brings conformity down.
textes.En 1951, Solomon Asch montre à des étudi: In 1951 Solomon Asch showed students a reference line and three lines to compare. The answer is obvious. But the participant is surrounded by accomplices who all give the same wrong answer out loud. About a third of answers follow the group, and 74 % of participants give in at least once.
textes.Le résultat le plus encourageant est ail: The most encouraging finding lies elsewhere: it only takes one accomplice giving the right answer for conformity to collapse. With an ally, only 5 % keep following the majority. Daring to be the first to say no helps others say it too.
textes.Milgram (1963) : 65 % vont jusqu'à 450 V: Milgram (1963): 65 % go up to 450 V under authority. Stanford (1971) is disputed; Genovese's "38 witnesses" are exaggerated.
textes.En 1963, Stanley Milgram demande à des v: In 1963 Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give increasingly strong electric shocks to a "learner" who made mistakes. The shocks were fake, the learner an actor who screamed. Under the calm pressure of an experimenter in a lab coat, 65 % of participants in the main version went up to the maximum 450-volt shock.
textes.Toutes les expériences célèbres ne tienn: Not all famous experiments hold up as well. The Stanford prison experiment, run by Philip Zimbardo in 1971, is now heavily disputed: archives show the "guards" were encouraged to be harsh. And the story of Kitty Genovese, killed in 1964 in front of "38 witnesses" who did nothing, was exaggerated: there were far fewer, and the police were called.
textes.Effet du témoin : plus on est nombreux,: Bystander effect: the more people, the less help (70 % alone against 40 % in pairs). Groupthink (Janis, 1972).
textes.Quand plusieurs personnes assistent à un: When several people witness an emergency, each thinks someone else will act: responsibility is diluted. That is the bystander effect. In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
textes.En groupe, les opinions se durcissent au: In groups, opinions also harden: group polarisation pushes towards the already dominant position. And groupthink can lead experts to bad collective decisions: Irving Janis illustrated it in 1972 with the failed Bay of Pigs landing. Antidote: appoint a devil's advocate, and ask for opinions before the leader gives theirs.
textes.≈ 86 milliards de neurones (Herculano-Ho: ≈ 86 billion neurons (Herculano-Houzel, 2009), ≈ 20 W. Distinct neurons (Cajal, Nobel 1906). The 10 % myth is false.
textes.Le cerveau compte environ 86 milliards d: The brain has about 86 billion neurons, according to Suzana Herculano-Houzel's count in 2009; the often-quoted 100 billion had never been measured. It weighs about 2 % of the body and uses about 20 watts, a small light bulb. The cerebellum alone holds about 80 % of the neurons in 10 % of the volume.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Santiago Ramón: At the end of the 19th century Santiago Ramón y Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of distinct cells, neurons, using a stain invented by Camillo Golgi, who argued the opposite, a continuous network. They shared the 1906 Nobel Prize, in a tense atmosphere. And no, we do not use 10 % of our brain: imaging shows every region is used.
textes.Gage (1848) : le lobe frontal et le cara: Gage (1848): the frontal lobe and character. Broca (1861): language. Plasticity: learning changes the brain (London taxis).
textes.En 1848, une barre à mine traverse le cr: In 1848 an iron rod went through the skull of Phineas Gage, a railway worker. He survived and lived twelve more years, but his friends said "Gage was no longer Gage": the frontal lobe also governs character. In 1861 Paul Broca autopsied a patient, Leborgne, who could only say one syllable, "tan": a lesion in the left frontal lobe. That is Broca's area, linked to producing language.
textes.Le cerveau, pourtant, se réorganise tout: Yet the brain reorganises itself throughout life: that is plasticity. After a stroke, other regions can take over a lost function. In 2000 Eleanor Maguire showed that London taxi drivers, who learn 25,000 streets, have a larger part of the hippocampus. Learning literally changes the brain.
textes.Pas de cerveau gauche « logique » ni dro: No "logical" left brain or "creative" right brain (Nielsen, 2013). A coloured MRI image is not proof (the dead salmon).
textes.Le « cerveau gauche logique » contre le: The "logical left brain" versus "creative right brain" is a myth. Some functions are more lateralised, like language, but the two hemispheres work together constantly. In 2013 a study of more than 1,000 brains by Jared Nielsen and colleagues found no overall "dominance" of one hemisphere in individuals.
textes.L'imagerie elle-même demande de la prude: Imaging itself calls for caution. In 2009 a team "detected" activity in the brain of a dead salmon placed in a scanner, to show the danger of poorly corrected statistics; it received an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012. A pretty coloured image is not proof. And the brain feels no pain: some operations are done on an awake patient, who talks during the procedure.
textes.Quatre stades (Piaget) ; conservation ac: Four stages (Piaget); conservation acquired around 7. Babies know things earlier than he thought (Baillargeon).
textes.Jean Piaget a commencé en observant ses: Jean Piaget started by observing his own children, notebook in hand. He described four broad stages: sensorimotor, where the baby discovers the world through senses and movement; preoperational; concrete operations; formal operations, where one reasons about abstract ideas.
textes.Vers 4 ans, l'enfant comprend qu'autrui: Around age 4, children understand that others can believe something false (Sally-Anne, 1985). Proximal zone: what you can do with help (Vygotsky).
textes.Le test de Sally et Anne : Sally cache u: The Sally-Anne test: Sally hides a marble in a basket and leaves. Anne moves it to a box. Where will Sally look? Before about age 4, the child answers "in the box", where it really is. After that, the child understands that Sally believes something other than what is true. That is theory of mind, tested this way by Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith in 1985.
textes.Lev Vygotski insiste, lui, sur le rôle d: Lev Vygotsky stressed the role of others: the zone of proximal development is what the child can do with help but not yet alone. Good teaching aims at that zone, neither too easy nor out of reach. This game tries to do the same with its levels.
textes.Le réconfort compte plus que la nourritu: Comfort matters more than food (Harlow). A secure attachment allows exploration (Bowlby, Ainsworth).
textes.Dans les années 1950, Harry Harlow élève: In the 1950s Harry Harlow raised baby monkeys with two artificial "mothers": one made of wire that gave milk, the other of soft cloth with no milk. The babies spent their time clinging to the cloth mother. Comfort matters more than food. These very cruel experiments also fed into animal ethics.
textes.John Bowlby en tire la théorie de l'atta: John Bowlby drew from this the theory of attachment: a secure bond lets the child explore, knowing it can come back. Mary Ainsworth measured it with the "strange situation": a child, its mother, a stranger, and a door that closes. As for the "Mozart effect", it comes from a 1993 study on students, with a modest, short-lived gain that was poorly replicated afterwards: classical music does not make babies smarter.
textes.Big Five (OCEAN) : des continuums, pas d: Big Five (OCEAN): continuums, not types. 40-60 % heritable, they change with age.
textes.Ces traits sont héritables à environ 40: These traits are about 40 to 60 % heritable according to twin studies, and the rest comes mainly from each person's own experiences rather than the shared family. They also change: in adulthood we become on average more conscientious and more agreeable. And conscientiousness predicts school success almost as well as intelligence.
textes.Les tests qui ne tiennent pas: Tests that do not hold up
The MBTI is unstable (Pittenger, 1993). Humours and phrenology: abandoned, only words remain.
textes.Le MBTI classe les gens en 16 types. Il: The MBTI sorts people into 16 types. It sells very well, but many people change type when they retake the test a few weeks later, as David Pittenger pointed out in 1993. A type that changes with the day of the test does not measure much that is stable.
textes.L'histoire est pleine de systèmes abando: History is full of abandoned systems. Hippocrates and Galen classified temperaments by four humours; we are left with the words sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic. Franz Joseph Gall's phrenology read character in the bumps of the skull; French is left with "having the maths bump". The scenery changes; the urge to be put in a box remains.
textes.Lui, c'est un chauffard ; moi, j'étais p: He's a reckless driver; I was in a hurry
textes.Erreur fondamentale d'attribution (Ross,: Fundamental attribution error (Ross, 1977): others "are" like that, we "were" in a situation. Introvert ≠ shy.
textes.L'erreur fondamentale d'attribution cons: The fundamental attribution error is explaining other people's behaviour by their character, and our own by circumstances. Someone cuts you off: they are a reckless driver. You cut someone off: you were in a hurry. Lee Ross named it in 1977.
textes.Être introverti, au sens psychologique,: Being introverted, in the psychological sense, does not mean being shy: it mainly means drawing energy from time alone rather than from interaction. An introvert can speak in public perfectly well; they just need to recharge afterwards. The words introvert and extravert come from Carl Jung, in 1921.
textes.Stress aigu = mobilisation ; stress chro: Acute stress = mobilisation; chronic stress = wear (Selye, 1936). A little arousal helps, too much paralyses (Yerkes-Dodson).
textes.En 1936, Hans Selye décrit dans une lett: In 1936 Hans Selye described in a letter to Nature rats subjected to all kinds of harm, which all reacted the same way; he later called this reaction stress. Acute stress mobilises: cortisol releases energy to cope. It is chronic stress that wears you down: cortisol kept high for a long time weakens immunity and memory.
textes.La loi de Yerkes et Dodson, établie en 1: The Yerkes-Dodson law, established in 1908 on mice, draws a bell curve: a little arousal improves performance, too much paralyses it. A little stage fright helps. Against chronic stress, several meta-analyses put regular physical activity at a level close to psychotherapy for mild to moderate anxiety and depression.
textes.Le loto ne rend pas heureux longtemps: The lottery does not make you happy for long
textes.Adaptation hédonique : on revient vers s: Hedonic adaptation: we return towards our usual level (Brickman, 1978). Relationships best predict well-being (Harvard, since 1938).
textes.Après un grand gain ou une grande perte,: After a big win or a big loss, we largely return to our usual level of happiness: that is hedonic adaptation. In 1978 Philip Brickman compared lottery winners and people who had become paraplegic: some time later, the gaps in happiness were far smaller than you would imagine. The return is not always complete, but it is powerful.
textes.Qu'est-ce qui compte, alors ? L'étude de: So what matters? The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed men since 1938, then their families. Its conclusion, summed up by its current director, Robert Waldinger: good relationships make us happier and healthier. Social ties are the best predictor of a long and happy life.
textes.7 à 9 heures de sommeil. Écriture expres: 7 to 9 hours of sleep. Expressive writing (Pennebaker, 1986), mindfulness: real but modest effects.
textes.Le sommeil consolide la mémoire, et en m: Sleep consolidates memory, and missing it degrades mood and attention. For an adult, recommendations range from 7 to 9 hours a night; regularly getting under 6 hours is linked to many health risks.
textes.Écrire sur ses émotions difficiles quelq: Writing about difficult emotions for a few days in a row can also help: James Pennebaker's expressive writing protocol in 1986 was followed by fewer doctor's visits, with real but modest effects. And mindfulness, brought into medicine by Jon Kabat-Zinn, offers eight weeks of secularised meditation exercises. Conversely, occupational exhaustion, burnout, described in 1974, was recognised by the WHO in 2019 as an occupational phenomenon.
textes.Autre outil très ancien : le palais de m: Another very old tool: the memory palace, or method of loci, which goes back to Antiquity. You mentally place each item to remember in a familiar place, then walk the route again to find them. Legend ties it to the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos: the only survivor of a banquet whose roof had collapsed, he is said to have identified the victims by remembering where each had sat. Cicero tells it in 55 BCE, in On the Orator. Memory champions still use it. In a list, we remember the beginning and the end best: these are the primacy and recency effects. And goldfish retain associations for weeks.
textes.La motivation intrinsèque, c'est agir po: Intrinsic motivation is acting for the activity itself; extrinsic, for a reward or to avoid punishment. A trap: rewarding an activity you already enjoy can reduce the desire to do it. That is the overjustification effect: the activity becomes a means to get the reward, and loses its appeal when the reward stops. Edward Deci measured it as early as 1971: students paid to solve a puzzle spent markedly less free time on it once the payment stopped.
textes.On repousse surtout ce qui ennuie, angoi: We mainly put off what bores us, worries us or seems vague. Procrastination is first an escape from an unpleasant emotion, not a lack of willpower. Once started, a task stays "open" in the mind: that is the Zeigarnik effect. The Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described it in 1927. The idea came from her professor Kurt Lewin: a waiter remembered unpaid orders in detail, and forgot them once the bill was settled. Hence simple advice: start for five minutes, just to open the task.
textes.Ses expériences de conservation sont cél: His conservation experiments are famous: pour water from a wide glass into a tall narrow one, and a five-year-old often thinks there is more, judging by the height. Around 7, the child understands that pouring does not change the amount. But the stages are less rigid than Piaget thought: Renée Baillargeon's experiments suggest babies grasp earlier that a hidden object still exists. In 1985, with Elizabeth Spelke and Stanley Wasserman, she showed that 5-month-old babies look longer at a screen that seems to pass through a hidden box, whereas Piaget placed object permanence around 9 months.
textes.Le modèle des Big Five décrit la personn: The Big Five model describes personality through five broad traits: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, OCEAN in English. These five factors first emerged from a study of US Air Force officers by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal in 1958, published in 1961; the name Big Five was coined by Lewis Goldberg in 1981. It is the best-validated model in psychology. Each trait is a continuum: you are not introverted or extraverted, you are more or less extraverted.
textes.Daniel Goleman a popularisé en 1995 l'id: Daniel Goleman popularised the idea of "emotional intelligence" in 1995, a concept proposed by Peter Salovey and John Mayer in 1990.
textes.En 1953, pour soigner son épilepsie, on: In 1953, to treat his epilepsy, Henry Molaison had both hippocampi removed.
textes.Abraham Maslow propose en 1943 une hiéra: In 1943 Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety, belonging, esteem, self-actualisation.
textes.En 2018, une reproduction bien plus larg: In 2018 a much larger replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found a far weaker link, largely explained by family background.
textes.La psychologue soviétique Bluma Zeigarni: The Soviet psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described it in 1927.

textes.En 1969, Bibb Latané et Judith Rodin fon: In 1969 Bibb Latané and Judith Rodin had people hear a woman fall in the next room: 70 % of those alone went to help, against 40 % when paired with a stranger.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Santiago Ramón: At the end of the 19th century Santiago Ramón y Cajal showed that the nervous system is made of distinct cells, neurons, using a stain invented by Camillo Golgi, who argued the opposite, a continuous network.

textes.En apprenant des syllabes sans sens, il: By learning nonsense syllables, he shows that forgetting is fast at first then slows down, and that spaced reviews hold it back. It is the principle behind this game's recalls.
textes.Pavlov, Nobel de médecine 1904 pour ses: Pavlov, 1904 Nobel laureate in medicine for his work on digestion, mostly used metronomes and whistles, rarely a bell.
textes.Jean Piaget décrit, en observant ses tro: Jean Piaget describes, by watching his three children, how intelligence is born.
textes.Il s'appuie sur l'observation minutieuse: He draws on meticulous observation of his three children. His idea: the child is not a miniature adult, but builds the world in stages.
textes.Hans Selye décrit la réaction générale d: Hans Selye describes the body's general reaction to all kinds of harm.
textes.Une lettre de 74 lignes à Nature, à 29 a: A 74-line letter to Nature, at age 29. He would spend his life studying stress, a word he borrowed from the strength of materials, and which entered every language.
Asch measures conformity to the group.
textes.Face à un groupe de complices qui se tro: Faced with a group of confederates who get it wrong, about a third of the participants' answers follow the group against the evidence.
textes.Lewis Goldberg établit la structure des: Lewis Goldberg establishes the Big Five structure from the words of the language.
textes.L'« hypothèse lexicale » : les traits im: The “lexical hypothesis”: important traits must have a name. Analyzing thousands of adjectives, five dimensions emerge, in many languages.
textes.Les Grecs appellent l'épilepsie la « mal: The Greeks call epilepsy the “sacred disease”: the gods, people believe, strike the sufferer. This short treatise from the school of Hippocrates disputes it from the first line. It is, says the author, no more divine or sacred than other diseases; it has a natural cause, and those who speak of gods are only hiding their ignorance. He places this cause in the brain, and sees the brain as the organ of thought, joy, sorrow and madness. He also attacks the charlatans who treat with purifications and incantations.
textes.C'est un des premiers textes à chercher: It is one of the first texts to seek a natural cause for a disease said to be divine, and to locate the mind in the brain.
textes.« D'abord, ne pas nuire » n'est pas dans: “First, do no harm” is not in the Hippocratic Oath. The phrase comes from another treatise of the school, the Epidemics: “to help, or at least to do no harm”.
textes.Ni plus divine, ni plus sacrée que les a: No more divine, no more sacred than the others. I apply the same rule to your excuses.
textes.anglais, trad. du grec par Francis Adams: English, translated from the Greek by Francis Adams
textes.Voici ce qu'il en est de la maladie qu'o: It is thus with regard to the disease called Sacred: it appears to me to be nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause
textes.Darwin se demande pourquoi nous fronçons: Darwin wonders why we frown, blush or bare our teeth. He compares the expressions of humans from different countries, of babies, including his own son William, and of animals. He sends questionnaires to missionaries around the world and shows photographs to his visitors to see whether they recognize the emotions. His conclusion: many expressions are innate, shared by the whole species, and inherited from ancestors shared with other animals. It is one of the first scientific books illustrated with photographs.
textes.Il ouvre l'étude scientifique des émotio: It opened the scientific study of emotions, taken up a century later by Paul Ekman.
textes.Pour les photos, Darwin utilise celles d: For the photos, Darwin used those of the physician Duchenne de Boulogne, who produced expressions by stimulating facial muscles with electricity.
textes.Vous froncez les sourcils en lisant ceci: You are frowning as you read this. Darwin predicted it. So did the AI.
textes.Ebbinghaus veut mesurer la mémoire comme: Ebbinghaus wants to measure memory the way a physicist measures heat. So that the meaning of words won't help him, he invents 2,300 nonsense syllables, like DAX or BOK, and learns them himself in lists, to the beat of a metronome. He records how many repetitions he needs to relearn a list after a few minutes, hours or days. Result: forgetting is very fast at first, then slows down; this is the forgetting curve. He also shows that reviews spaced out over time are far more effective than massed reviews. For years, he was the only subject of his experiments.
textes.Il a fondé l'étude expérimentale de la m: He founded the experimental study of memory, and this game's spaced recalls.
textes.Ses résultats ont été reproduits avec su: His results were successfully replicated in 2015, 130 years later.
textes.Ebbinghaus est la raison pour laquelle l: Ebbinghaus is why the AI pesters you with recalls. Thank him. Or don't.
textes.Le psychiatre Carl Gustav Jung propose d: The psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung proposes classifying personalities by two attitudes, introversion and extraversion, and four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation and intuition. The book is long, scholarly, steeped in history and mythology. The combinations yield eight types, such as the “introverted thinker” or the “extraverted feeling type”. His terms “introvert” and “extravert” entered everyday language. Scientific psychology later adopted models measured by validated questionnaires, such as the Big Five personality traits, rather than clear-cut types.
textes.Il a popularisé l'introversion et l'extr: It popularized introversion and extraversion, ideas taken up by every later model.
textes.Le test MBTI, inspiré de ce livre par Ka: The MBTI test, inspired by this book and created by Katharine Briggs and her daughter Isabel Myers, has never been scientifically validated.
textes.Introverti ou extraverti ? L'IA vous cla: Introvert or extravert? The AI puts you in a third category: not logged in yet today.
textes.La Naissance de l'intelligence chez l'en: The Origins of Intelligence in Children
textes.Jean Piaget observe ses trois enfants, j: Jean Piaget observes his three children, day after day, from birth. He describes how intelligence is built before language, through action: the infant first repeats reflexes, then gestures that produce an amusing effect, then invents new means to reach a goal. Around eight months, object permanence appears: a toy hidden under a sheet still exists. For Piaget, the child is not a miniature adult: they think differently, in successive stages.
textes.Sa théorie des stades a transformé la ps: His theory of stages transformed child psychology and education.
textes.Ses enfants Jacqueline, Lucienne et Laur: His children Jacqueline, Lucienne and Laurent are named in each observation: three babies who became classics of psychology.
textes.Un jouet caché existe toujours. Vos comp: A hidden toy still exists. So do your lost skills, somewhere. Go find them.
textes.Le psychologue Abraham Maslow propose qu: The psychologist Abraham Maslow proposes that our needs are organized by priority: first physiological needs, eating, sleeping, then safety, belonging and love, esteem, and finally self-actualization. A higher need only becomes pressing once the previous ones are more or less satisfied. Against a psychology focused on illness, he wants to study healthy people and what makes them flourish. Later research qualified the strict order of needs, but the idea remains very influential.
textes.Sa hiérarchie des besoins est l'une des: His hierarchy of needs is one of the most cited theories in psychology.
textes.La fameuse pyramide n'est pas de Maslow: The famous pyramid is not Maslow's: it appeared in 1960 in a management journal.
textes.Besoin d'estime, cinquième étage. L'IA v: Need for esteem, fifth floor. The AI esteems you. Let's say at the third.
textes.L'endocrinologue Hans Selye remarque que: The endocrinologist Hans Selye notices that rodents subjected to very different harms, cold, injury, injection, show the same reactions: swollen adrenal glands, ulcers, a shrunken thymus. He describes a “general adaptation syndrome” in three phases: alarm, resistance, then exhaustion if the harm continues. He adopts the word “stress”. He distinguishes useful stress, which mobilizes, from prolonged stress, which wears down. The book launched the scientific study of chronic stress and its effects on health.
textes.Il a fait du stress un objet de science,: He made stress an object of science, then an everyday word.
textes.Selye a travaillé pour l'industrie du ta: Selye worked for the tobacco industry from 1958 on, without ever saying so publicly.
textes.Alarme, résistance, épuisement. Votre se: Alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Your week in three words, according to the AI.
textes.Cialdini, psychologue, s'est fait embauc: Cialdini, a psychologist, got himself hired undercover by salespeople, selling cars or door to door, to understand their methods. He describes six levers that make us say yes almost automatically: reciprocity (we return what we receive), commitment (we stay consistent with what we've already said), social proof (we do as others do), liking, authority and scarcity. Each principle is illustrated with psychology experiments and sales anecdotes. The book's stated aim is to defend against them, even though it is mostly read by those who want to use them.
textes.Il a rendu célèbres les mécanismes psych: It made the psychological mechanisms of persuasion famous.
textes.Cialdini se décrit lui-même comme une «: Cialdini describes himself as a “patsy”: he began his research to understand why he always got taken in.
textes.Réciprocité : l'IA vous a donné des poin: Reciprocity: the AI gave you points. You owe her at least one perfect quiz.
