textes.Le neurologue Oliver Sacks raconte une v: The neurologist Oliver Sacks tells some twenty cases of patients whose brains were affected. A music teacher no longer recognizes faces or objects, and reaches for his wife's head to put on his hat. A sailor has lost the memory of everything after 1945. Autistic twins play at finding very large prime numbers; Sacks would privately admit to having embellished their case. Sacks describes these patients as people, not cases, and shows what their disorders reveal about how the normal brain works.
textes.Il a fait connaître au grand public la n: It brought neuropsychology to the general public, with humanity.
textes.Le professeur de musique, atteint d'agno: The music teacher, who had visual agnosia, kept all his musical gifts intact.
textes.L'IA reconnaît très bien les visages. Le: The AI recognizes faces very well. Yours, right now, expresses hesitation.
textes.En 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum écrit un prog: In 1966, Joseph Weizenbaum writes a program that imitates a psychotherapist by rephrasing your sentences. His secretary asks him to leave the room so she can talk to the machine alone. Weizenbaum would spend the rest of his life warning against AI.
textes.« Et que ressentez-vous face à cet échec: “And how do you feel about this failure?” A failed recall does not move you back.
textes.Des listes de syllabes absurdes, du genr: Lists of nonsense syllables, such as “DAX” or “BOK” (he left no examples), learned to measure forgetting without the help of meaning.
textes.Des syllabes d'Ebbinghaus. DAX. BOK. J'a: Ebbinghaus syllables. DAX. BOK. I've already forgotten where your pawn was. I'll put it back one square, just in case.
textes.Ebbinghaus apprend lui-même des listes d: Ebbinghaus learns lists of nonsense syllables himself and measures the time saved in relearning them: a large part fades within the first hour.

textes.Le philosophe allemand Theodor Lipps emp: German philosopher Theodor Lipps used the word Einfühlung, "feeling into", in 1903. Psychologist Edward Titchener rendered it in English as empathy in 1909, from the Greek empatheia.
textes.L'expression apparaît peut-être dès 1964: The phrase may first appear in 1964 in Michael Beldoch's work. Peter Salovey and John Mayer defined it in 1990, and journalist Daniel Goleman turned it into a bestseller in 1995. The scientific validity of these measures is still criticised.
textes.Le physiologiste américain Walter Cannon: American physiologist Walter Cannon described this response in 1914 and wrote of "fighting or flight" in 1915. He showed the role of adrenaline, released by the adrenal glands.
textes.En 2007, Matthew Lieberman et son équipe: In 2007, Matthew Lieberman and colleagues showed that naming what you feel lowers amygdala activity. Talk therapies have used it for more than a century.
textes.Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo et Richar: Elaine Hatfield, John Cacioppo and Richard Rapson devoted a book to emotional contagion in 1993. In 2014, a Facebook and Cornell University study that altered users' news feeds without their knowledge drew strong criticism.
textes.Le psychologue James Gross propose en 19: Psychologist James Gross proposed his process model of emotion regulation in 1998. Reappraisal is classed in it among the adaptive strategies.
textes.Dans le modèle de James Gross (1998), la: In James Gross's model (1998), expressive suppression is classed among the maladaptive strategies, unlike reappraisal.
textes.L'équipe de Giacomo Rizzolatti, à Parme,: Giacomo Rizzolatti's team in Parma discovered them in the 1980s-1990s in the macaque's area F5: neurons that fire both when the monkey grasps an object and when it sees someone do it (di Pellegrino et al., 1992). Their role in human empathy remains poorly established.
textes.Dans Über das Gedächtnis (1885), Hermann: In Über das Gedächtnis (1885), Hermann Ebbinghaus used himself as the subject, learning lists of nonsense syllables drawn from 2,300 of them. From this he derived the forgetting curve.
textes.L'article de George Miller paraît en 195: George Miller's paper appeared in 1956 in Psychological Review and is among the most cited in psychology. Nelson Cowan has since proposed a lower limit of about 4 chunks.
textes.C'est Hermann Ebbinghaus qui découvre l': It was Hermann Ebbinghaus who discovered the spacing effect, by studying himself in Über das Gedächtnis (1885).
textes.L'anatomiste Giulio Cesare Aranzi la com: Anatomist Giulio Cesare Aranzi compared it in 1587 to a silkworm, then to a seahorse, which gave it its name. In 1971, John O'Keefe and Jonathan Dostrovsky found "place cells" in it.
textes.Le chirurgien William Scoville l'opère l: Surgeon William Scoville operated on him on 1 September 1953 in Hartford to treat his epilepsy. Scoville and Brenda Milner reported the case in 1957. Henry Molaison could no longer retain anything new, yet he learned mirror drawing without remembering having practised.
Henry Molaison died on 2 December 2008. On 4 December 2009, Jacopo Annese's team cut his brain into 2,401 slices to study it.
textes.En 1974, avec John Palmer, Elizabeth Lof: In 1974, with John Palmer, Elizabeth Loftus showed that a crash video was judged faster depending on the question's verb: 34 mph for "hit", 41 for "smashed". She has testified as an expert in more than 300 court cases.
Cicero tells, in De Oratore (55 BC), how the poet Simonides identified the dead of a collapsed banquet hall by where each had sat. The method is described around 90 BC in the Rhetorica ad Herennium, and memory champions still use it.
textes.En 1924, John Jenkins et Karl Dallenbach: In 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach found that people remember a list better after sleeping than after the same time spent awake.
textes.William James le décrit dès 1890. En 196: William James described it as early as 1890. In 1966, Roger Brown and David McNeill induced it in the laboratory at Harvard. According to Bennett Schwartz (1999), 45 of 51 languages have an idiom for it.
textes.Des études montrent qu'un poisson rouge: Studies show goldfish keep memories for at least three months. In 1994, at the University of Plymouth, goldfish learned to push a lever to get food. The show MythBusters also debunked the legend.
textes.Le terme d'effet de position sérielle vi: The term serial position effect comes from Hermann Ebbinghaus. In 1962, Bennet Murdock plotted its U-shaped curve: the start and end of a list are remembered better than the middle.
textes.Edward Deci et Richard Ryan bâtissent le: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan built their self-determination theory from their mid-1980s book. In 1971, Deci paid $1 per solved puzzle (the Soma puzzle) to measure the urge to keep going without reward.
textes.Edward Deci et Richard Ryan posent ces t: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan set out these three needs, autonomy, competence and relatedness, in their theory from the mid-1980s.
textes.En 1971, Edward Deci montre que des étud: In 1971, Edward Deci showed that students paid to solve puzzles came back to them less of their own accord afterwards than those who received nothing.
textes.Abraham Maslow expose sa hiérarchie des: Abraham Maslow set out his hierarchy of needs in 1943 in Psychological Review. He never drew a pyramid: it is due to consultant Charles McDermid, in the journal Business Horizons.
textes.Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi part de l'observ: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi started from watching painters, so absorbed they forgot hunger and fatigue. He described flow in Beyond Boredom and Anxiety (1975), then in a popular book in 1990.
textes.Edwin Locke lance la théorie de la fixat: Edwin Locke launched goal-setting theory in 1968. With Gary Latham, he summarised it in 1990 and again in 2002, from about 400 studies.
textes.La première expérience a lieu en 1970 à: The first experiment took place in 1970 at Stanford's Bing Nursery School. A 1990 follow-up linked waiting to better SAT scores, but a 2018 replication by Tyler Watts and colleagues found much smaller effects.
textes.Le mot vient du latin procrastinare, de: The word comes from the Latin procrastinare, from cras, "tomorrow". Psychologist Piers Steel defined it in 2007 as voluntarily delaying an intended course of action despite expecting to be worse off.
textes.Bluma Zeigarnik publie en 1927 dans Psyc: Bluma Zeigarnik published in 1927 in Psychologische Forschung, after Kurt Lewin noticed that a waiter remembered orders only until they were paid. A 2025 meta-analysis found no memory advantage for unfinished tasks.
textes.L'idée vient des recherches de Carol Dwe: The idea comes from Carol Dweck's research at Stanford. Large classroom trials have been disappointing: the Education Endowment Foundation's in 2019, then a 2024 study, found no gain.
textes.En 2009, Phillippa Lally suit des volont: In 2009, Phillippa Lally followed volunteers: on average it took them 66 days for an action to become automatic, from 18 to 254 depending on the case. William James already said we are "bundles of habits".
textes.Solomon Asch mène ses expériences en 195: Solomon Asch ran his experiments in 1951 at Swarthmore College. 74% of participants went along with the group's wrong answer at least once; with a single ally in the room, they gave in only 5% of the time.
textes.Stanley Milgram commence en août 1961, t: Stanley Milgram began in August 1961, three months after the trial of Adolf Eichmann opened in Jerusalem: he wanted to understand how ordinary people obey atrocious orders. He published in 1963.
textes.Dans la version de base, 65 % des partic: In the baseline version, 65% of participants went up to 450 volts. Jerry Burger in 2009 found similar rates, halting after the 150-volt switch; Gina Perry, in 2012, reported a troubling mismatch between the published descriptions and what actually happened.
textes.L'idée naît du meurtre de Kitty Genovese: The idea was born from the murder of Kitty Genovese in New York on 13 March 1964, whose story of neighbours who stayed passive was exaggerated: The New York Times itself acknowledged it in 2016. In 2019, Richard Philpot showed from street videos that someone intervened in over 90% of conflicts.
textes.Edward Thorndike nomme l'effet en 1920 :: Edward Thorndike named the effect in 1920: officers rated their soldiers good or bad at everything at once. In 1972, Karen Dion and colleagues showed that people credit attractive faces with more qualities.
textes.Leon Festinger publie sa théorie en 1957: Leon Festinger published his theory in 1957. With James Carlsmith, he showed that students paid $1 to praise a boring task ended up finding it more enjoyable than those paid $20.
textes.En 1966, Jonathan Freedman et Scott Fras: In 1966, Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser asked residents to accept a large sign in their yard: 76% said yes after a small prior request, against 17% without.
textes.En 1971, Dennis Regan montre que des par: In 1971, Dennis Regan showed that participants given a soft drink later bought more raffle tickets. Sociologist Phillip Kunz sent greeting cards to strangers: many sent one back.
textes.En 1975, Stephen Worchel et ses collègue: In 1975, Stephen Worchel and colleagues offered cookies from a jar: those from a jar holding only 2 were rated better than those from a jar holding 10.
textes.Tout part du mémoire de master de James: It all started with James Stoner's master's thesis at MIT in 1961, on the "risky shift" of groups. Serge Moscovici and Marisa Zavalloni generalised the effect in 1969: the group pushes in the direction it already leaned.
textes.William Whyte forge le mot groupthink en: William Whyte coined the word groupthink in 1952 in Fortune magazine. Irving Janis studied it through fiascos such as the Bay of Pigs invasion; the decision to launch the Challenger shuttle is another example often cited.
textes.En août 1971, 24 étudiants jouent gardie: In August 1971, 24 students played guards and prisoners; the experiment, planned for two weeks, was stopped on day 6 after Christina Maslach intervened. In 2018, Thibault Le Texier argued in Histoire d'un mensonge that the guards' behaviour was caused by Zimbardo's instructions.
textes.Le chiffre de 86 milliards vient de Suza: The figure of 86 billion comes from Suzana Herculano-Houzel: in 2005 she developed a method that dissolves the brain into a "soup" of cell nuclei that can be counted.
textes.Le mythe se répand en 1936, dans la préf: The myth spread in 1936, in Lowell Thomas's foreword to Dale Carnegie's book, which attributed the figure to William James. It is wrongly attributed to Einstein. Brain imaging shows that every region is active.
textes.Le 13 septembre 1848, à Cavendish (Vermo: On 13 September 1848, in Cavendish, Vermont, an iron bar 1.1 m long and weighing 6 kg went through the skull of this railroad foreman. According to his doctor John Harlow, he was "no longer Gage". Yet he ended up a stagecoach driver in Chile and died on 21 May 1860.
textes.Paul Broca examine en 1861 le cerveau de: In 1861, Paul Broca examined the brain of Louis Victor Leborgne, nicknamed "Tan", the only word he could say: a lesion of the left frontal lobe. Physician Marc Dax had made a similar observation a generation earlier.
textes.Santiago Ramón y Cajal colore les neuron: Santiago Ramón y Cajal stained neurons with Camillo Golgi's method, though Golgi believed in a continuous network. They shared the Nobel Prize in 1906, and Cajal's drawings are still used in textbooks.
textes.Le mythe vient d'une lecture abusive des: The myth comes from an overstretched reading of Roger Sperry and Michael Gazzaniga's 1960s studies of split-brain patients. In 2013, a University of Utah study found no "dominant side" in individuals.
textes.William James parle de plasticité dès 18: William James spoke of plasticity as early as 1890, and Pole Jerzy Konorski was the first to write "neural plasticity". Paul Bach-y-Rita showed that people can learn to "see" through touch.
textes.Eleanor Maguire a observé chez les chauf: Eleanor Maguire observed changes in the hippocampus of London taxi drivers, the region for memory of places.
textes.Seiji Ogawa découvre le signal BOLD en 1: Seiji Ogawa discovered the BOLD signal in 1990 at Bell Labs. The idea is old: Angelo Mosso already weighed blood flow to the brain, and Charles Roy and Charles Sherrington linked activity and blood flow in 1890. In 2009, a dead salmon "responded" in a badly analysed scan.
textes.Le neurochirurgien Wilder Penfield opère: Neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield operated on awake patients under local anaesthesia, a technique learned in Germany in 1928. By stimulating their cortex, he mapped the body's "little man", the homunculus. He founded the Montreal Neurological Institute in 1934.
textes.Cervelet veut dire « petit cerveau ». Ga: Cerebellum means "little brain". Galen already described it; Luigi Rolando in 1809, then Pierre Flourens showed its role in movement. It holds more neurons than all the rest of the brain.
textes.Chez Binet, à Paris, Jean Piaget corrige: At Binet's in Paris, Jean Piaget marked intelligence tests and became interested in children's mistakes. He then closely observed his own three children, and founded the International Centre for Genetic Epistemology in Geneva in 1955.
textes.Jean Piaget tire ses quatre stades en bo: Jean Piaget drew his four stages largely from observing his own three children.
textes.Piaget décrit « l'erreur A-non-B » : le: Piaget described the "A-not-B error": the baby looks for the toy where it found it before, not where it saw it hidden. In 1991, Renée Baillargeon and Julie DeVos showed that a baby of three and a half months is already surprised when a hidden object vanishes.
textes.En 1985, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie: In 1985, Simon Baron-Cohen, Alan Leslie and Uta Frith ran the test: 85% of non-autistic children passed (23 of 27), against 20% of autistic children (4 of 20).
textes.Lev Vygotski introduit cette notion dans: Lev Vygotsky introduced this idea in the last three years of his life, before his death in 1934. The word "scaffolding", often linked to it, came later from Jerome Bruner, David Wood and Gail Ross.
textes.Harry Harlow présente ses résultats en 1: Harry Harlow presented his results in 1958 in "The Nature of Love": baby monkeys preferred the cloth mother to the wire mother that gave milk. These experiments are now considered unethical.
textes.Le psychiatre John Bowlby pose la théori: Psychiatrist John Bowlby set out the theory, and Mary Ainsworth devised the "Strange Situation" in the 1970s, observing a baby's reaction when its mother leaves and comes back.
textes.Selon Piaget, la conservation s'acquiert: According to Piaget, conservation is acquired around age 7. But when a "naughty teddy" messes up the row, in James McGarrigle and Margaret Donaldson's experiment, younger children succeed far more often.
textes.Janet Werker et Richard Tees le montrent: Janet Werker and Richard Tees showed it: at 6-8 months, babies tell apart the sounds of a foreign language better than at 8-10 months, when their ear has already tuned to the language they hear.
textes.En 1993, Frances Rauscher fait écouter M: In 1993, Frances Rauscher played Mozart to 36 students (not babies): a slight gain on a spatial task, lasting about fifteen minutes. Georgia governor Zell Miller nonetheless proposed in 1998 to give every newborn a classical music CD. Meta-analyses by Chabris (1999) and Pietschnig (2010) found no notable effect.
textes.Eleanor Gibson et Richard Walk testent 3: Eleanor Gibson and Richard Walk tested 36 babies aged 6 to 14 months; 27 of them crawled to their mother on the shallow side. More recent work indicates that this caution is not innate: it comes with experience.
textes.Francis Galton propose dès 1884 de cherc: Francis Galton proposed as early as 1884 looking for traits in the words of the language. In 1936, Gordon Allport and Henry Odbert listed 4,504 adjectives. Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal found five factors in 1961, and Lewis Goldberg named them the "Big Five" in 1981.
textes.Katharine Briggs et sa fille Isabel Myer: Katharine Briggs and her daughter Isabel Myers, with no training in psychology, drew on Jung (1921) and began during the Second World War; the manual came out in 1962. Between 39 and 76% of people get a different type when retaking it five weeks later.
textes.Le névrosisme fait partie des cinq facte: Neuroticism is one of the five factors found by Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal in 1961, which Lewis Goldberg named the "Big Five" in 1981.
textes.Pour Hans Eysenck, l'introverti a un cer: For Hans Eysenck, the introvert has an already highly aroused brain and seeks less stimulation. In 2012, Susan Cain's book Quiet popularised the defence of introverts.
textes.Carl Jung les introduit dans Psychologis: Carl Jung introduced them in Psychologische Typen in 1921, translated into English in 1923.
textes.Delroy Paulhus et Kevin Williams nomment: Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams named the dark triad in 2002. Machiavellianism was already measured with Richard Christie and Florence Geis's MACH-IV scale (1970). Sadism is sometimes added: the "dark tetrad".
textes.La théorie des quatre humeurs vient d'Hi: The theory of the four humours comes from Hippocrates; Galen drew from it the four temperaments: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric and melancholic. Kant still used them in 1798.
textes.Franz Joseph Gall lance sa « cranioscopi: Franz Joseph Gall launched his "cranioscopy" around 1796; his collaborator Johann Spurzheim popularised the word "phrenology". Pierre Flourens's experiments helped discredit it by the 1840s.
textes.À partir de 1979, Thomas Bouchard étudie: From 1979, Thomas Bouchard studied identical twins raised apart in Minneapolis: they are about 50% alike in personality.
textes.Lee Ross nomme cette erreur en 1977, d'a: Lee Ross named this error in 1977, based on Edward Jones and Victor Harris's experiment (1967): even knowing a writer had been assigned to argue for Fidel Castro, readers credited the writer with that opinion.
textes.Le modèle des Big Five vient de Tupes et: The Big Five model comes from Tupes and Christal (1961) and Goldberg (1981); of the five traits, conscientiousness best predicts exam success.
textes.En 1936, Hans Selye publie « A Syndrome: In 1936, Hans Selye published "A Syndrome Produced by Diverse Nocuous Agents": he observed that rats exposed to cold, drugs or injury all reacted the same way, in three phases. He later distinguished good stress (eustress) from bad (distress).
textes.Robert Yerkes et John Dodson publient en: Robert Yerkes and John Dodson published in 1908 in the Journal of Comparative Neurology and Psychology, from experiments on dancing mice. The paper was cited only ten times in fifty years before becoming famous.
textes.L'étude commence en 1938 à la faculté de: The study began in 1938 at Harvard Medical School, funded by William Thomas Grant, with 268 students. George Vaillant directed it for more than thirty years; Robert Waldinger took over. One of its conclusions: success depends on warmth of relationships, not on intelligence.
textes.Philip Brickman et Donald Campbell parle: Philip Brickman and Donald Campbell spoke of the "hedonic treadmill" in 1971. In 1978, Brickman, Dan Coates and Ronnie Janoff-Bulman compared 22 lottery winners and 29 paraplegics: the winners were no happier than before, and the paraplegics expected to get back to their level within a couple of years.
textes.Martin Seligman en fait le thème de sa p: Martin Seligman made it the theme of his term as president of the American Psychological Association in 1998, feeling the field focused too much on illness. The phrase dates back at least to 1954, the title of a chapter by Maslow.
textes.En 1967, à l'université de Pennsylvanie,: In 1967, at the University of Pennsylvania, dogs that had no way to stop shocks later lay down in a box they could have escaped with one jump. In 2016, Steven Maier and Seligman turned the theory around: by default the brain assumes it has no control, and it is control that is learned.
textes.Le record est détenu par Randy Gardner,: The record belongs to Randy Gardner, who stayed awake 264 hours, 11 days, without stimulants. The US National Sleep Foundation recommends that adults aim for 7 hours a night.
textes.Jon Kabat-Zinn crée son programme de réd: Jon Kabat-Zinn created his stress reduction programme in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. It lasts eight weeks; its roots are in Zen Buddhism, but the programme is secular.
textes.Le psychologue Herbert Freudenberger s'o: Psychologist Herbert Freudenberger observed himself and his fellow volunteers at a free clinic for drug addicts, in "Staff Burn-Out" in 1974. Christina Maslach published her inventory in 1981, and the WHO recognised it in 2019 as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition.
textes.En 1986, James Pennebaker et Sandra Beal: In 1986, James Pennebaker and Sandra Beall had students write 15 minutes a day, 4 days in a row, about their deepest thoughts on a trauma. Over the following months, they visited the doctor significantly less than those who wrote about neutral topics.
textes.{comp}. Ebbinghaus apprenait des syllabe: {comp}. Ebbinghaus learned syllables with no meaning at all. I give you some. Make the most of it.
textes.Psychologie. William James disait que no: Psychology. William James said we are sad because we cry. Don't cry too soon: {comp}.
textes.Pavlov sonnait, les chiens salivaient. J: Pavlov rang, the dogs salivated. I launch {comp}, you tap the screen.
textes.Juste. Votre hippocampe travaille. Henry: Right. Your hippocampus is working. Henry Molaison would have envied yours.
textes.Bonne réponse. Piaget vous aurait noté d: Correct. Piaget would have noted you in his notebook, between two of his children.
textes.Correct. Milgram aurait voulu savoir qui: Correct. Milgram would have wanted to know who ordered you to succeed. Me.
textes.Bien vu. Je ressens quelque chose. Proba: Well spotted. I feel something. Probably a bug.
textes.Raté. Phineas Gage s'est remis d'une bar: Missed. Phineas Gage recovered from an iron bar through his skull. You'll recover from this.
textes.Faux. Gall lisait le caractère dans les: Wrong. Gall read character in the bumps of the skull. I read the error in your answer. It's more reliable.
textes.Erreur. La courbe de l'oubli d'Ebbinghau: Error. Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve was lying in wait. It got you.
textes.Je compatis. C'est faux, mais l'intentio: I sympathize. It's wrong, but the intention is there.
textes.Avec son mari Kenneth, elle présente à d: With her husband Kenneth, she shows Black children two identical dolls, one white, one Black, and asks them which one is nice, which one is pretty. Most choose the white one. This work was cited in 1954 by the Supreme Court in the ruling that ended school segregation.
textes.Pour lui, nous ne pleurons pas parce que: For him, we don't cry because we are sad: we are sad because we cry. The body reacts first, the emotion follows. At Harvard he taught the first course in experimental psychology in the United States, and noted that the first lecture on psychology he ever heard was his own.
textes.Seul cobaye de ses propres expériences,: The only guinea pig of his own experiments, he learns thousands of nonsense syllables (textbooks cite DAX or BOK), to the beat of a metronome, and measures how fast he forgets them. This is the forgetting curve, published in 1885. This game applies it to your recalls.
textes.Il reçoit le Nobel en 1904 pour ses trav: He received the Nobel in 1904 for his work on digestion, not for the conditioned reflex. His laboratory ran like a factory, with dozens of assistants and dogs. To announce food, he mostly used a metronome, a buzzer or a whistle, far more often than a bell.
textes.En 1961, il fait croire à des volontaire: In 1961, he leads volunteers to believe they are sending electric shocks to a “learner” who makes mistakes. On the calm orders of a man in a gray lab coat, twenty-six out of forty go up to 450 volts. The shocks were fake. The volunteers' distress was very real.
textes.Avec une coloration à l'argent inventée: Using a silver stain invented by his rival Golgi, he shows that the brain is made of separate cells, neurons, and draws thousands of them. They share the 1906 Nobel and contradict each other in their speeches. As a child, he had built a cannon and demolished a neighbor's gate.
textes.Médecin des gladiateurs de Pergame, puis: Physician to the gladiators of Pergamon, then to Emperor Marcus Aurelius, he derives four temperaments from Hippocrates' four humors: sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric, melancholic. The theory is wrong, the words stayed. He dissected monkeys for lack of human bodies, and his errors stood until Vesalius.
textes.Jeune chercheur à Montréal, maladroit, i: A clumsy young researcher in Montreal, he injects all sorts of extracts into struggling rodents, and always gets the same lesions, whatever the extract. From this he derives the concept of “stress”. He later took money from the tobacco industry, delighted that people talked about stress rather than cigarettes.
Master the first diamond of Empathy.
textes.Le cœur a ses raisons, que la raison ne: The heart has its reasons, which reason knows nothing of.
textes.Maîtriser l'influence sociale. Vous saur: Master social influence. At least you'll know why nobody moved.
textes.Le meurtre de Kitty Genovese (1964) a la: The murder of Kitty Genovese (1964) launched the study of the bystander effect, with “38 witnesses who did nothing”. The figure was greatly exaggerated: few neighbors understood what was happening, and some called the police. The New York Times acknowledged it in 2016.
textes.Maîtriser 7 compétences. L'arbre de la P: Master 7 skills. The Psychology tree opens.
textes.L'art d'être sage est l'art de savoir ce: The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
textes.Maîtriser les émotions. Sourire de force: Master emotions. Forcing a smile doesn't make things funnier. The AI does.
textes.En 1988, une étude célèbre fait tenir un: In 1988, a famous study had people hold a pen between their teeth (which forces a smile) or between their lips: cartoons seemed funnier to the involuntary smilers. In 2016, seventeen laboratories carefully redid the experiment. No effect.
textes.Maîtriser la mémoire. Vous retiendrez ce: Master memory. You'll remember this one; he couldn't.
textes.En 1953, on retire à Henry Molaison une: In 1953, part of both of Henry Molaison's hippocampi is removed to treat his epilepsy. He can no longer form new memories. Yet he learns to draw in a mirror, better and better, without ever remembering having done it. So there are several kinds of memory.
textes.Maîtriser la motivation. Vous avez atten: Master motivation. You waited for this achievement without eating it. Well done.
textes.Dans les années 1970, des enfants qui ré: In the 1970s, children who resisted one marshmallow to get two seemed to do better later on. In 2018, a replication with over 900 children found a much weaker effect, largely explained by family background.
textes.Maîtriser le cerveau. Le cerveau répare: Master the brain. The brain repairs more than people say.
textes.En 1848, une barre de fer traverse le cr: In 1848, an iron bar goes through the skull of Phineas Gage, a railroad foreman. The story goes that he stayed brutish and unstable until his death. In fact, he later drove stagecoaches in Chile for years, a job that demands patience and organization.
Master child development. Your parents observed you too. Less scientifically.
textes.Jean Piaget a bâti une bonne partie de s: Jean Piaget built a good part of his theory by observing his three children, Jacqueline, Lucienne and Laurent, from the cradle to school: he notes their gestures, hides objects from them under a cushion, and watches whether they look for them.
textes.Maîtriser la personnalité. Vous n'êtes p: Master personality. You are not a type. You are a distribution.
textes.Le test MBTI, qui range chacun dans l'un: The MBTI test, which sorts everyone into one of sixteen types, was designed by Katharine Briggs and her daughter Isabel Myers, with no training in psychology, based on Jung. Retaken five weeks later, it changes the type of 39 to 76% of people. Psychologists prefer the Big Five traits.
textes.Maîtriser le bien-être et le stress. L'h: Master well-being and stress. The habit of playing here, you have picked up.
textes.Il faudrait 21 jours pour prendre une ha: It supposedly takes 21 days to form a habit. The figure comes from a cosmetic surgeon, Maxwell Maltz, who noted in 1960 that his patients got used to their new face in about three weeks. Measured in 2010: from 18 to 254 days, 66 on average.
textes.Réussir trois quiz d'Empathie sans faute: Pass three Empathy quizzes without a mistake. The AI expected the worst. You disappointed her.
textes.En 1968, Rosenthal et Jacobson annoncent: In 1968, Rosenthal and Jacobson announce that pupils randomly labeled “promising” progress more, because their teachers believe in them. The effect exists, but reanalyses show it is much weaker than promised, and mostly in the youngest children.
The next enemy on your path leaves. Even the one blocking you.
textes.Je le chasse. Pas pour vous : il encombr: I'm chasing it off. Not for you: it was cluttering my road.
textes.Les rois de France vendaient des lettres: The kings of France sold lettres de cachet. I sell letters of dismissal. The enemy is gone.
textes.Un ennemi de plus devant ton pion. Plus: One more enemy in front of your pawn. More duels, more loot.
textes.Vous payez pour qu'on vous barre la rout: You pay to have your path blocked? I love customers like you.
textes.Un ennemi de plus, livré devant votre pi: One more enemy, delivered in front of your pawn. Win the duel: the loot is better.
textes.Il vend des raisonnements au poids. Plus: He sells arguments by the pound. The more false they are, the more expensive. Protagoras boasted he could make the weaker argument win; Aristophanes mocks it in The Clouds, and Xenophon accuses the sophists of hunting rich young men.
textes.Je vais te prouver que tu as perdu avant: I'll prove you've lost before we even start. The proof: you're listening to me.
textes.Bon. Disons que c'était un exercice de s: Fine. Let's call that a stylistic exercise.
textes.Tu vois ? Tout se démontre. Surtout le f: See? Everything can be proven. Especially what's false.
textes.Une caricature. Les vrais sophistes étai: A caricature. The real sophists were paid teachers of eloquence in 5th-century BC Greece, like Protagoras or Gorgias. Plato portrayed them as word merchants. The AI kept the merchant.
textes.Un argument se juge sur sa structure, pa: An argument is judged by its structure, not by the self-assurance of whoever defends it.
textes.Il n'a jamais vu la courbure de la Terre: He has never seen the curvature of the Earth. He has never looked either. Eratosthenes measured it around 240 BC with a stick and two shadows.
textes.Avance si tu l'oses. Au bout du plateau,: Go ahead if you dare. At the end of the board, you fall into the void.

textes.Les saisons viennent de l'inclinaison de: The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the Northern Hemisphere's winter.

textes.L'oiseau naturalisé est toujours exposé: The stuffed bird is still on display at the University of Rostock.

textes.James Clerk Maxwell réunit électricité e: James Clerk Maxwell united electricity and magnetism in a few equations and showed that electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light: light is one of them. Heinrich Hertz would produce these waves twenty years later, paving the way for radio. In 1861, Maxwell also had the first color photograph projected, of a tartan ribbon.
textes.Maxwell a unifié la lumière, l'électrici: Maxwell unified light, electricity and magnetism. The AI unifies your mistakes in a single report.

textes.En série, une seule boucle : une lampe g: In series, a single loop: one burnt-out bulb turns everything off.
textes.En dérivation, chaque branche a sa boucl: In parallel, each branch has its own loop: the bulbs are independent, as in a house.
textes.Les métaux conduisent grâce à leurs élec: Metals conduct thanks to their free electrons; plastic and glass insulate.

textes.Un courant crée un champ magnétique (Ørs: A current creates a magnetic field (Ørsted, 1820): that's the principle of the electromagnet.
textes.Un champ magnétique qui varie crée un co: A changing magnetic field creates a current (induction, Faraday 1831): that's the generator.
textes.Un moteur électrique transforme l'énergi: An electric motor turns electrical energy into motion; a generator does the reverse.
textes.Le pôle nord d'une boussole pointe vers: A compass's north pole points toward the geographic North Pole, which is a magnetic south pole.
textes.Casser un aimant en deux ne sépare pas l: Breaking a magnet in two doesn't separate the poles: you get two complete magnets.

textes.Radio, micro-ondes, infrarouge, visible,: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma: the same wave at different frequencies.
textes.Toutes se propagent à la vitesse de la l: They all travel at the speed of light in a vacuum (Maxwell, 1865).
textes.Plus la fréquence est élevée, plus chaqu: The higher the frequency, the more energy each photon carries: only part of the UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionizing.
textes.Le micro-ondes chauffe surtout l'eau des: A microwave oven mainly heats the water in food by shaking its molecules.
textes.Les ondes radio et Wi-Fi ne sont pas ion: Radio waves and Wi-Fi are not ionizing: they don't have enough energy to break DNA.

textes.Éolien et solaire sont intermittents : i: Wind and solar are intermittent: you need storage or backup.

textes.Une centrale nucléaire ne rejette pas de: A nuclear plant doesn't emit smoke: the white plumes are water vapor.

textes.Le binaire n'utilise que 0 et 1 : 1011 e: Binary uses only 0 and 1: 1011 in binary equals 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.
textes.Portes logiques ET, OU, NON : construite: AND, OR, NOT logic gates: built from transistors, they do all the computing.
textes.Loi de Moore : le nombre de transistors: Moore's law: the number of transistors per chip doubled roughly every two years for decades.
textes.Un kilooctet vaut 1 000 octets selon le: A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes in SI terms; 1,024 bytes is called a kibibyte.
textes.Tables des portes ET et OU: Truth tables of the AND and OR gates
textes.Même signe : répulsion ; signes opposés: Same sign: repulsion; opposite signs: attraction. Rubbing moves electrons, creating nothing. The word "charge": Franklin.
textes.Les Grecs avaient remarqué que l'ambre f: The Greeks had noticed that rubbed amber attracts twigs. In 1600, in De Magnete, the English physician William Gilbert drew from the Greek elektron, amber, a Latin word for bodies that attract: that is where our "electricity" comes from. In the 18th century Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of charge positive and negative, and coined the word "charge".
textes.Les charges de même signe se repoussent,: Charges of the same sign repel, opposite charges attract. Rubbing creates nothing: electrons change place. A balloon rubbed on hair takes electrons from it, becomes negative and attracts it. Franklin's choice was arbitrary, and he fixed the conventional direction of current before electrons were discovered: in a wire they actually go the other way.
textes.Boucle fermée obligatoire. Série : tout: A closed loop is required. Series: everything goes out together. Parallel: each branch is independent, like at home.
textes.En série, une seule boucle : retirer une: In series, a single loop: remove one lamp and all the others go out, like old fairy lights. In parallel, each lamp has its own loop: they are independent. That is how a house's sockets are wired. If the current finds an almost resistance-free path, that is a short circuit: the current runs away and heats the wires, hence fuses and circuit breakers that cut off before a fire.
Galvani (1780s): the frogs. Volta (1800): the battery, copper, zinc and salt water. The volt is named after him.
textes.Dans les années 1780, à Bologne, Luigi G: In the 1780s in Bologna, Luigi Galvani saw frogs' legs twitch when touched with two different metals. He took it for an electricity specific to living beings. Alessandro Volta disagreed: for him the electricity came from the contact between the two metals, and the frog was only a detector.
textes.Pour le prouver, Volta empile des disque: To prove it, Volta stacked discs of copper and zinc separated by cardboard soaked in salt water. Connect top and bottom with a wire: a continuous current flows. He described this first true battery in a letter to the Royal Society in London on 20 March 1800. It was later understood that the salt water takes part in the reactions, which Volta overlooked. The volt is named after him.
textes.U = R × I (Ohm, 1827). 9 V sur 3 Ω = 3 A: U = R × I (Ohm, 1827). 9 V across 3 Ω = 3 A. Current is not used up, energy is.
textes.La tension U, en volts, pousse le couran: Voltage U, in volts, pushes the current. Resistance R, in ohms, slows it down. Current I, in amperes, is the resulting flow. Georg Ohm related them in 1827 in Die galvanische Kette: U = R × I. With a 9 V battery on a 3 Ω resistor, I = U ÷ R = 9 V ÷ 3 Ω = 3 A. His work was at first received with little enthusiasm; yet the unit of resistance bears his name.
textes.L'image de l'eau aide : la tension est l: The water picture helps: voltage is the pressure, current the flow, resistance the narrowness of the pipe. A long thin wire resists more than a short thick one. And current does not get used up going through a lamp: the same current comes out, it is energy that is given up. Current is measured with an ammeter connected in series, voltage with a voltmeter connected across the terminals.
textes.Série : R = R₁ + R₂. Dérivation : 1/R =: Series: R = R₁ + R₂. Parallel: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ (two 100 Ω = 50 Ω). Kirchhoff's laws, 1845.
textes.En série, le courant traverse les résist: In series, the current goes through the resistors one after the other: they add up, R = R₁ + R₂. The current is the same everywhere, the voltage is shared. In parallel, the current has several paths: 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂. For two 100 Ω resistors: 1/R = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so R = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 Ω. Two paths let twice as much current through.
textes.Ces règles se déduisent de la loi d'Ohm: These rules follow from Ohm's law and the two laws Gustav Kirchhoff published in 1845, while still a student. Junction rule: all the current arriving at a junction leaves it again, nothing is lost. Loop rule: around a loop, the voltages balance out. With these two laws you can work out any circuit, however complicated.
textes.C'est le courant qui tue: It is the current that kills
textes.Le danger, c'est le courant à travers le: The danger is current through the body: 30 mA for the RCD. One wire, no current: the bird survives.
textes.Ce qui blesse, c'est le courant qui trav: What harms is the current passing through the body, more than voltage alone. A few tens of milliamperes are enough to cause serious heart trouble. That is why homes have a 30 mA residual-current device: it compares the current going out and the current coming back, and cuts off within a fraction of a second if some escapes, for example through someone.
textes.Un oiseau posé sur un seul câble haute t: A bird sitting on a single high-voltage line is safe: both its feet are at the same potential, no current passes through it. The danger would come from touching two lines at once, or a line and the pylon. In France the household supply is 230 V AC, 50 Hz; North America uses about 120 V at 60 Hz.
textes.P = U × I : 230 V × 10 A = 2 300 W. Watt: P = U × I: 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. Watt = joule per second.
textes.Le watt et le joule ne mesurent pas la m: The watt and the joule do not measure the same thing. The joule is an energy, the watt a power, that is, energy per second: 1 W = 1 J/s. A 5 W bulb spends 5 joules every second. An LED gives as much light as an incandescent bulb using about 5 to 8 times less, because the old one turned most of the electricity into heat.
textes.E = P × t : 2 kW pendant 3 h = 6 kWh. 1: E = P × t: 2 kW for 3 h = 6 kWh. 1 kWh = 3.6 million joules. Standby costs through its duration.
textes.Sur une facture, on paie une énergie, en: On a bill you pay for energy, in kilowatt-hours: power multiplied by time, E = P × t. A 2,000 W heater, that is 2 kW, on for 3 hours uses E = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kWh. A 5 W bulb on for 1,000 hours: E = 5 W × 1,000 h = 5,000 Wh = 5 kWh. One kilowatt-hour is 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3,600,000 joules.
textes.Le piège : un appareil en veille consomm: The trap: an appliance on standby uses little per hour, often a few watts, but 24 hours a day. A few watts all year round end up weighing more than a powerful appliance used for a few minutes. To know what costs money, always multiply the power by the time in use.
textes.P = R × I² (Joule, 1841). Haute tension: P = R × I² (Joule, 1841). High voltage = low current = losses divided by the square.
textes.En 1841, James Prescott Joule mesure la: In 1841 James Prescott Joule measured the heat given off by a wire carrying a current: it is proportional to the resistance and to the square of the current. Combining P = U × I with Ohm's law U = R × I gives P = R × I². That is Joule heating: the toaster, the kettle, the heater and the fuse that melts all use it.
textes.Ce carré explique le transport à très ha: That square explains transmission at very high voltage. For the same power P = U × I, raising the voltage lowers the current. Yet losses in the cables equal R × I²: dividing the current by 10 divides the losses by 10 × 10 = 100. That is why lines leave power stations at hundreds of thousands of volts.
textes.Un courant crée un champ magnétique (Ørs: A current creates a magnetic field (Ørsted, 1820). Electromagnet: Sturgeon, 1824. Motor: electricity → motion.
textes.En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820 Hans Christian Ørsted noticed that a wire carrying a current deflects the needle of a nearby compass. Tradition says it happened during a lecture. It is the proof that electricity and magnetism are linked: a current creates a magnetic field around it. André-Marie Ampère worked out the laws within a few weeks; the unit of current bears his name.
textes.Enroulez le fil autour d'un noyau de fer: Wind the wire around an iron core and the field concentrates: that is the electromagnet, invented by William Sturgeon in 1824. Unlike a magnet, it can be switched on and off: scrapyard cranes, doorbells, loudspeakers. In an electric motor, these forces turn a shaft: electrical energy becomes motion.
textes.Un champ qui varie crée un courant (Fara: A changing field creates a current (Faraday, 1831). Alternator = magnet turning past coils.
textes.En 1831, Michael Faraday fait l'inverse: In 1831 Michael Faraday did the reverse: he moved a magnet near a coil of wire, and a current appeared in it. Not when the magnet is still, only when the field changes. That is electromagnetic induction. Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice who became Humphry Davy's assistant, used little beyond the simplest algebra: he thought in lines of force, an image that would guide Maxwell.
textes.Presque toute notre électricité vient de: Almost all our electricity comes from this. In an alternator, a magnet turns past coils: coal, gas, nuclear, dam or wind turbine only serve to turn it. The motor does the reverse, and some electric cars do both, recovering energy when braking. The induction hob too: its changing field creates currents in the bottom of the pan, which heats by Joule heating.
Earth's field = liquid iron in the core. The Arctic holds a magnetic south pole. Auroras = solar particles guided to the poles.
textes.Ce champ nous protège. Il dévie la plupa: This field protects us. It deflects most of the charged particles coming from the Sun. Near the poles some get in and excite the oxygen and nitrogen of the upper atmosphere, which give off green, red or violet light: those are the polar auroras.
textes.Maxwell (1865) : la lumière est une onde: Maxwell (1865): light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz (1886): radio waves exist. Marconi (1901): the Atlantic.
textes.En 1865, James Clerk Maxwell met en équa: In 1865 James Clerk Maxwell put electricity and magnetism into equations. His equations predict waves travelling at a speed he calculates: that of light. He concluded that light is itself an electromagnetic wave. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which in turn creates an electric field: the wave sustains itself, even in a vacuum.
textes.Restait à le prouver. À partir de 1886,: It still had to be proved. From 1886 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves in his laboratory. Asked about their applications, he is said to have answered: "Nothing, I guess." Fifteen years later, in 1901, Guglielmo Marconi sent an "S" in Morse across the Atlantic, from Cornwall to Newfoundland.
textes.Même onde, fréquences différentes. c = λ: Same wave, different frequencies. c = λ × f: Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz = 12.5 cm. Ionising: part of UV, X, gamma.
textes.Plus la fréquence est haute, plus chaque: The higher the frequency, the more energy each grain of light, each photon, carries. Only part of the ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays have enough to tear off electrons and damage DNA: they are ionising radiation, hence sunburn. Radio waves and Wi-Fi do not have enough: they can heat, not break DNA.
textes.Röntgen (1895) : rayons X, premier Nobel: Röntgen (1895): X-rays, first Nobel Prize in Physics (1901). Spencer (1945): the microwave, born of a melted chocolate bar.
textes.En 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen découvre des ra: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen discovered unknown rays, which he called X, able to pass through flesh and reveal bones. In 1901 he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, and refused to patent his discovery. About six weeks after the discovery he was already X-raying his wife's hand.
textes.Le radar, développé intensément pendant: Radar, developed intensively during the Second World War, sends out waves and listens for their echo. In 1945 at Raytheon, engineer Percy Spencer was working near a radar magnetron when a chocolate bar melted in his pocket: from this came the microwave oven, which agitates the water molecules in food.
textes.ENIAC : plus de 17 000 tubes. Diode = se: ENIAC: more than 17,000 tubes. Diode = one way. Capacitor = store of charges released at once.
textes.Les premiers ordinateurs calculaient ave: The first computers calculated with vacuum tubes, glass bulbs that let a current of electrons through or block it. ENIAC, completed in 1945 in the United States, had more than 17,000 of them. They got hot, used a lot of power and burned out regularly: finding the dead tube was part of the job.
textes.Tout l'enjeu de l'électronique est là :: That is what electronics is all about: controlling one current with another. The diode, the simplest component, lets current through in one direction only; it is used to turn alternating current into direct current. The capacitor stores charges and releases them in one go, as in a camera flash.
textes.Un interrupteur sans pièce mobile: A switch with no moving parts
textes.Transistor : Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobe: Transistor: Bell, 1947, germanium, Nobel 1956. A small signal controls a large current.
textes.En décembre 1947, aux laboratoires Bell,: In December 1947, at Bell Labs, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain got the first transistor working, a small germanium device; William Shockley, their boss, soon designed a more practical version. The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics. Bardeen received a second in 1972, for superconductivity.
textes.Le transistor est fait d'un semi-conduct: The transistor is made of a semiconductor: a material that conducts less well than a metal, but whose conduction can be controlled. A small current or voltage on one terminal controls a large current between the other two. It serves as an amplifier in a radio, and as an ultra-fast switch in a computer. Silicon replaced germanium, hence Silicon Valley.
textes.Circuit intégré : Kilby 1958 (germanium): Integrated circuit: Kilby 1958 (germanium), Noyce 1959 (silicon). Moore's law: doubling every two years.
textes.Le 12 septembre 1958, chez Texas Instrum: On 12 September 1958 at Texas Instruments, Jack Kilby demonstrated the first integrated circuit: several components on a single piece of germanium. About six months later Robert Noyce, at Fairchild, made a silicon version, much easier to manufacture. Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000; Noyce, who died in 1990, could no longer share it.
textes.En 1965, Gordon Moore remarque que le no: In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of transistors per chip was doubling at a steady rate: every year, then, in 1975, he revised it to every two years. This "Moore's law" held for decades. A large 2023 processor has from a few tens to more than a hundred billion transistors. LEDs are diodes too: the blue LED, which made white light possible, won the 2014 Nobel Prize.
textes.Thermique = eau chauffée, vapeur, turbin: Thermal = heated water, steam, turbine, alternator. Plumes = water vapour. Solar: Becquerel, 1839.
textes.Une centrale thermique, au charbon, au g: A thermal power station, coal, gas or nuclear, always does the same thing: heat water. The steam turns a turbine, the turbine drives an alternator, and Faraday's induction does the rest. In a nuclear plant the heat comes from the fission of uranium nuclei. The big white plumes from the cooling towers are not smoke but water vapour.
textes.Les éoliennes et les barrages font tourn: Wind turbines and dams turn the alternator directly, without steam. The solar panel has nothing that turns: it converts light into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839, at 19. In 2023, according to RTE, nuclear power produced about 65 % of France's electricity.
textes.Edison : continu. Westinghouse et Tesla: Edison: direct current. Westinghouse and Tesla: alternating current. AC won thanks to the transformer.
textes.À la fin du XIXe siècle, Thomas Edison d: At the end of the 19th century Thomas Edison championed direct current; George Westinghouse, who licensed Nikola Tesla's motor patents, championed alternating current. Edison's 110 V DC did not reach beyond about a mile: a small power station was needed for each neighbourhood. In 1882 his lighting company set up in New York on that model.
textes.L'alternatif gagne grâce au transformate: Alternating current won thanks to the transformer, which only works with a varying current, since it relies on induction. It lets you raise the voltage to transmit far with few losses, then lower it again at the user's end. In France the current changes direction a hundred times a second: 50 Hz. The 1892 merger that created General Electric ended the battle.
textes.Production = consommation à chaque insta: Production = consumption at every moment, otherwise the frequency drifts. Storage: pumped storage, batteries (Nobel 2019).
textes.Le réseau a une contrainte que peu de ge: The grid has a constraint few people know: at every moment, production must equal consumption. If more is consumed than produced, the frequency drops below 50 Hz; too large a gap, and outages are triggered to protect the grid. On a winter evening, when everyone gets home and cooks, you need sources that start fast.
textes.Le vent et le soleil ne se commandent pa: Wind and sun cannot be ordered: you have to store or supplement. Pumped-storage stations pump water up into a lake when electricity is plentiful and run it through turbines when it is short. Lithium-ion batteries play the same role on a smaller scale; they earned Goodenough, Whittingham and Yoshino the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
textes.1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 (Leibniz, 1705). 8 bits = 256 values. A transistor: on or off.
textes.En binaire, on n'a que deux chiffres, 0: In binary there are only two digits, 0 and 1, and each place is worth double the one before: 1, 2, 4, 8… So 1011 = 1 × 8 + 0 × 4 + 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 11. Leibniz set out this arithmetic in a memoir published in 1705. With 3 bits you can code 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 values; with an 8-bit byte, 2⁸ = 256.
textes.Pourquoi deux chiffres ? Parce qu'un tra: Why two digits? Because a transistor is very good at two things: letting through or blocking. Text, images, sounds: everything is coded in 0s and 1s. A detail about units: under the International System, a kilobyte is 1,000 bytes; 1,024 bytes is called a kibibyte.
textes.Boole : la logique devient algèbre. Shan: Boole: logic becomes algebra. Shannon (1937): circuits compute it. AND, OR, NOT are enough for everything.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, George Boole fait de la: In the 19th century George Boole turned logic into algebra: true and false become 1 and 0, and "and", "or", "not" become operations. In 1937, aged 21, Claude Shannon showed in his master's thesis at MIT, published in 1938, that relay circuits can carry out all of this algebra. It has been called possibly the most important master's thesis of the century.
textes.La porte ET donne 1 seulement si ses deu: The AND gate gives 1 only if both its inputs are 1; the OR gate gives 1 if at least one is 1; the NOT gate inverts. Built from a few transistors, these gates are assembled into adders, memories, then processors. A computer is, at bottom, just a huge assembly of these three decisions.
textes.Des plans de Babbage au bug de 1947: From Babbage's plans to the 1947 bug
textes.Babbage : la machine jamais construite ;: Babbage: the machine never built; Lovelace (1843): the first program. Von Neumann (1945): program and data together.
textes.Au XIXe siècle, Charles Babbage conçoit: In the 19th century Charles Babbage designed the analytical engine, a programmable mechanical calculator. It was never built in his lifetime. Yet in 1843 Ada Lovelace published its first program: a calculation of the Bernoulli numbers. She also sensed that the machine could handle things other than numbers, music for example.
textes.La guerre accélère tout. En 1943-1944, C: The war sped everything up. In 1943-1944 Colossus helped Bletchley Park break encrypted German messages; it remained secret until the 1970s. In 1945 John von Neumann described the architecture in which program and data share the same memory, that of almost all our computers. And in 1947 Grace Hopper's team taped into their logbook a moth found in a relay: "first actual case of bug being found".
textes.Un courant ne circule que dans une boucl: A current flows only in a closed loop: from the battery, through the wires, through the lamp, and back to the battery. An open switch breaks the loop and the lamp goes out. Metals conduct because some of their electrons are free to move; plastic, glass or rubber hold them back: they are insulators, hence cable sheathing. This difference between conductors and insulators was discovered by the Englishman Stephen Gray in 1729: a thread held up by metal lost its charge, one held up by silk kept it, and he made electricity travel 800 feet, about 240 m.
textes.La puissance électrique P, en watts, est: Electrical power P, in watts, is the product of voltage U and current I: P = U × I. An appliance on 230 V drawing 10 A uses P = 230 V × 10 A = 2,300 W. The other way round, a 2,000 W kettle draws I = P ÷ U = 2,000 ÷ 230 ≈ 8.7 A. The watt is named after James Watt, the steam-engine engineer. His great improvement to Newcomen's engine, the separate condenser, dates from 1769.
textes.L'aiguille d'une boussole s'aligne sur l: A compass needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, produced by the motion of liquid iron in the outer core. Classic trap: the needle's north pole is attracted by a magnetic south pole. The pole in the Arctic is therefore, magnetically speaking, a south pole. And breaking a magnet in two does not separate its poles: each piece becomes a complete magnet. That the Earth itself is a magnet was proposed by the Englishman William Gilbert, physician to Elizabeth I, in 1600 in De Magnete, after moving a needle around a small sphere of lodestone, the terrella.
textes.Radio, micro-ondes, infrarouge, visible,: Radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays: it is the same wave at different frequencies. All travel at the speed of light c, about 300,000 km/s, and satisfy c = λ × f: wavelength times frequency. For Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz: λ = c ÷ f = 300,000,000 m/s ÷ 2,400,000,000 Hz = 0.125 m, that is 12.5 cm. Our eye sees only a thin slice, from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). The two invisible neighbours of that slice were discovered one after the other: infrared in 1800 by William Herschel, with a thermometer placed beyond the red of a prism's spectrum, and ultraviolet in 1801 by Johann Ritter, with silver chloride paper that darkened beyond the violet.

textes.Professeur de lycée à Cologne, Georg Ohm: A secondary-school teacher in Cologne, Georg Ohm passes current through wires of different lengths and measures what happens. He derives a simple law: the current is proportional to the voltage, and inversely proportional to the circuit's resistance. He takes inspiration from how heat spreads along a bar, studied by Fourier. The German scientific community gives this work a poor reception, calling it a “web of naked fancies”, and Ohm leaves his post. Not until 1841 does the Royal Society honor him.

textes.Fils de brasseur, James Joule mesure ave: A brewer's son, James Joule measures with obsessive precision the heat given off by a wire carrying a current. He shows it is proportional to the wire's resistance and to the square of the current: doubling the current quadruples the heat. This is Joule heating, which makes filament bulbs glow and toasters heat up, but also wastes energy in power lines, which is why electricity is transmitted at very high voltage. These measurements later lead him to the equivalence between work and heat, which he defended alone against the scientific establishment.

textes.En décembre 1733, le Français Charles du: In December 1733, Frenchman Charles du Fay concluded that there are two kinds of electricity, which he called "vitreous" and "resinous": our positive and negative charges.
textes.C'est Benjamin Franklin qui nomme les ch: It was Benjamin Franklin who named charges positive and negative, in the 18th century, without knowing which case was a surplus. The electron was only named in 1891 by George Johnstone Stoney, and J. J. Thomson showed in 1897 that it is a particle.
textes.En 1729, l'Anglais Stephen Gray montre q: In 1729, Englishman Stephen Gray showed that electricity travels along a hemp thread but not along silk, which he used to insulate it. For his "flying boy", he hung a child from silk cords and electrified him.
textes.Stephen Gray est le premier à étudier la: Stephen Gray was the first to study conduction systematically, around 1729: he showed that metals carry electricity. His colleague John Desaguliers coined the words "conductor" and "insulator".
textes.Les règles des circuits en série et en d: The rules for series and parallel circuits were first described in 1845 by German physicist Gustav Kirchhoff.
textes.Gustav Kirchhoff énonce en 1845 les lois: Gustav Kirchhoff set out in 1845 the laws that say how current divides between the branches of a circuit.

In 1785, with his torsion balance, he showed that the force between two charges falls off as the square of the distance. The unit was named after him in 1880.
textes.En 1600, le médecin anglais William Gilb: In 1600, English physician William Gilbert coined the Latin word electricus from the Greek word for amber.
textes.Le physicien Louis Breguet recommande de: Physicist Louis Breguet recommended thinner wires to protect telegraph stations from lightning: they melt first. Thomas Edison patented a fuse in 1890 for his network, and circuit breakers replaced it in new homes from the 1950s.
textes.Tout part d'une dispute : dans les année: It all began with a dispute: in the 1780s, Luigi Galvani saw a frog's leg twitch in contact with two metals. Volta thought the electricity came from the metals, not the animal, and described his pile in a letter to the Royal Society on 20 March 1800. That same year, it was used to split water.
textes.Henry Cavendish avait trouvé la même loi: Henry Cavendish had found the same law in 1781, measuring current by the strength of the shock he took through his own body; he published nothing, and Maxwell revealed his results in 1879.
textes.Le livre d'Ohm est très mal reçu : un cr: Ohm's book was very badly received: a critic called it "a web of naked fancies" and the Minister of Education judged that a professor preaching such heresies was unworthy to teach science. The law only won acceptance in the 1840s.
textes.L'ampère porte le nom d'André-Marie Ampè: The ampere is named after André-Marie Ampère (1775-1836). It became an international unit in 1881, at the International Exposition of Electricity; since 2019, it has been defined from the elementary charge.
textes.Le mot « volt » est inventé en 1861 par: The word "volt" was coined in 1861 by Latimer Clark and Charles Bright, in honour of Volta. The 1881 International Electrical Congress adopted it as the unit of voltage.
textes.En 1899, la compagnie d'électricité de B: In 1899, Berlin's electricity company switched to 220 V, a model taken up across Europe, while the United Kingdom chose 240 V. A 1983 standard set 230 V for all, phased in from 1987.
textes.Le nom de watt, en hommage à James Watt,: The name watt, in honour of James Watt, was proposed in August 1882 by engineer William Siemens before the British Association. It was officially adopted at the 1908 London international conference.

Joseph Swan showed his lamp to 700 people on 3 February 1879, and Thomas Edison succeeded in his first test on 22 October 1879: thirteen and a half hours. A filament bulb turns less than 5% of its energy into light.
textes.En 1884, une ligne de 34 km en courant a: In 1884, a 34 km alternating-current line was built for the Turin exhibition. In 1891, the Lauffen-Frankfurt line carried three-phase current at 15,000 volts over about 175 km.
