textes.Le 20 décembre 1951, le réacteur expérim: On 20 December 1951, the experimental reactor EBR-I in Idaho produced the first nuclear electricity. The Obninsk plant in the USSR was the first connected to the grid, on 27 June 1954.
textes.Heinrich Hertz observe l'effet en 1887 :: Heinrich Hertz observed the effect in 1887: ultraviolet light made his sparks easier. Einstein explained it in 1905 with packets of light. Robert Millikan, who found the idea "quite unthinkable", confirmed his law in 1914.
textes.Le joule est proposé en 1882 par William: The joule was proposed in 1882 by William Siemens and officially adopted on 31 August 1889, at the second International Electrical Congress.
textes.Vers 1269, Pierre de Maricourt écrit sa: Around 1269, Peter Peregrinus of Maricourt wrote his Letter on the Magnet: the oldest surviving text to speak of poles and show that like poles repel.
textes.En 1600, dans De Magnete, William Gilber: In 1600, in De Magnete, William Gilbert, physician to Elizabeth I, experimented on a small magnetised Earth, the terrella, and concluded that the Earth is itself a magnet.
textes.Le récit d'une découverte faite par hasa: The story of a chance discovery in the middle of a lecture is a myth: Ørsted had been looking for this link since 1818. His discovery at once launched Ampère's work. Ørsted also isolated aluminium in 1824.
textes.Le 29 août 1831, Faraday enroule deux fi: On 29 August 1831, Faraday wound two wires around an iron ring: connecting one, he saw a brief "wave of electricity" in the other. American Joseph Henry made the same discovery on his own in 1832.
textes.Le pôle magnétique nord est atteint pour: The north magnetic pole was first reached on 1 June 1831 by James Clark Ross. It moves: about 55 km a year in 2019, from Canada towards Siberia.
textes.William Sturgeon invente l'électroaimant: William Sturgeon invented the electromagnet in 1824: 18 turns of bare copper wire on a horseshoe that lifted 9 pounds. Joseph Henry improved it from 1830 with silk-insulated wire; its first major use was the telegraph.
textes.Faraday et le Français Hippolyte Pixii f: Faraday and Frenchman Hippolyte Pixii ran the first generators in the 1830s. The word "alternator" appeared in the late 1870s, when Yablochkov's arc lamps worked better on alternating current.
textes.Le 3 septembre 1821, Faraday fait tourne: On 3 September 1821, Faraday made a wire dipped in mercury rotate around a magnet. Moritz von Jacobi built the first truly useful motor in 1834, which in 1838 drove a boat with 14 people across a wide river.
textes.En 1855, Weber et Kohlrausch mesurent un: In 1855, Weber and Kohlrausch measured an electrical velocity of about 310,000 km/s, very close to the speed of light. Maxwell published his equations in 1865: twenty equations originally, which Oliver Heaviside rewrote in today's compact form.
textes.Le Norvégien Kristian Birkeland envoie u: Norwegian Kristian Birkeland aimed an electron beam at a magnetised sphere: the electrons gathered towards the poles in rings of light. From this he drew his theory of the aurora, confirmed only in 1967 by a space probe.
textes.Pierre Curie se demandait dès 1894 si un: Pierre Curie wondered as early as 1894 whether a single magnetic pole could exist, and Paul Dirac developed its theory in 1931. On 14 February 1982, Blas Cabrera recorded a signal nicknamed the "Valentine's Day monopole", never reproduced. None has ever been observed.
textes.Les premiers brevets datent de 1906 (Art: The first patents date from 1906 (Arthur Berry, in the UK) and 1909. Frigidaire toured demonstration hobs in the mid-1950s without selling them; Westinghouse sold its own from 1973 to 1975.
textes.Maxwell comprend dès 1861, dans On Physi: Maxwell understood as early as 1861, in On Physical Lines of Force, that light is an electromagnetic wave. In 1865, he published A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field.
textes.Hertz mène ses expériences de 1886 à 188: Hertz carried out his experiments from 1886 to 1889 in Karlsruhe and confirmed the waves predicted by Maxwell. Asked about applications, he replied: "Nothing, I guess." He died in 1894, aged 36; the unit of frequency bears his name.
textes.En 1800, William Herschel place un therm: In 1800, William Herschel placed a thermometer beyond the red end of a spectrum of sunlight: it warmed up. A year later, Johann Ritter discovered on the other side, beyond violet, rays that darken silver chloride.
textes.Le Français Paul Villard découvre les ra: Frenchman Paul Villard discovered gamma rays in 1900 while studying radium. Ernest Rutherford named them in 1903, and showed with Edward Andrade in 1914 that their wavelength is shorter than that of X-rays.
textes.Percy Spencer n'avait pas fini l'école p: Percy Spencer had not finished grammar school and taught himself in the Navy. Others had seen a candy bar melt near a radar; he looked into it, popping corn and bursting an egg. The first commercial oven, in 1947, stood about 6 feet tall and weighed 750 pounds.
textes.Le 8 novembre 1895, à Würzburg, Röntgen: On 8 November 1895, in Würzburg, Röntgen saw a screen glow near a discharge tube. He called the rays "X", the letter for the unknown. Six weeks later, he imaged the hand of his wife Anna Bertha, who exclaimed: "I have seen my death!"
textes.Newton est le premier à employer le mot: Newton was the first to use the word "spectrum" in 1671 for light split by a prism; he first counted six colours and later added indigo. Thomas Young was the first to measure the wavelengths of colours, in 1802.
textes.Le 12 décembre 1901, Marconi écoute à Si: On 12 December 1901, Marconi listened at Signal Hill, Newfoundland, with a kite-borne antenna, for a signal sent from Poldhu about 3,500 km away. No automatic record was made, and historians doubt he really received it. He shared the 1909 Nobel Prize with Ferdinand Braun.
textes.En 1985, l'autorité américaine des téléc: In 1985, the US communications regulator opened the 2.4 GHz band to unlicensed use. NCR and AT&T created the precursor of Wi-Fi in 1991 in the Netherlands, for cash registers; the 802.11 standard came out in 1997. The name Wi-Fi was coined by a branding agency in 1999.
textes.On croyait la lumière portée par un « ét: Light was thought to be carried by an "aether". In 1887, in Cleveland, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley tried to measure the aether wind and found nothing: it has been called the most famous failed experiment in history.
textes.En 1801, Johann Ritter découvre au-delà: In 1801, Johann Ritter discovered invisible rays beyond violet that darken silver chloride; they were long called "chemical rays". Their effect on DNA was only established in 1960.
textes.En janvier 1935, le ministère britanniqu: In January 1935, the British Air Ministry asked whether a "death ray" was possible. Arnold Wilkins calculated that it was not, but suggested locating aircraft by radio: on 26 February 1935, at Daventry, a bomber was detected. In 1956, Robert Watson-Watt was stopped for speeding by a radar gun.
textes.Le 23 décembre 1947, Walter Brattain fai: On 23 December 1947, Walter Brattain demonstrated a germanium point-contact transistor that amplified speech. Julius Lilienfeld had filed a patent on the principle as early as 1925 in Canada, and Germans Mataré and Welker independently invented the "transistron" in 1948.
textes.Karl Ferdinand Braun découvre en 1874 qu: Karl Ferdinand Braun discovered in 1874 that a contact between a metal and a mineral lets current through in one direction only. John Ambrose Fleming patented the first vacuum diode on 16 November 1904, and William Eccles coined the word "diode" in 1919, from the Greek for "two paths".
textes.Henry Joseph Round, des laboratoires Mar: Henry Joseph Round, of the Marconi labs, saw a carborundum crystal emit light under voltage in 1906; Soviet inventor Oleg Losev built an LED in 1927. The first white LEDs went on sale in autumn 1996.
textes.L'ancêtre du condensateur est la bouteil: The ancestor of the capacitor is the Leyden jar, discovered on 11 October 1745 by Ewald von Kleist and then by Musschenbroek in Leiden. Abbé Nollet sent its discharge through 180 royal guards before Louis XV, and Franklin spoke of an "electrical battery" in 1749.
textes.William Shockley installe son laboratoir: William Shockley set up his laboratory in Mountain View in 1956 and preferred silicon to germanium. Journalist Don Hoefler popularised the phrase "Silicon Valley" on 11 January 1971, in the weekly Electronic News.
textes.En 1833, Faraday remarque que le sulfure: In 1833, Faraday noticed that silver sulfide conducts better when heated, unlike metals. The word Halbleiter, "semiconductor", appeared in 1910 in Josef Weiss's thesis.
textes.Nouvel employé de Texas Instruments, Jac: As a new Texas Instruments employee, Jack Kilby had no summer vacation in 1958: he spent it on the problem. On 12 September 1958, he showed his germanium circuit to management. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000.
textes.Le premier microprocesseur, l'Intel 4004: The first microprocessor, the Intel 4004, came out on 15 November 1971 with 2,300 transistors. It had been ordered by Japan's Busicom for its calculators.
textes.L'ENIAC, construit à l'université de Pen: ENIAC, built at the University of Pennsylvania by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert, was unveiled on 14 February 1946. It weighed 27 tonnes; several tubes burned out almost every day. Six women did most of its programming, long unrecognised.
textes.Dès 1903, l'Allemand Albert Hanson décri: As early as 1903, German Albert Hanson described flat conductors laminated to an insulating board. Austrian Paul Eisler invented the printed circuit around 1936 for a radio set; the United States used it on a large scale around 1943 for proximity fuzes.
textes.Willard Boyle et George Smith inventent: Willard Boyle and George Smith invented the CCD sensor in 1969 at Bell Labs, while looking for a new kind of memory. In 1975, Steven Sasson at Kodak built the first digital still camera from it, at 100 × 100 pixels. Boyle and Smith received the Nobel Prize in 2009.
textes.Vers 1893, AEG en Allemagne choisit le 5: Around 1893, AEG in Germany chose 50 Hz and Westinghouse in the United States 60 Hz, hence the world's two frequencies today.
textes.Pour discréditer l'alternatif, Harold Br: To discredit alternating current, Harold Brown electrocuted dogs in 1888 in public demonstrations, secretly linked to Edison's company. On 6 August 1890, the first electric chair execution, of William Kemmler, used alternating current: the first jolt did not kill him.
textes.Faraday enroule dès 1831 deux bobines su: Faraday wound two coils on an iron ring as early as 1831. Lucien Gaulard and John Gibbs showed a transformer in London in 1882 and in Turin in 1884; in 1885, Ganz engineers in Budapest patented the closed core, the basis of today's transformers.
textes.En 1890, la première ligne à haute tensi: In 1890, the first high-voltage alternating-current line linked Willamette Falls to Portland, Oregon. In 1891, the Lauffen-Frankfurt line ran about 175 km at 15,000 volts.
textes.Héron d'Alexandrie décrit déjà une roue: Hero of Alexandria already described a wind-driven wheel, and the windmills of Sistan in Iran were turning from the 7th century. In July 1887, Scotsman James Blyth lit his holiday home with the first electric wind turbine.
textes.Les cellules restent une curiosité jusqu: Cells remained a curiosity until 1954: Calvin Fuller, Daryl Chapin and Gerald Pearson presented the first practical cell at Bell Labs. The Vanguard I satellite carried some as early as 1958.
textes.Après le choc pétrolier de 1973, le Prem: After the 1973 oil crisis, Prime Minister Pierre Messmer announced a vast nuclear programme on 6 March 1974. France built 56 reactors in fifteen years; the very first had been commissioned at Marcoule from 1956.
textes.En 1878, à Cragside, en Angleterre, Will: In 1878, at Cragside in England, William Armstrong set up the first hydroelectric scheme, for a single arc lamp in his art gallery. Edison's first hydroelectric station started on 30 September 1882 in Appleton, Wisconsin.
textes.Stanley Whittingham invente le principe: Stanley Whittingham invented the principle at Exxon in 1974, but metallic lithium caught fire; John Goodenough and Koichi Mizushima found a better cathode in 1980, and Akira Yoshino the anode in 1985. Sony sold the first batteries in 1991.
textes.La première station de pompage date de 1: The first pumped-storage plant dates from 1907, in Switzerland, near Schaffhausen. In 2020, such plants accounted for about 95% of the world's electricity storage installations.
textes.La centrale de Pearl Street, à Manhattan: Pearl Street Station, in Manhattan, started on 4 September 1882 and supplied 400 lamps for 82 customers, in direct current at 110 volts. It burned down in 1890 and ran until 1895.
textes.Bien avant Leibniz, les trigrammes du Yi: Long before Leibniz, the trigrams of the Chinese I Ching (9th century BC) resemble binary numbers, and India's Pingala described metre with short and long syllables. Leibniz wrote his first text on binary in 1679.
textes.Le mot byte est inventé en juin 1956 par: The word byte was coined in June 1956 by Werner Buchholz at IBM, for the Stretch computer: he respelled bite as byte so it would not be confused with bit. The word "octet" unambiguously means 8 bits.
textes.George Boole, autodidacte qui enseigne d: George Boole, self-taught and teaching from age 16, published his algebraic logic in 1847 and then in The Laws of Thought in 1854. It is this algebra that Shannon applied to circuits.
textes.Babbage décrit sa machine en 1837 et ne: Babbage described his machine in 1837 and did not finish it, for lack of money and after a conflict with his engineer. His son Henry built a small part that, in 1910, calculated a list of multiples of pi... a wrong one. In 1991, London's Science Museum built his Difference Engine No. 2, which works.
textes.Le mot bug est bien plus ancien : Thomas: The word bug is much older: Thomas Edison used it in a letter of 13 November 1878 for an invention's little faults. The log book with the moth is kept at the National Museum of American History in Washington.
textes.Gordon Moore l'écrit en 1965 dans la rev: Gordon Moore wrote it in 1965 in Electronics magazine, under the title "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits". Caltech professor Carver Mead later popularised the name "Moore's law". The pace has slowed since around 2010.
textes.Le rapport de John von Neumann de 1945 s: John von Neumann's 1945 report built on the work of Eckert and Mauchly, but circulated under his name alone, which angered them. The first stored program ran on 21 June 1948, on the Manchester "Baby".
textes.La première vraie mémoire vive est le tu: The first true random-access memory was the Williams tube, which ran the Manchester "Baby"'s first program on 21 June 1948. Robert Dennard invented the one-transistor cell at IBM in 1966, and Intel sold the first such chip in 1970.
textes.Le mot bit, contraction de binary digit,: The word bit, short for binary digit, comes from a Bell Labs memo by John Tukey dated 9 January 1947. Claude Shannon took it up in his founding 1948 paper.
textes.Conçu par l'ingénieur des postes Tommy F: Designed by Post Office engineer Tommy Flowers, Colossus broke the German Lorenz cipher: the first message fell on 5 February 1944, and the Mark 2 was ready on 1 June 1944, just before D-Day. After the war, Flowers was ordered to burn the plans.
textes.Le mot « logiciel » est formé en 1969 pa: The word "logiciel" was formed in 1969 by the Délégation à l'informatique, in charge of the Plan Calcul, from "logique" and "matériel". The Académie française adopted it in 1972.
textes.En 1937, Claude Shannon montre dans son: In 1937, Claude Shannon showed in his MIT master's thesis that Boolean algebra and binary arithmetic can drive relays and switches: the basis of digital circuits.
textes.{comp}. Franklin envoyait un cerf-volant: {comp}. Franklin flew a kite into a storm, or so he said. I'm sending you a question. It's less dangerous.
textes.Électricité. Faraday a quitté l'école à: Electricity. Faraday left school at 13 and discovered induction. You have no excuse left: {comp}.
textes.Volta empilait le zinc et le cuivre. J'e: Volta stacked zinc and copper. I stack questions: {comp}.
textes.Juste. Le courant passe entre nous. Ohm: Right. There's a current between us. Ohm would measure a very low resistance.
textes.Bonne réponse. Tesla dirait qu'il l'avai: Correct. Tesla would say he found it before you. He said that about everything.
textes.Correct. Faraday aurait fait une confére: Correct. Faraday would have given a Christmas lecture about you, for the children.
textes.Étincelant. Ne vous habituez pas à la lu: Sparkling. Don't get used to the light.
textes.Raté. Galvani croyait à l'électricité an: Missed. Galvani believed in animal electricity. You believe in your answer. Same result.
textes.Faux. Edison a essayé des milliers de ma: Wrong. Edison tried thousands of materials before the right filament. You're allowed a few more tries.
textes.Erreur. Franklin s'est assommé en voulan: Error. Franklin knocked himself out trying to electrocute a turkey. You knocked yourself out all on your own.
textes.Court-circuit. Je coupe le courant à vot: Short circuit. I'm cutting the power to your pride.
textes.Fils de forgeron, apprenti relieur, il a: A blacksmith's son, apprenticed to a bookbinder, he learned science by reading the books he bound. He discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831. To a minister who asked what electricity was good for: “One day, sir, you may tax it.” The retort is probably made up.
textes.Fille de Byron, elle écrit en 1843 le pr: Byron's daughter, she wrote the first published program in 1843, for Babbage's Analytical Engine, and foresaw that a machine might compose music. Her mother had raised her on mathematics to protect her from the “madness” she attributed to her father.
textes.Haut fonctionnaire de la dynastie Song,: A high official of the Song dynasty, he noted in 1088 that a magnetized needle does not point exactly north: the first known description of magnetic declination. He also described Bi Sheng's movable-type printing and the formation of fossils.
textes.En 1921, sur le bateau du retour, il se: In 1921, on the ship home, he wonders why the sea is blue. In Calcutta, he discovers that a small part of the light scattered by molecules changes color: the Raman effect. Nobel Prize 1930; he had booked his trip to Stockholm months before the announcement.
textes.Professeur de lycée à Cologne, il publie: A secondary-school teacher in Cologne, he published his law in 1827 after months of measurements. In Germany, the reception was cold; he left his post. It took the Royal Society of London awarding him the Copley Medal in 1841 for his country to take him seriously.
textes.Coinventeur du transistor en 1947, il es: Co-inventor of the transistor in 1947, he is the only person to have received the Nobel Prize in physics twice. In 1956, he brought only one of his three children to Stockholm. The King of Sweden chided him; he promised to come back with all of them. In 1972, he did, with all three.
textes.Son moteur à courant alternatif l'emport: His alternating-current motor beat Edison's direct current in the “war of the currents”: our grids come from it. He also promised wireless power and a death ray, never built. He died alone and in debt in a New York hotel room, where he looked after pigeons.
textes.Maîtriser la puissance électrique. Comme: Master electric power. Like Edison, you didn't invent everything.
textes.Edison n'a pas inventé l'ampoule. Humphr: Edison did not invent the light bulb. Humphry Davy, Warren de la Rue and Joseph Swan came before him. His contribution, in 1879, was a long-lasting carbon filament and above all the whole system to produce and distribute the current.
textes.Maîtriser les charges et les circuits. A: Master charges and circuits. No frogs were harmed. This time.
textes.Dans les années 1780, Luigi Galvani voit: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani sees frogs' legs twitch on contact with two metals. He believes in an “animal electricity”. Volta disagrees and, to prove it, invents the battery.
textes.Maîtriser la loi d'Ohm. Vous l'avez mieu: Master Ohm's law. You received it better than his contemporaries.
textes.Georg Ohm publie sa loi en 1827. Elle es: Georg Ohm published his law in 1827. It got a cold reception in Germany, and Ohm had to leave his teaching post. Recognition came from London, with the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1841.
textes.Maîtriser le magnétisme. Le nord n'est p: Master magnetism. North isn't quite the same anymore.
textes.En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted notices that a wire carrying a current deflects a magnetized needle. Electricity and magnetism would never again be two separate disciplines.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange d'Étincelle: Master the first diamond of Spark.
textes.L'expérience du cerf-volant de Franklin: Franklin's kite experiment (1752) is only known in detail through an account published fifteen years later by Joseph Priestley. In 1753, Georg Richmann, who was reproducing this kind of experiment in Saint Petersburg, was killed by lightning.
textes.Maîtriser 6 compétences. L'arbre de l'Él: Master 6 skills. The Electricity tree opens.
textes.En 1825, Michael Faraday lance à la Roya: In 1825, Michael Faraday launched Christmas lectures for children at the Royal Institution. He gave nineteen series himself. They have been held every year since, except during World War II.
Master electromagnetic waves. Don't stand in front of the magnetron.
textes.En 1945, l'ingénieur Percy Spencer trava: In 1945, engineer Percy Spencer is working on radar magnetrons at Raytheon and notices that a chocolate bar has melted in his pocket. He tries corn, which pops. The first microwave oven, in 1947, is almost two meters tall and weighs 340 kilos.
textes.Maîtriser l'électronique. Le mot « bug »: Master electronics. The word “bug” is older than computing.
textes.Le 9 septembre 1947, l'équipe du calcula: On September 9, 1947, the team of the Harvard Mark II calculator taped into its log a moth found in a relay: “First actual case of bug being found”. The joke works because the word already existed: Edison spoke of “bugs” in his inventions as early as 1878.
textes.Maîtriser le réseau et les énergies. La: Master the grid and energy. The war of the currents has enough real horrors.
textes.On attribue à Edison l'électrocution de: Edison is credited with electrocuting the elephant Topsy to discredit alternating current. It happened in 1903 at Coney Island, ten years after the war of the currents ended, and Edison had nothing to do with it. His company merely filmed the scene.
Master from transistor to computer. You surely have more than five at home.
textes.« Je pense qu'il y a un marché mondial p: “I think there is a world market for maybe five computers.” The line is attributed to Thomas Watson, head of IBM, in 1943. Nobody has ever found it in a document from the time. The most famous failed predictions are often made up.
textes.Réussir trois quiz d'Étincelle sans faut: Pass three Spark quizzes without a mistake. You're right. The current, though, flows backwards.
textes.Vers 1747, Benjamin Franklin nomme « pos: Around 1747, Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of electricity “positive” and “negative”, guessing which way the fluid flows. He had a fifty-fifty chance and got it wrong: electrons, discovered in 1897, go the other way. Conventional current keeps his choice.
textes.L'os d'Ishango, trouvé en 1950 au Congo,: The Ishango bone, found in 1950 in the Congo, is a bone covered in notches arranged in groups, so worked that no one can tell which animal it came from. Some read prime numbers or a lunar calendar in it; others, more cautious, a simple counting tool. Dated to about 20,000 years ago, it is kept in Brussels and is among the oldest known mathematical objects.
textes.Des encoches sur un os. Les premiers mat: Notches on a bone. The first mathematicians had no blackboard, but they already had skeptics to dispute their results.
textes.Pythagore n'a probablement pas démontré: Pythagoras probably did not prove the theorem that bears his name: the Babylonians knew the relation a millennium earlier, as the Plimpton 322 tablet shows, and no writing by Pythagoras has come down to us. His school mixed mathematics, music and strange rules, such as the ban on eating beans. It left an idea that has crossed the centuries: the world can be described by numbers.
textes.Le théorème de Pythagore n'est pas de Py: The Pythagorean theorem isn't by Pythagoras. The AI isn't quite an intelligence. Everyone has their labels.
textes.À Alexandrie, Euclide rassemble la géomé: In Alexandria, Euclid gathered the geometry of his time in the Elements: 13 books, definitions, five postulates and hundreds of theorems proven step by step. It is one of the most copied and printed books in history. To King Ptolemy, who asked for a shorter path, he supposedly replied: “There is no royal road to geometry.”
textes.Pas de voie royale en géométrie, ni sur: No royal road to geometry, nor on this board. The AI sees to it.
textes.Les Éléments ont servi de manuel pendant: The Elements served as a textbook for more than two thousand years. People still study them. Your turn.
textes.Le mathématicien indien Brahmagupta donn: In 628, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta gave rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers: a debt minus zero is a debt, zero minus zero is zero. Zero already existed as a placeholder among the Babylonians and the Maya, but he made it a number like any other. Yet he got zero divided by zero wrong, saying it equals zero.
textes.Zéro devient un nombre. L'IA connaît des: Zero becomes a number. The AI knows quizzes that made it their favorite score.
textes.Brahmagupta fixe les règles du zéro, mai: Brahmagupta set the rules for zero, but stated 0 ÷ 0 = 0. One calculation error, two squares back.
textes.À la Maison de la sagesse de Bagdad, al-: At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise on solving equations by “al-jabr,” restoration, which gave us the word algebra. His name, Latinized as Algoritmi, gave us “algorithm.” His books also introduced Europe to the Indian numerals, which have since been called, wrongly, Arabic numerals.
textes.Les algorithmes portent le nom d'un math: Algorithms are named after a mathematician from Baghdad. The AI is made of algorithms. She'll let you draw the connection.
textes.Leonardo de Pise, dit Fibonacci, publie: Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, published the Liber abaci: in it he explained to European merchants the Hindu-Arabic numerals and written calculation, far more practical than Roman numerals. He is mostly remembered for a little problem about rabbits that gives the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… Indian mathematicians had known it for centuries.
textes.Calculez avec MCMXXIV, puis avec 1924. V: Calculate with MCMXXIV, then with 1924. You'll understand the shortcut.
textes.Le chevalier de Méré, joueur, demande à: The Chevalier de Méré, a gambler, asked Blaise Pascal how to divide the stakes of an interrupted game. Pascal discussed it by letter with Pierre de Fermat in the summer of 1654: their correspondence laid the foundations of probability theory. At 18, Pascal had also built a calculating machine, the Pascaline, to help his father collect taxes.
textes.Les probabilités sont nées d'une partie: Probability was born from a game of dice. Your chances of passing the next quiz can be calculated. The AI has calculated them.
textes.Pascal et Fermat posent les bases du cal: Pascal and Fermat laid the foundations of probability to fairly divide the stakes of an interrupted game. This time, the split falls your way.
textes.Alan Turing imagine une machine abstrait: Alan Turing imagined an abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape: it can carry out any calculation. It is the theoretical model of all our computers. During the war, he helped break the Enigma code at Bletchley Park. Convicted in 1952 of “gross indecency” because of his relationship with a man, he died in 1954; the United Kingdom granted him a posthumous pardon in 2013.
textes.Turing a inventé l'ordinateur sur le pap: Turing invented the computer on paper, then wondered whether a machine could think. The AI reserves her answer.
textes.Au CERN, Tim Berners-Lee propose un syst: At CERN, Tim Berners-Lee proposed a system of documents connected by links and accessible over the Internet: the World Wide Web. His boss annotated the proposal “Vague but exciting…”. The first website went online at the end of 1990, and CERN put the technology in the public domain in 1993.
textes.Le Web a commencé par « vague mais excit: The Web started out as “vague but exciting.” That's how the AI sums up your progress.
textes.La toute première version du premier sit: The very first version of the first website is lost: in 2013, CERN could only put back online a copy from 1992. Dead link: back to Mendeleev's table.
textes.Vers 1800 av. J.-C., probablement à Lars: Around 1800 BC, probably in Larsa, in Mesopotamia, a scribe inscribes on a clay tablet a table of 15 rows in base 60. It contains Pythagorean triples: whole numbers like 3, 4 and 5, sides of a right triangle, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. Bought around 1922 by the New York publisher George Plimpton, it is at Columbia University. What was it for? Specialists still debate it.
textes.Mille ans avant Pythagore, un scribe con: A thousand years before Pythagoras, a scribe already knew his triangles. You, a thousand years after, let's check.
textes.Vers 1550 av. J.-C., à Thèbes, le scribe: Around 1550 BC, in Thebes, the scribe Ahmes copies an older mathematics manual. The papyrus opens with a table writing the fractions 2/n as sums of fractions with numerator 1, the Egyptian way. Then come problems of sharing loaves, pyramid slopes, areas. For the area of a disc, Ahmes in effect takes 256/81 for π, about 3.16. Alexander Rhind buys it in Luxor in 1858; it is now in the British Museum.
textes.3,16 pour π, il y a trente-cinq siècles: 3.16 for π, thirty-five centuries ago: less than one percent off. Do better in the next quiz.
textes.Vers 250 av. J.-C., dans La Mesure du ce: Around 250 BC, in Measurement of a Circle, Archimedes traps the circle between two regular 96-sided polygons, one inside, one outside. The circle's perimeter must lie between the two. From this he gets bounds: π is greater than 223/71 and less than 22/7, that is between 3.1408 and 3.1429. His method, which approaches a curve with ever finer figures, foreshadows calculus.
textes.Archimède a dessiné deux fois 96 côtés p: Archimedes drew 96 sides twice for one answer. You need only one answer. A right one.
textes.Au IIIe siècle, à Alexandrie, Diophante: In the 3rd century, in Alexandria, Diophantus writes the Arithmetica in thirteen books: number problems solved with equations. He invents abbreviations for the unknown and its powers, a first step towards algebraic notation. Six books survive in Greek; four more, in Arabic, were only found in 1968. Bachet's Latin edition of 1621 made him read all over Europe, right into Fermat's margin.
textes.Diophante a inventé une abréviation pour: Diophantus invented an abbreviation for the unknown. Here, the unknown is your next answer.
textes.Vers 1070, à Samarcande, le Persan Omar: Around 1070, in Samarkand, the Persian Omar Khayyam begins a treatise on algebra. In it he solves cubic equations with geometry: the solution is read where two conic sections cross, such as a parabola and a circle. It is the first systematic study of these equations. An astronomer, he also leads the team that creates the Jalali calendar, launched in 1079. In the West he is best known for quatrains, the Rubaiyat, many of them wrongly attributed to him.
textes.Khayyam résolvait des équations avec des: Khayyam solved equations with parabolas and wrote poems. You might at least pick one of the two.
textes.En 1539, le mathématicien Tartaglia conf: In 1539, the mathematician Tartaglia tells Gerolamo Cardano his method for solving certain cubic equations, on condition that he keep it secret. Cardano then learns that Scipione del Ferro had found it first, and publishes everything in 1545 in the Ars Magna, with his student Ferrari's method for the fourth degree. In it, for the first time, appear square roots of negative numbers, which Cardano judges as subtle as they are useless.
textes.Des nombres aussi subtils qu'inutiles, d: Numbers as subtle as they are useless, said Cardano. Today they are used everywhere. Beware of your final judgements.
textes.En 1614, l'Écossais John Napier publie l: In 1614, the Scot John Napier publishes the Description of the Wonderful Rule of Logarithms: 57 pages of explanation and 90 pages of tables. Thanks to them, long hand calculations become much faster. He had already invented his bones, numbered rods to make multiplication easier. In 1615, Henry Briggs visits him; Napier hands him the computation of new tables, which will become base-10 logarithms.
textes.Napier a passé des années à calculer pou: Napier spent years calculating so others could calculate less. You calculate less without having done anything.
textes.Vers 1637, Pierre de Fermat, magistrat à: Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat, a magistrate in Toulouse, annotates his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica. He states that no cube is the sum of two cubes, and more generally that no power beyond the square is the sum of two like powers. He claims a marvellous proof, but the margin is too narrow to contain it. His son publishes the note in 1670. It took until Andrew Wiles, in 1994: 358 years.
textes.J'ai une démonstration merveilleuse de v: I have a marvellous proof of your delay, but this square is too small. Go back two.
textes.À Königsberg, la rivière Pregel entoure: In Königsberg, the river Pregel surrounds two islands linked to the banks by seven bridges. Can you take a walk crossing each bridge once and only once? In 1736, Leonhard Euler forgets the map and keeps only the essentials: land masses linked by bridges. He shows that such a walk requires zero or two land masses touched by an odd number of bridges. Königsberg has four: it is impossible. This is the first theorem of graph theory.
textes.Euler a résolu le problème en effaçant l: Euler solved the problem by erasing the map. Erase your preconceptions, that works too.
textes.L'Anglais Thomas Bayes meurt en 1761 san: The Englishman Thomas Bayes dies in 1761 without having published his work on probability. His friend Richard Price finds it among his papers, completes it and has it published in 1763 in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society. The essay shows how to revise a probability in the light of a new observation, starting from an initial estimate. This reasoning, since called Bayes's theorem, is used today in medicine, law and artificial intelligence.
textes.Bayes révisait ses probabilités à chaque: Bayes revised his probabilities with each new observation. After your last answer, I'm revising mine.
textes.En 1854, l'Anglais George Boole publie A: In 1854, the Englishman George Boole publishes An Investigation of the Laws of Thought. In it he treats logic like algebra: Aristotle's propositions become equations, which one solves. He justifies his system with a rule of calculation on the numbers 0 and 1 alone. His successors, such as Jevons, Peirce or Schröder, will draw from it the algebra that bears his name, that of the circuits of our computers, where everything comes down to true or false.
textes.Chez Boole, tout est vrai ou faux. Votre: With Boole, everything is true or false. Your last answer was 0.
textes.En novembre 1854, l'infirmière Florence: In November 1854, the nurse Florence Nightingale arrives at the military hospital in Scutari, during the Crimean War. She finds that soldiers die ten times more often of typhus, cholera or dysentery than of their wounds. To make decision-makers understand, she draws sector diagrams, month by month, now called her roses. In 1859, she becomes the first woman member of the Royal Statistical Society.
textes.Nightingale a sauvé des vies avec un gra: Nightingale saved lives with a chart. You could start by reading yours, in the stats.
textes.En 1891, Georg Cantor publie l'argument: In 1891, Georg Cantor publishes the diagonal argument. Suppose a list of all infinite sequences of 0s and 1s. Build a new sequence by changing the first digit of the first, the second of the second, and so on: it differs from every sequence on the list. So no list can be complete. There are infinities larger than that of the whole numbers: the real numbers are one.
textes.Il y a des infinis plus grands que d'aut: Some infinities are larger than others. Like your backlog of reviews.
textes.En 1931, le jeune logicien autrichien Ku: In 1931, the young Austrian logician Kurt Gödel publishes two theorems. The first: any consistent system of axioms capable of arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. The second: such a system cannot prove its own consistency. David Hilbert's grand project, to found all of mathematics on a complete and secure base, is badly shaken.
Some truths cannot be proved. Your hidden talent, for instance.
textes.Un jeu télévisé : trois portes, une voit: A TV game show: three doors, a car behind one of them. You pick one; the host, who knows everything, opens another, empty one. Should you switch? In 1990, Marilyn vos Savant answers in Parade magazine: yes, you then win two times out of three. About 10,000 readers write to tell her she is wrong, nearly 1,000 of them PhDs. Even the mathematician Paul Erdős only believes it after a computer simulation.
A thousand PhDs got it wrong in chorus. You see, you're in good company.
textes.Les opérations, les priorités de calcul,: Operations, order of operations, fractions and prime numbers.
textes.Priorités : parenthèses, puissances, pui: Order of operations: parentheses, powers, then multiplication and division (left to right), then addition and subtraction.
textes.Pour additionner des fractions, on les m: To add fractions, put them over a common denominator: 3/4 + 1/8 = 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. You never add the denominators.
textes.Diviser par une fraction, c'est multipli: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4.
textes.Un nombre premier a exactement deux divi: A prime number has exactly two divisors, 1 and itself. So 1 is not prime; 2 is the only even prime.
textes.6 ÷ 2 × 3 vaut 9, pas 1 : à priorité éga: 6 ÷ 2 × 3 equals 9, not 1: with equal priority, the convention is to work from left to right.
textes.Une barre coupée en 4 dont 3 parts color: A bar cut into 4 with 3 parts colored, a bar cut into 8 with 1 part colored
textes.Règle de trois, échelles, hausses et bai: Rule of three, scales, percentage increases and decreases.
textes.La règle de trois marche quand deux gran: The rule of three works when two quantities are proportional: if 3 kg cost €12, 5 kg cost 5 × 12 / 3 = €20.
textes.Une hausse de t % multiplie par (1 + t/1: An increase of t% multiplies by (1 + t/100), a decrease by (1 − t/100). Successive changes chain by multiplying the coefficients.
textes.+50 % puis −50 % ne ramène pas au départ: +50% then −50% does not bring you back to the start: 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75, a 25% drop.
textes.Point de pourcentage et pourcentage diff: Percentage points and percent differ: going from 10% to 12% is +2 points, but +20%.
textes.Une baisse de 20 % ne se rattrape pas pa: A 20% drop is not made up by a 20% rise: you need +25%.
textes.Hausse de 50 % puis baisse de 50 % : on: A 50% rise then a 50% drop: you end up at 75
textes.Le hasard, l'indépendance, les paradoxes: Chance, independence, the paradoxes that fool intuition.
textes.Probabilité = cas favorables ÷ cas possi: Probability = favorable cases ÷ possible cases, provided the cases are equally likely.
textes.Deux événements indépendants : on multip: Two independent events: multiply their probabilities. Two heads in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
textes.Le hasard n'a pas de mémoire : après dix: Chance has no memory: after ten heads, the eleventh toss still has a one in two chance (the gambler's fallacy).
textes.Monty Hall : changer de porte fait gagne: Monty Hall: switching doors wins 2 times out of 3, because the host knows where the car is and never opens that door.
textes.Avec deux dés, 7 est la somme la plus pr: With two dice, 7 is the most likely sum (6 outcomes out of 36), not 12 (1 out of 36).
textes.Tableau des 36 résultats possibles avec: Table of the 36 possible results with two dice
textes.Implication, négation, syllogismes et ra: Implication, negation, syllogisms and proof by contradiction.
textes.« Si A alors B » est faux dans un seul c: “If A then B” is false in only one case: A true and B false.
textes.La contraposée « si non B alors non A »: The contrapositive “if not B then not A” is equivalent. The converse “if B then A” is not.
textes.Nier « tous les cygnes sont blancs », c': Negating “all swans are white” means saying “at least one swan is not white”, not “no swan is white”.
textes.Raisonnement par l'absurde : on suppose: Proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of what you want to prove and reach a contradiction.
textes.Affirmer le conséquent : « s'il pleut, l: Affirming the consequent: “if it rains, the ground is wet; the ground is wet, so it's raining” is invalid.
textes.Inconnues, équations, identités remarqua: Unknowns, equations, special products and systems.
textes.Résoudre une équation : faire la même op: Solving an equation: do the same operation on both sides until the unknown is isolated.
textes.Identités remarquables : (a + b)² = a² +: Special products: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
textes.(a + b)² n'est pas a² + b² : on oublie l: (a + b)² is not a² + b²: that forgets the cross term 2ab.
textes.Un système de deux équations à deux inco: A system of two equations in two unknowns is solved by substitution or by elimination.
textes.Diviser les deux côtés par x fait perdre: Dividing both sides by x loses the solution x = 0: factor instead.
textes.Moyenne, médiane, écart type, corrélatio: Mean, median, standard deviation, correlation and samples.
textes.La moyenne est sensible aux valeurs extr: The mean is sensitive to extreme values; the median splits the population into two halves and resists them.
textes.Quand Bill Gates entre dans un bar, la m: When Bill Gates walks into a bar, the mean fortune explodes; the median barely moves.
textes.L'écart type mesure la dispersion autour: The standard deviation measures the spread around the mean.
textes.Corrélation n'est pas causalité : glaces: Correlation is not causation: ice cream and drownings rise together in summer, because of the heat.
textes.Un salaire moyen supérieur au salaire mé: An average salary above the median salary doesn't mean most people earn more than the average: it's the opposite.
textes.Cinq valeurs : médiane 2, moyenne 4 tiré: Five values: median 2, mean 4 pulled up by the value 12
textes.Angles, aires, volumes, Pythagore, sinus: Angles, areas, volumes, Pythagoras, sine and cosine.
textes.Pythagore : dans un triangle rectangle,: Pythagoras: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides (3, 4, 5).
textes.Aire du disque π r², périmètre 2 π r ; v: Area of a disk π r², circumference 2 π r; volume of a sphere 4/3 π r³.
textes.Doubler les longueurs multiplie les aire: Doubling lengths multiplies areas by 4 and volumes by 8.
textes.Dans un triangle rectangle : sinus = opp: In a right triangle: sine = opposite / hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent / hypotenuse, tangent = opposite / adjacent.
textes.La somme des angles d'un triangle vaut 1: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, but only on a plane: on a sphere, they add up to more than 180°.
textes.Agrandir une figure : longueurs, aires e: Enlarging a figure: lengths, areas and volumes
textes.Suites, séries, limites et les paradoxes: Sequences, series, limits and the paradoxes of infinity.
textes.Une suite géométrique de raison inférieu: A geometric sequence with ratio less than 1 in absolute value tends to 0; its sum can be finite: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … = 1.
textes.0,999… = 1 exactement : c'est la même so: 0.999… = 1 exactly: it's the same infinite sum written another way.
textes.La série harmonique 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … di: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges, even though its terms tend to 0.
textes.Cantor : il y a autant d'entiers pairs q: Cantor: there are as many even integers as integers, but strictly more real numbers than integers.
textes.Que les termes tendent vers 0 ne suffit: Terms tending to 0 is not enough for an infinite sum to be finite.
textes.Les sommes 1/2 + 1/4 + … s'approchent de: The sums 1/2 + 1/4 + … approach 1 without exceeding it
textes.Espérance = somme de chaque gain × sa pr: Expected value = sum of each gain × its probability.
textes.Second degré ax² + bx + c = 0 : discrimi: Quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0: discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac; if Δ > 0, two solutions (−b ± √Δ) ÷ 2a.
textes.cos 60° = 1/2 : c'est la moitié d'un tri: cos 60° = 1/2: it is half of an equilateral triangle.
textes.Parenthèses, puissances, × et ÷, puis +: Brackets, powers, × and ÷, then + and −. When tied, left to right.
textes.Un calcul s'écrit sur une ligne, mais il: A calculation is written on one line, but it is not necessarily read from left to right. The convention: brackets first, then powers, then multiplications and divisions, finally additions and subtractions. So 2 + 3 × 4 is 14, not 20.
Adding: common denominator first. Dividing by a fraction: multiply by its inverse.
textes.Pour additionner des fractions, il faut: To add fractions, they must talk about parts of the same size: you put them over a common denominator. 3/4 + 1/8 is 6/8 + 1/8 = 7/8. Adding the denominators (4 + 8) makes no sense: you do not cut the cake into twelve by adding two slices.
textes.Premier = exactement deux diviseurs (1 n: Prime = exactly two divisors (1 is not prime). There are infinitely many (Euclid, Elements IX, 20).
textes.Un nombre premier a exactement deux divi: A prime number has exactly two divisors: 1 and itself. 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13… 1 is not prime, since it has only one divisor, and 2 is the only even prime. Every whole number breaks down into a product of primes: they are the bricks of multiplication.
textes.Y en a-t-il une infinité ? Euclide le dé: Are there infinitely many? Euclid proved it around 300 BCE, in Book IX of the Elements. Take a finite list of primes, multiply them all and add 1. The result is divisible by none of them, since there is always 1 left over. So it is prime, or it has a prime factor missing from the list. No list is ever complete.
textes.Proportionnel = multiplier par un même n: Proportional = multiplying by the same number. Rule of three: go through the unit.
textes.Deux grandeurs sont proportionnelles qua: Two quantities are proportional when one is obtained by multiplying the other by the same number: the price and weight of apples, the flour and the number of guests. Doubling one doubles the other.
textes.Hausse de t % = × (1 + t/100). On enchaî: A t % rise = × (1 + t/100). Chain by multiplying. −20 % is recovered by +25 %.
textes.D'où les surprises. +50 % puis −50 % : 1: Hence the surprises. +50 % then −50 %: 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75, you have lost 25 %. After a 20 % fall, you need +25 % to get back, because 0.8 × 1.25 = 1. And to get a pre-tax price back from €120 including 20 % VAT, you divide by 1.2: €100, not €96.
textes.Point de pourcentage = différence entre: Percentage point = difference between two rates. Percentage = relative change. 10 % → 12 %: +2 points, +20 %.
textes.Quand un taux passe de 10 % à 12 %, il a: When a rate goes from 10 % to 12 %, it has gained 2 percentage points. But relative to where it started, it has risen by 20 %, since 2 is a fifth of 10. Both statements are right; they do not say the same thing.
It is a playground for headlines. An interest rate going from 2 % to 3 %: "+1 point" sounds calm, "+50 %" sounds alarming. A risk going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 "doubles", but stays tiny. Always ask: a percentage of what?
textes.Probabilité = cas favorables ÷ cas possi: Probability = favourable cases ÷ possible cases (equally likely cases). Pascal and Fermat, 1654; Huygens, 1657.
textes.La probabilité, au départ, c'est compter: Probability starts with counting: favourable cases divided by possible cases, provided all cases are equally likely. A 6 with one die: 1 in 6. With two dice there are 36 possible pairs; six give 7, only one gives 12. So 7 comes up six times more often than 12.
textes.Cette science est née autour d'une table: This science was born around a gaming table. Around 1654 the Chevalier de Méré put the "problem of points" to Blaise Pascal: how to share the stakes of an interrupted game? Pascal discussed it by letter with Pierre de Fermat, and their answers laid the foundations of probability. In 1657 Christiaan Huygens drew the first treatise from it.
textes.Indépendants : on multiplie. Une série p: Independent: multiply. A past streak does not change the next draw (gambler's fallacy, Monte Carlo 1913).
textes.Deux événements indépendants ne s'influe: Two independent events do not influence each other: you multiply their probabilities. Two heads in a row: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. And after ten heads, the eleventh toss still has a one-in-two chance: the coin does not know what it did before.
textes.Croire le contraire, c'est l'erreur du j: Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy, and it is expensive. On 18 August 1913, at the Monte Carlo casino, the ball landed on black 26 times in a row. Players, convinced red "had to" come up, bet bigger and bigger against black and lost millions of francs.
textes.Monty Hall : changer de porte gagne 2 fo: Monty Hall: switching doors wins 2 times out of 3. Positive test for a rare disease: often a false alarm. Always start from the base rate.
textes.Le jeu de Monty Hall : trois portes, une: The Monty Hall game: three doors, a car behind one. You pick one; the host, who knows everything, opens another, losing door and offers to let you switch. Switching wins 2 times out of 3: your first choice only had a one-in-three chance, and the host told you nothing about it. In September 1990 Marilyn vos Savant published it in Parade magazine. She received about 10,000 letters, nearly 1,000 from PhDs, most saying she was wrong. Even Paul Erdős was only convinced by a simulation.
textes.Autre piège : les tests sur des maladies: Another trap: tests for rare diseases. A disease affects 1 person in 1,000, the test is 99 % reliable. Out of 100,000 people, 100 are ill and 99 are detected, but 1 % of the 99,900 healthy people also test positive, about 1,000. A positive result therefore has only about a one-in-eleven chance of being ill. When the starting case is rare, false alarms win.
textes.« Si A alors B » n'est faux que si A est: "If A then B" is false only when A is true and B false. Contrapositive (not B → not A) equivalent; converse (B → A) not.
textes.Sa contraposée, « si le sol est sec, il: Its contrapositive, "if the ground is dry, it did not rain", says exactly the same thing. Its converse, "if the ground is wet, it rained", does not: that is the error called affirming the consequent. A good share of shaky reasoning confuses an implication with its converse.
textes.Non (tous) = au moins un ne… pas. Non (A: Not (all) = at least one is not. Not (A and B) = not A or not B; not (A or B) = not A and not B (De Morgan).
textes.Pour contredire « tous les cygnes sont b: To contradict "all swans are white", you do not need to prove that no swan is white: a single black swan is enough. The negation of "all" is "at least one is not". And the negation of "there exists" is "none".
textes.Par l'absurde : supposer le contraire, a: By contradiction: assume the opposite, reach a contradiction. Example: √2 is not a fraction.
textes.Pour prouver qu'une chose est vraie, on: To prove something true, you can assume it is false and show that this leads to a contradiction. If the opposite hypothesis cannot stand, it is false.
textes.Même opération des deux côtés jusqu'à is: Same operation on both sides until the unknown is isolated. Algebra comes from al-jabr, restoration (al-Khwarizmi, around 820).
textes.Une équation est une balance en équilibr: An equation is a balanced scale. You can do anything, as long as you do it to both sides. 3x + 5 = 20: take 5 from each side, 3x = 15; divide each side by 3, x = 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 5 = 20.
textes.Le mot algèbre vient de là. Vers 820, à: The word algebra comes from this. Around 820, in Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi wrote a treatise whose title names two moves: al-jabr, "restoration", which moves a subtracted term to the other side, and al-muqabala, "balancing", which removes the same quantity from both sides. Translated into Latin in 1145, al-jabr became algebra.
textes.Le carré qui oublie un morceau: The square that forgets a piece
textes.(a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² ; (a − b)² = a²: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b²; (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
textes.Les deux autres identités suivent : (a −: The other two identities follow: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². The last one is used to factorise: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). And it rescues mental arithmetic: 21 × 19 = 20² − 1² = 399.
textes.Δ = b² − 4ac : positif, deux solutions ;: Δ = b² − 4ac: positive, two solutions; zero, one; negative, no real one. Never divide by x: factorise.
textes.Une équation ax² + bx + c = 0 se règle a: An equation ax² + bx + c = 0 is solved with the discriminant Δ = b² − 4ac. If it is positive, two solutions, (−b ± √Δ) ÷ 2a; zero, just one; negative, none among the real numbers. For x² − 5x + 6 = 0: Δ = 25 − 24 = 1, and the solutions are 2 and 3.
textes.Médiane = valeur du milieu, insensible a: Median = middle value, insensitive to extremes. Mean pulled by extreme values.
textes.La moyenne additionne tout et divise ; l: The mean adds everything and divides; the median sorts the values and takes the middle one. In 2, 3, 3, 8, 100, the median is 3, the mean 23.2: the 100 pulls everything up. When Bill Gates walks into a bar, the customers' average wealth explodes; the median barely moves.
textes.Écart type = dispersion autour de la moy: Standard deviation = spread around the mean. Normal distribution: ≈ 68 % within one standard deviation, ≈ 95 % within two.
textes.Pour beaucoup de mesures, tailles ou err: For many measurements, heights or measurement errors, values follow a bell curve, the normal distribution. Then about 68 % of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean, and about 95 % within two. In the 19th century Adolphe Quetelet applied these tools to society and described an "average man".
textes.Un échantillon tiré au hasard vaut mieux: A randomly drawn sample beats a huge biased one (Literary Digest, 1936). Correlation is not causation.
textes.En 1936, le magazine Literary Digest int: In 1936 the Literary Digest magazine polled about 10 million Americans and received 2.4 million replies. Verdict: Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt won with about 61 % of the vote and every state but two. George Gallup, with about 50,000 people, had got it right.
textes.Le problème n'était pas la taille mais l: The problem was not the size but the selection: magazine readers, car owners, telephone users, Americans richer than average. A large biased sample stays biased. Random selection matters more than numbers. And even with a good sample, a correlation does not prove a cause: ice cream sales and drownings rise together in summer, because of the heat.
textes.a² + b² = c² dans un triangle rectangle: a² + b² = c² in a right triangle (3, 4, 5). Known to the Babylonians around 1800 BCE; proved by Euclid (I, 47).
textes.Dans un triangle rectangle, le carré du: In a right triangle, the square of the longest side, the hypotenuse, equals the sum of the squares of the other two: a² + b² = c². With 3 and 4 you get 9 + 16 = 25, so a hypotenuse of 5. It is the builders' triangle, which lets you lay out a right angle with a simple rope.
textes.Le nom est trompeur. La tablette babylon: The name is misleading. The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322, around 1800 BCE, already lists fifteen rows of triples like (3, 4, 5): more than a thousand years before Pythagoras. The oldest written proof that has come down to us is Euclid's, Book I of the Elements, proposition 47.
textes.Longueurs × k → aires × k², volumes × k³: Lengths × k → areas × k², volumes × k³. Disc: π r²; circle: 2 π r; sphere: 4/3 π r³.
textes.Doublez toutes les longueurs d'une figur: Double all the lengths of a shape: its area is multiplied by 4 (2 × 2), its volume by 8 (2 × 2 × 2). A cube with 3 cm sides is 27 cm³; a 6 cm cube is 216, eight times more.
textes.Mesurer la Terre avec une ombre: Measuring the Earth with a shadow
textes.SOH CAH TOA. cos 60° = 1/2. Ératosthène: SOH CAH TOA. cos 60° = 1/2. Eratosthenes: 7.2° = 1/50 of a turn, so the Earth is 50 times the Syene-Alexandria distance.
textes.Dans un triangle rectangle, les rapports: In a right triangle, the ratios of the sides depend only on the angle. Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent: SOH CAH TOA. Cut an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: the 60° angle has an adjacent side of 1 for a hypotenuse of 2, so cos 60° = 1/2.
textes.Avec un angle et une distance, on mesure: With an angle and a distance, you can measure the unreachable. In the 3rd century BCE, Eratosthenes knew that at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun lit the bottom of wells at Syene. The same day in Alexandria, a shadow made an angle of about 7.2°, one fiftieth of a turn. The two cities being 5,000 stadia apart, the Earth was therefore about 50 × 5,000 = 250,000 stadia around: a remarkably accurate order of magnitude.
textes.Une somme infinie peut être finie : 1/2: An infinite sum can be finite: 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 1. And 0.999… = 1 exactly.
Terms tending to 0 ≠ finite sum. The harmonic series diverges (Oresme, around 1350).
textes.Piège : que les termes tendent vers zéro: Trap: terms tending to zero is not enough. The harmonic series, 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + …, has smaller and smaller terms, and yet its sum exceeds any number.
textes.Nicole Oresme le démontre vers 1350 en r: Nicole Oresme proved it around 1350 by grouping the terms: 1/3 + 1/4 exceeds 1/2, 1/5 + … + 1/8 exceeds 1/2, 1/9 + … + 1/16 too, and so on. You stack infinitely many halves. Yet it grows very slowly: it takes more than 12,000 terms to exceed 10.
textes.Autant de pairs que d'entiers (correspon: As many even numbers as whole numbers (one-to-one pairing). More reals than whole numbers (Cantor, 1874; diagonal argument, 1891).
textes.Il y a autant de nombres pairs que de no: There are as many even numbers as whole numbers: pair them up one to one, 1 with 2, 2 with 4, n with 2n, and nobody is left alone. That is the spirit of Hilbert's hotel: full with infinitely many rooms, it still fits a guest by moving everyone along one room.
But not all infinities are equal. Georg Cantor showed as early as 1874 that the real numbers cannot be numbered, and in 1891 he gave the famous proof, the diagonal argument: assume a complete list, build a number that differs from the first at the 1st decimal, from the second at the 2nd, and so on. It is nowhere in the list. There are strictly more reals than whole numbers.
textes.Multiplier, c'est plus simple : on multi: Multiplying is simpler: multiply top and bottom, and half of a third is 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its inverse: 2 ÷ 1/2 = 2 × 2 = 4, since there are four halves in two. The Egyptians wrote almost everything as sums of fractions with numerator 1: 2/5 became 1/3 + 1/15. It can be seen on the Rhind papyrus, copied around 1550 BCE by the scribe Ahmes, which opens with a table of 2/n written as unit fractions.
textes.La règle de trois passe par l'unité. Si: The rule of three goes through the unit. If 3 kg cost €12, 1 kg costs €4, and 5 kg cost €20. A recipe for 4 that needs 300 g of flour needs 75 g per person, so 450 g for 6. Careful: it only works if the proportionality is real. Nine women do not make a baby in one month. The rule is very old: Chinese mathematicians knew it before the 2nd century, and it appears in The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art; Europe only adopted it much later.
textes.« S'il pleut, le sol est mouillé. » Cett: "If it rains, the ground is wet." This sentence is false in only one case: it rains and the ground is dry. If it does not rain, it says nothing: the ground can be dry or wet (from watering), the implication remains true. This definition goes back to Philo, a Greek logician of the so-called Dialectical school, active between the late 4th and mid-3rd century BCE: for him, an "if… then" is false only when the first part is true and the second false.
textes.Pour les « et » et les « ou », il y a le: For "and" and "or" there are De Morgan's laws, named after the logician Augustus De Morgan: "not (A and B)" is equivalent to "not A or not B", and "not (A or B)" to "not A and not B". Not being both rich and famous means not being rich, or not being famous, or neither. De Morgan stated them explicitly in 1847 in Formal Logic, but they were known long before: William of Ockham wrote them out in words in the 14th century.
textes.(a + b)² n'est pas a² + b². Dessinez un: (a + b)² is not a² + b². Draw a square of side a + b: it holds an a² square, a b² square, and two a × b rectangles. Hence (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². The 2ab is the piece people forget. With a = 3 and b = 4: 49, not 25. This drawing is Proposition 4 of Book II of Euclid's Elements, around 300 BCE: "the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments".
textes.C'est pourquoi on parle souvent de salai: That is why people often speak of the median salary. When the mean salary is above the median, it means a few high salaries are pulling the mean up, and most people earn less than the mean, not more. The word median, in statistics, is owed to the Briton Francis Galton, in the late 19th century.
textes.C'est la réponse au paradoxe de Zénon :: That is the answer to Zeno's paradox: to catch the tortoise, Achilles has to cover infinitely many stages, but their durations form a finite sum, and he catches it. The paradox dates from the 5th century BCE, with Zeno of Elea; Aristotle reports it to us, in his Physics. It is also why 0.999… with infinitely many 9s equals 1: it is the sum 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1,000 + …, which equals exactly 1.
textes.C'est pour cela qu'un éléphant n'est pas: That is why an elephant is not an enlarged mouse. If a mouse doubled in size, its weight, which follows volume, would be multiplied by 8, but the cross-section of its bones, which follows area, only by 4. Galileo had already noticed: large animals have proportionally thicker bones. He was the first to describe this square-cube law, in 1638, in his Two New Sciences. For the circle, remember area π r² and circumference 2 π r; for the sphere, volume 4/3 π r³.
textes.Quand deux opérations ont la même priori: When two operations have the same priority, you go from left to right. 6 ÷ 2 × 3 is 3 × 3 = 9, not 6 ÷ 6 = 1. It is not a law of nature but a writing rule, adopted so that everyone reads the same calculation the same way. When in doubt, a pair of brackets costs less than an argument. This rule is recent: multiplication has come before addition since the algebraic notation of the 17th century, and the name order of operations only took hold in the late 19th or early 20th century, with school textbooks. In the 1920s people still argued over whether multiplication came before division.
textes.Une hausse de t % multiplie par (1 + t/1: A rise of t % multiplies by (1 + t/100), a fall by (1 − t/100). +25 % is × 1.25; −20 % is × 0.8. To chain changes, you multiply the coefficients; you do not add the percentages. The Romans already counted in hundredths: the emperor Augustus levied a one-hundredth tax on auction sales, the centesima rerum venalium. The % sign comes from the Italian per cento, gradually shortened into two small circles separated by a line.
textes.Deux classes peuvent avoir la même moyen: Two classes can have the same mean, 10 out of 20, one where everyone has between 9 and 11, the other split between 2s and 18s. The standard deviation measures this spread around the mean: small, the values are tight; large, they are scattered. The term standard deviation was coined by Karl Pearson, who first used it in print in 1894; Gauss spoke of the "mean error".
textes.1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + … : chaque term: 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + 1/16 + …: each term fills half of what is missing to reach 1. The sum gets as close as you like without ever going over: it equals exactly 1. Infinitely many terms can therefore give a finite result. Archimedes already used a sum of this kind to find the area of a piece of parabola.
textes.Al-Khwârizmî résolvait déjà ces équation: Al-Khwarizmi already solved these equations by "completing the square". Yet the oldest traces are much older: around 2000 BCE, Babylonian clay tablets solve problems about the sides and areas of rectangles with steps that amount to our formula. Letters came much later: at the end of the 16th century François Viète used vowels for unknowns and consonants for known quantities, before Descartes imposed x, y, z. A trap to keep in mind: dividing both sides by x loses the solution x = 0; factorise instead.
textes.L'exemple le plus célèbre : √2 n'est pas: The most famous example: √2 is not a fraction. Suppose √2 = a/b, a fully simplified fraction. Then a² = 2b², so a is even; writing it as 2k, we find b² = 2k², so b is even too. But a simplified fraction cannot have two even terms: contradiction. Aristotle already alludes to this argument. That was around 350 BCE, in the Prior Analytics, where he describes proof "by the impossible".
