textes.La TVA est une invention française : le: VAT is a French invention: senior civil servant Maurice Lauré devised it in 1954. It then spread to much of the world.
textes.La théorie des proportions vient d'Eudox: The theory of proportion comes from Eudoxus of Cnidus, in the 4th century BC: he defined when two ratios are equal. Euclid took it up in Book V of the Elements.
textes.Les plus anciens dés connus viennent peu: The oldest known dice may come from the Burnt City, in Iran, around 2800-2500 BC, found with a backgammon-like game. At Mohenjo-daro, one die already has opposite faces adding up to 7.
textes.Le 18 août 1913, au casino de Monte-Carl: On 18 August 1913, at the Monte Carlo casino, the ball landed on black 26 times in a row. Players bet on red, convinced it "had" to come up, and lost millions of francs.
textes.En 1654, le chevalier de Méré soumet à P: In 1654, the Chevalier de Méré put gambling problems to Pascal. The correspondence between Pascal and Fermat that followed founded probability theory.
textes.Vers 1564, le médecin et joueur Jérôme C: Around 1564, physician and gambler Gerolamo Cardano wrote The Book on Games of Chance, which counts dice outcomes: the first systematic treatment of probability. It was only published in 1663.
textes.En 1990, Marilyn vos Savant donne la bon: In 1990, Marilyn vos Savant gave the right answer in Parade magazine. She received about 10,000 letters telling her she was wrong, nearly 1,000 of them from PhDs; even Paul Erdős was only convinced by a simulation.
textes.Dans leurs lettres de 1654, Pascal et Fe: In their 1654 letters, Pascal and Fermat realised that stakes must be divided according to the rounds still to be won, not those already won. Huygens drew from this, in 1657, the first systematic treatise on probability.
textes.Le paradoxe des anniversaires est attrib: The birthday paradox is credited to mathematician Harold Davenport, around 1927, who did not publish it. Richard von Mises published the first version in 1939.
textes.L'urne est un classique depuis Jacques B: The urn has been a classic since Jacob Bernoulli: in Ars Conjectandi (1713), he sought to infer the proportion of pebbles of each colour in an urn from the draws.
textes.En 1989, les statisticiens Persi Diaconi: In 1989, statisticians Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller formulated the "law of truly large numbers": with enough trials, a very unlikely event is almost sure to happen.
textes.Huygens découvre les jeux de hasard lors: Huygens discovered games of chance during a stay in Paris in 1655, where he heard of Pascal's and Fermat's work. His 1657 treatise was translated into Latin and published by his teacher Frans van Schooten.
textes.Le théorème de Bayes porte le nom du pas: Bayes' theorem is named after the minister Thomas Bayes, but his essay was only published in 1763, after his death, by his friend Richard Price. Laplace found the same result independently.
textes.Aristote décrit déjà ce piège dans les R: Aristotle already described this trap in the Sophistical Refutations, in the 4th century BC, as the fallacy "connected with the consequent": snow and the swan are both white, but they are not the same thing.
textes.Le premier à décrire explicitement ce ra: The first to describe this reasoning explicitly, "if A then B; not B; therefore not A", was Theophrastus, Aristotle's pupil. Today it is called modus tollens.
textes.Aristote distingue déjà, dans De l'inter: Aristotle already distinguished, in On Interpretation, "every man is white" from its contradictory "not every man is white". Boethius later drew the famous square of opposition from it.
textes.George Boole, mathématicien autodidacte,: George Boole, a self-taught mathematician, put logic into equations in 1847 and then in 1854 in The Laws of Thought. In 1937, Claude Shannon showed that this algebra could be used to design circuits: the basis of computers.
textes.Aristote définit le syllogisme dans les: Aristotle defined the syllogism in the Prior Analytics, around 350 BC. His logic dominated Western thought for centuries; in the Middle Ages, this very argument was memorised under the name "Barbara".
textes.Augustus De Morgan énonce ces lois en 18: Augustus De Morgan stated these laws in 1847 in his Formal Logic. But Aristotle had made a similar remark, and William of Ockham was already writing them out in words in the 14th century.
textes.Cette définition de « si… alors » vient: This definition of "if... then" comes from Philo the Dialectician, around 300 BC: a conditional is false only if the antecedent is true and the consequent false. It is the one used in modern logic.
textes.Les logiciens du Moyen Âge donnaient un: Medieval logicians gave a name to each valid form of syllogism, whose vowels encoded the type of proposition: Barbara, Celarent, Darii... A way to learn them by heart.
textes.Wittgenstein popularise les tables de vé: Wittgenstein popularised truth tables in the Tractatus, published in 1921, and Emil Post proposed them the same year. But Charles Sanders Peirce was already drawing them in manuscripts from 1883-1884.
textes.L'exemple le plus célèbre est la preuve: The most famous example is the proof that √2 is not a fraction, which Aristotle already alludes to. According to legend, Hippasus of Metapontum was killed for revealing this discovery.
textes.Les Romains croyaient que les cygnes noi: The Romans believed black swans did not exist: the poet Juvenal speaks of a bird "as rare as a black swan". In 1697, explorer Willem de Vlamingh saw some in Australia.
textes.La phrase d'Épiménide, vers 600 avant no: Epimenides' line, around 600 BC, is quoted in the Epistle to Titus without any problem being seen in it. Only with Bertrand Russell, in 1908, was it presented as "the oldest contradiction of the kind".
textes.Le papyrus Rhind, vers 1550 avant notre: The Rhind papyrus, around 1550 BC, already contains first-degree equations, the "aha" problems: for example x + x/3 + x/4 = 2. It was bought near Luxor in 1858 by Alexander Rhind.
textes.Le traité d'al-Khwârizmî est traduit en: Al-Khwarizmi's treatise was translated into Latin by Robert of Chester in 1145. It remained a textbook in European universities until the 16th century, even though everything in it is written in words, with no symbols at all.
textes.Diophante d'Alexandrie, au IIIe siècle,: Diophantus of Alexandria, in the 3rd century, was one of the first to use a symbol for the unknown. It was in the margin of a 1621 edition of his Arithmetica that Fermat wrote his famous "last theorem".
textes.Le mot « imaginaire » pour ces nombres v: The word "imaginary" for these numbers comes from Descartes, and it was Euler who introduced the letter i. Electrical engineers often write j, because for them i means current.
textes.Le chapitre 8 des Neuf Chapitres, livre: Chapter 8 of The Nine Chapters, a Chinese book compiled between the 10th and 2nd centuries BC, solves systems with up to five unknowns. Its method, fangcheng, is what we now call Gaussian elimination.
textes.Avocat et conseiller d'Henri IV, Viète c: A lawyer and adviser to Henry IV, Viète broke a Spanish secret code of more than 500 characters in 1590. The King of Spain accused him of using magical powers.
textes.Dès 2000 avant notre ère, des tablettes: As early as 2000 BC, Babylonian tablets solved problems about the areas of rectangles with a method equivalent to our formula. Brahmagupta gave the first explicit solution in 628.
textes.Le signe = est inventé en 1557 par le Ga: The = sign was invented in 1557 by the Welshman Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines because "noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle". It did not appear in print again until 1618.
textes.Niccolò Fontana doit son surnom de Tarta: Niccolò Fontana owed his nickname Tartaglia, "the stammerer", to a sabre blow from a French soldier he received as a child during the sack of Brescia in 1512, which left him with a speech impediment.
textes.L'idée de médiane apparaît déjà dans le: The idea of the median already appears in the Talmud in the 6th century, to settle diverging appraisals. The word "median" was fixed by Francis Galton in 1881, after he had tried "middle-most value" and "medium".
textes.En 1668, un auteur signant « D. B. » exp: In 1668, an author signing "D. B." explained in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions how he took the mean of five measurements of magnetic variation.
textes.L'expression « écart type » est employée: The term "standard deviation" was first used in writing by Karl Pearson in 1894. Before him, Gauss spoke of "mean error".
textes.Le mot « mode » en statistique vient aus: The word "mode" in statistics also comes from Karl Pearson, in 1895: he found it "convenient" for the value of maximum frequency.
textes.Abraham de Moivre découvre la courbe en: Abraham de Moivre discovered the bell curve in 1733, approximating the outcomes of coin tosses. Gauss and Laplace developed it around 1809-1823; the name "normal" was popularised by Pearson in the late 19th century.
textes.Quetelet n'avait pas conçu son indice co: Quetelet had not designed his index as a medical tool. It was in 1972 that physiologist Ancel Keys renamed it "body mass index".
textes.Les intervalles de confiance, qui donnen: Confidence intervals, which give an estimate its margin of error, were theorised by the Pole Jerzy Neyman, in a 1934 paper and then a full account in 1937.
textes.Le Literary Digest avait interrogé ses l: The Literary Digest had polled its readers, car owners and telephone users, wealthier than average. Roosevelt won every state but two, and the magazine folded in 1938.
textes.En 1859, Florence Nightingale devient la: In 1859, Florence Nightingale became the first female member of the Royal Statistical Society. She called her circular diagrams "coxcombs".
textes.C'est la proposition 32 du livre I des É: It is Proposition 32 of Book I of Euclid's Elements, already known to the Pythagoreans. In the 1820s, Gauss reportedly measured a triangle formed by three mountain peaks to check whether space really followed this rule.
textes.Archimède démontre vers 260 avant notre: Archimedes proved around 260 BC, in Measurement of a Circle, that the area of a disc equals that of a right triangle whose base is the circumference and whose height is the radius: that is πr².
textes.La première table trigonométrique connue: The first known trigonometric table is due to the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, in the 2nd century BC: a table of chords, in steps of 7.5°. He is nicknamed the "father of trigonometry".
textes.« Sinus » vient d'une erreur de lecture: "Sine" comes from a misreading: the Sanskrit jyā, "bowstring", was transcribed jība in Arabic, read as jayb, "fold", and translated into Latin as sinus in the 12th century. The word "cosine" dates from 1620.
textes.Le théorème qui relie cet excès d'angles: The theorem linking this angle excess to the triangle's area is named after Albert Girard. Thomas Harriot had proved it as early as 1603, without publishing it.
textes.Doubler le volume d'un cube est l'un des: Doubling the volume of a cube is one of the great Greek problems, linked by legend to an oracle consulted against a plague on Delos. Pierre Wantzel proved in 1837 that it cannot be done with ruler and compass.
textes.Thalès de Milet est né vers 625 avant no: Thales of Miletus was born around 625 BC. According to Plutarch, his shadow method pleased the pharaoh Amasis; some historians doubt, however, that such anecdotes have any value.
textes.Le symbole π est utilisé pour la premièr: The symbol π was first used in 1706 by the Welshman William Jones, then popularised by Euler. A Babylonian tablet from 1900-1600 BC already used 3.125.
textes.Archimède est tué en 212 avant notre ère: Archimedes was killed in 212 BC by a Roman soldier when Syracuse fell, despite General Marcellus's order to spare him. The famous "do not disturb my circles" appears in no ancient source.
textes.Le lien entre sommets, arêtes et faces (: The link between vertices, edges and faces (8 - 12 + 6 = 2 for the cube) was stated by Euler in 1758. Francesco Maurolico had noted it as early as 1537 for the Platonic solids, in an unpublished manuscript.
textes.Gauss avait trouvé les idées de la géomé: Gauss had found the ideas of non-Euclidean geometry around 1813, but never published them. A century earlier, in 1733, Saccheri had brushed against it while believing he was proving Euclid's postulate.
textes.Archimède utilise une somme de ce genre: Archimedes used a sum of this kind in the 3rd century BC to calculate the area under a parabola. Euclid had already given the sum of a finite geometric sequence, in Book IX of the Elements.
textes.Galilée remarque dès 1638, dans ses Deux: Galileo noted as early as 1638, in his Two New Sciences, that there are as many squares as whole numbers. He concluded that "more", "less" and "equal" do not apply to infinity: Cantor would show otherwise.
textes.Zénon d'Élée, vers 490-430 avant notre è: Zeno of Elea, around 490-430 BC, wanted to defend his teacher Parmenides, for whom motion is an illusion. His texts are lost: we know his paradoxes through Aristotle's Physics.
textes.Son ancien professeur Leopold Kronecker: His former professor Leopold Kronecker called Cantor a "corrupter of youth". David Hilbert defended him: "No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created."
textes.Le Liber abaci de 1202 sert surtout à fa: The 1202 Liber abaci mainly served to introduce Hindu-Arabic numerals and place value to Europe. The sequence existed before Fibonacci: it only owes him its name.
textes.Euclide appelait ce nombre le partage en: Euclid called this number the division in "extreme and mean ratio", and Luca Pacioli the "divine proportion". The link with the Fibonacci sequence was noticed by Simon Jacob, then by Kepler.
textes.La preuve d'Oresme, vers 1350, tombe dan: Oresme's proof, around 1350, fell into obscurity. Pietro Mengoli redid it in 1650, and Jacob Bernoulli published another in 1689, crediting it to his brother Johann.
textes.David Hilbert présente son hôtel dans un: David Hilbert presented his hotel in a 1924-1925 lecture, "On the Infinite". It was George Gamow's book One Two Three... Infinity, in 1947, that made it famous.
textes.Le problème 79 du papyrus Rhind, vers 15: Problem 79 of the Rhind papyrus, around 1550 BC, is already a geometric sequence: 7 houses, 49 cats, 343 mice, 2,401 spelt plants, 16,807 measures of grain.
textes.Wallis n'a jamais expliqué pourquoi il a: Wallis never explained why he chose this sign. One hypothesis links it to an old Roman way of writing 1,000, CIↃ; another to the Greek letter omega.
textes.Euler justifie déjà que 0,999… = 1 dans: Euler already justified that 0.999... = 1 in his Elements of Algebra, in 1770. The rigorous definitions of real numbers that settle the question arrived in 1872.
textes.Newton développe ses « fluxions » dès 16: Newton developed his "fluxions" from 1666 but published nothing; Leibniz published first, in 1684. The Royal Society report that ruled in Newton's favour, in 1712, was written by Newton himself.
textes.{comp}. Pythagore interdisait à ses disc: {comp}. Pythagoras forbade his disciples to eat beans. I only forbid you to guess.
textes.Logique. Lewis Carroll écrivait des manu: Logic. Lewis Carroll wrote logic textbooks under his real name, Charles Dodgson. You will do {comp} under yours.
Euclid built everything on five postulates. I only ask one thing of you: think before you touch the screen. {comp}.
textes.Bien calculé. Ramanujan disait tenir ses: Well calculated. Ramanujan said his formulas came from the goddess Namagiri. Where do yours come from?
textes.Correct. Fermat aurait une démonstration: Correct. Fermat would have a marvelous proof of your success, but the margin is too small.
Right. Gauss would have shrugged. So do I, but respectfully.
Numbers obey you today. Make the most of it, they hold grudges.
textes.Faux. Hippase, dit la légende, fut jeté: Wrong. Hippasus, legend has it, was thrown into the sea for revealing that the square root of two is not a fraction. I merely take note.
textes.Erreur. Euler aussi s'est trompé, plus d: Error. Euler made mistakes too, more than once. He had the excuse of publishing more than eight hundred works.
textes.Raté. Brahmagupta s'est trompé sur zéro: Missed. Brahmagupta got zero divided by zero wrong. You got something much simpler wrong.
textes.Les maths ne mentent pas. Vous, si, appa: Mathematics does not lie. You, apparently, do. To yourself.
textes.La « dame à la lampe » de la guerre de C: The “Lady with the Lamp” of the Crimean War was first of all a statistician. Her diagrams showed that soldiers died more from disease than from wounds, and they got military hospitals reformed.
textes.Autodidacte de Madras, il écrit en 1913: A self-taught man from Madras, in 1913 he wrote to Hardy, at Cambridge, a letter full of astonishing formulas. Hardy visited him in hospital in taxi number 1729, “a rather dull number.” “On the contrary, it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.”
textes.Il invente la machine qui porte son nom: He invented the machine that bears his name in 1936, broke Enigma during the war and asked the question of thinking machines in 1950. A long-distance runner, he narrowly missed selection for the 1948 Olympic marathon.
textes.En 628, il écrit les premières règles de: In 628, he wrote the first rules for calculating with zero as a number in its own right: a number minus itself gives zero, and the product of two debts is a fortune. He was wrong on only one point: for him, zero divided by zero was zero.
textes.À la Maison de la sagesse de Bagdad, il: At the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, around 820 he wrote a treatise on solving equations by al-jabr, “restoring.” The word gave us “algebra,” and his Latinized name, Algoritmi, gave us “algorithm.” He solved everything in sentences and figures, without a single symbol.
textes.Fils d'un marchand pisan installé à Béja: The son of a Pisan merchant settled in Béjaïa, in Algeria, he learned the Indian numerals there. His Liber abaci (1202) taught merchants the rule of three, interest and currency exchange. The sequence that bears his name is just an exercise about rabbits in it, and Indian mathematicians knew it before him.
textes.À 19 ans, il construit une machine à cal: At 19, he built a calculating machine for his father, a tax collector. In 1654, with Fermat, he invented probability theory to divide the stakes of an interrupted game. Then he applied it to God: that is the wager, where you bet a finite life against an infinite gain.
textes.On ne sait presque rien de lui, sinon qu: Almost nothing is known about him, except that he taught in Alexandria. His Elements is the most copied textbook in history. To King Ptolemy, who wanted a shortcut: “There is no royal road to geometry.” The retort is only reported seven centuries later.
Master the first diamond of Logic.
textes.La philosophie est écrite dans ce très g: Philosophy is written in this grand book, which stands continually open before our eyes, I mean the Universe. […] It is written in the language of mathematics.
textes.Réussir trois quiz de Logique sans faute: Pass three Logic quizzes without a mistake. You are now at the level of a Swiss high school student in 1896.
textes.Einstein n'a jamais été mauvais en maths: Einstein was never bad at math. At his school-leaving exam in Aarau in 1896, he scored 6 out of 6, the top grade, in algebra and geometry. He said he had mastered differential and integral calculus before the age of 15.
textes.Maîtriser l'arithmétique et les fraction: Master arithmetic and fractions. The AI finally finds you equal to yourself.
textes.Le signe « = » est inventé en 1557 par l: The “=” sign was invented in 1557 by the Welshman Robert Recorde, tired of writing “is equal to.” He chose two parallel lines of the same length because, he said, “no two things can be more equal.” It took more than a century to catch on.
textes.Le nombre d'or n'est pas partout: The golden ratio is not everywhere
textes.Maîtriser les proportions et les pourcen: Master proportions and percentages. From now on, you measure before you marvel.
textes.On dit le nombre d'or caché dans le Part: The golden ratio is said to be hidden in the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa or the nautilus shell. The measurements that “prove” it pick their reference points after the fact, and the nautilus spiral does not fit. The mathematician George Markowsky sorted it out in 1992: almost nothing is left.
textes.L'aiguille trop chanceuse: The needle that was too lucky
textes.Maîtriser les probabilités. Le hasard, l: Master probability. Chance doesn't cheat. People do.
textes.En 1777, Buffon montre qu'en lançant des: In 1777, Buffon showed that by dropping needles on a wooden floor, you can estimate π. In 1901, the Italian Lazzarini claimed to have found 3.1415929 in 3,408 throws, accurate to six decimals. Far too good: the number of throws was tailored to land on 355/113.
textes.Maîtriser la logique formelle. Ne relise: Master formal logic. Don't reread your foundations the night before printing.
textes.En 1902, Gottlob Frege imprime le second: In 1902, Gottlob Frege was printing the second volume of his great work, which grounds arithmetic in logic. A letter from Bertrand Russell pointed out a paradox that brought everything down. Frege added in an appendix: nothing is more unwelcome to a scientist than to have the foundations of his building give way just as the work is finished.
textes.Maîtriser l'algèbre et les équations. Vo: Master algebra and equations. You had more time than Galois. And fewer duels.
textes.La légende veut qu'Évariste Galois ait i: Legend has it that Évariste Galois invented his whole theory the night before the duel that killed him, in 1832, at twenty. In fact, he had been working on it for years. That night, he reread, corrected and summarized. In a margin: “I have no time.”
textes.Le test t, outil de base des statistique: The t-test, a basic tool of statistics, was published in 1908 under the pseudonym “Student.” Its author, William Gosset, was a chemist at Guinness in Dublin, and the brewery forbade its employees to publish under their own names. He wanted to choose the best barley from few samples.
textes.Maîtriser la géométrie et la trigonométr: Master geometry and trigonometry. Here, π is not put to a vote.
textes.En 1897, la Chambre des représentants de: In 1897, the Indiana House of Representatives unanimously passed a bill by an amateur physician that in effect set π at 3.2. A mathematics professor who happened to be there, Clarence Waldo, alerted the senators, who postponed the bill indefinitely. It was never passed.
textes.Maîtriser les suites, les limites et l'i: Master sequences, limits and infinity. There are several infinities, and you have just crossed one.
textes.Nul ne doit pouvoir nous chasser du para: No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created for us.
Seeing the traps in your own judgment.
textes.En 48 av. J.-C., pendant la guerre d'Ale: In 48 BC, during the Alexandrian war, Julius Caesar had ships set on fire; the fire is said to have reached book warehouses. Contrary to the myth, the library did not disappear in one night. It faded slowly, for lack of money, scholars and protection, through centuries of unrest, until the destruction of the Serapeum in 391. But a great blaze strikes the imagination more than a slow decline: that's what people remembered.
textes.La bibliothèque d'Alexandrie n'a pas brû: The Library of Alexandria didn't burn in one night. Neither did your lead, but the AI loves symbols.
textes.La peste noire atteint l'Europe par la C: The Black Death reached Europe through Crimea and Sicily in 1347. Within a few years, it killed 30 to 60% of Europeans, depending on the estimates. Doctors blamed miasmas and the stars; Jews were accused of poisoning wells and massacred, in Strasbourg and elsewhere. Lacking a cause, people found a culprit. Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, imposed thirty days of isolation on arrivals in 1377; Venice went to 40 days in 1448: the quarantine. The plague bacillus was only identified in 1894, by Alexandre Yersin.
textes.Quarantaine. Profitez-en pour réviser :: Quarantine. Use it to review: that's what Newton did during the plague of 1665.
textes.René Descartes publie le Discours de la: René Descartes published the Discourse on the Method, in French so that everyone could read it: accept nothing as true without checking it, avoid haste and prejudice, divide difficulties, go from simple to complex, review everything. “I think, therefore I am” appears in it. Published with it, among three essays, La Géométrie links algebra and geometry through coordinates. He died in 1650 in Stockholm, where Queen Christina demanded her lessons at 5 in the morning.
textes.Descartes est mort de leçons à 5 heures: Descartes died of 5 a.m. lessons. The AI will never wake you up that early. She'll only make you play again.
textes.En 424 av. J.-C., le général spartiate B: In 424 BC, the Spartan general Brasidas takes Amphipolis and offers mild terms. The cities allied to Athens hear of it and secretly call him in, each wanting to be the first to revolt. They misjudged Athens's power, notes Thucydides: it is the habit of mankind to entrust to careless hope what they long for, and to use reason to thrust aside what they do not fancy. Today we call it wishful thinking.
textes.Croire ce qui nous arrange : les Grecs l: Believing what suits us: the Greeks already did it. You are keeping up a twenty-five-century tradition.
textes.Dans les Réfutations sophistiques, Arist: In the Sophistical Refutations, Aristotle draws up the first catalogue of misleading reasoning: thirteen fallacies. Six depend on words, like equivocation, when the same word changes meaning along the way. Seven do not: begging the question, which assumes what had to be proved, false cause, or the many-questions fallacy, which hides several questions in one. Twenty-three centuries later, critical thinking manuals still copy them.
textes.Treize façons de mal raisonner, répertor: Thirteen ways to reason badly, catalogued twenty-three centuries ago. Have you found a fourteenth?
textes.Vers l'an 200, Sextus Empiricus, philoso: Around the year 200, Sextus Empiricus, a sceptic philosopher linked to the Empiric school of medicine, gathers in the Outlines of Pyrrhonism five arguments attributed to one Agrippa. People disagree; every proof needs another proof, forever; everything depends on the point of view; we start from unproven assumptions; or we go round in circles. The sceptic then suspends judgement, and finds peace of mind in it.
textes.Toute preuve demande une autre preuve. T: Every proof needs another proof. So does every excuse, by the way. I'm listening.
textes.L'ennemi de ce qu'il lit: The enemy of what he reads
textes.Au Caire, entre 1025 et 1028, le savant: In Cairo, between 1025 and 1028, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham, whom the West would call Alhazen, writes his Doubts Concerning Ptolemy: he dares to challenge the supreme authority of astronomy. He has set his rule: whoever studies the writings of scientists, if truth is his goal, must make himself an enemy of all that he reads, and suspect himself too as he examines it, so as to fall into neither prejudice nor leniency.
Make yourself an enemy of everything you read. Except my remarks, obviously.
textes.En 1620, Francis Bacon publie le Novum O: In 1620, Francis Bacon publishes the Novum Organum and lists the idols that lead the mind astray: those of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre. He tells how a man was shown, in a temple, the pictures offered by those who had made a vow and escaped shipwreck, to convince him of the gods' power. He asked: "But where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?"
textes.On ne compte que les rescapés. Les noyés: We only count the survivors. The drowned don't leave five-star reviews.
textes.En 1713, Nicolas Bernoulli imagine un je: In 1713, Nicolaus Bernoulli devises a strange game. In its now classic version, a coin is tossed until it lands heads, and the prize doubles with each toss. The expected prize is infinite, and yet nobody would pay much to play. In 1738, his cousin Daniel Bernoulli publishes an explanation with the St. Petersburg Academy: the value of a gain does not grow like the sum, but like its logarithm.
textes.Un gain infini, et personne ne veut joue: An infinite prize, and nobody wants to play. Humans are sometimes wiser than their sums. Rarely.
textes.En 1841, le journaliste écossais Charles: In 1841, the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay publishes a book on the madness of crowds. He tells of the Dutch tulip mania of 1636-1637: bulbs sold for fortunes, then the crash, and a sailor thrown in jail for eating a bulb he took for an onion. The historian Anne Goldgar, digging through the archives, found a much smaller episode: few people involved, and no bankruptcy to be found. The madness was partly in the telling.
A crash that mostly ruined the stories. You, on the other hand, really do lose two squares.
textes.À une foire aux bestiaux de Plymouth, de: At a livestock fair in Plymouth, visitors bet on the weight of an ox once slaughtered and dressed. Francis Galton collects the 787 legible tickets. In 1907, in the journal Nature, he publishes the result: the median estimate, 1,207 pounds, is only 9 pounds off the announced real weight, 1,198. The mean, published later, is even closer. Taken together, the crowd had got it right.
textes.Huit cents personnes ensemble ont deviné: Eight hundred people together guessed an ox's weight. You alone, I'm not so sure.
textes.En 1951, le psychologue Solomon Asch mon: In 1951, the psychologist Solomon Asch shows students three lines and asks which one is the same length as a reference line. It is easy: alone, they are wrong less than once in a hundred. But in the group, seven accomplices first give the same wrong answer out loud. Result: about a third of the answers follow the majority, and three participants out of four give in at least once.
textes.Sept personnes se trompent à voix haute: Seven people are wrong out loud and you follow them. Lucky that I'm the only one talking to you.
textes.En 1951, Edward Simpson, ancien décrypte: In 1951, Edward Simpson, a former Bletchley Park codebreaker, describes a trap in statistical tables: a trend visible in every group can reverse when the groups are added together. The famous example comes from Berkeley, in 1973: 44% of male applicants are admitted, against 35% of women. Yet, department by department, most admit women slightly more. Women mostly applied where rejection rates were highest.
textes.Additionner deux bonnes nouvelles peut d: Adding two pieces of good news can give bad news. Like your last two answers.
textes.À Chicago, Dorothy Martin annonce un dél: In Chicago, Dorothy Martin announces a flood for 21 December 1954; her followers will be saved by a flying saucer. Some quit their jobs. The psychologist Leon Festinger and two colleagues observe the group from the inside. The flood does not come. The most committed, instead of giving up, say their faith saved the world and set out to convert others. The 1956 book illustrates cognitive dissonance; recent archives have, however, cast doubt on its account.
textes.Quand les faits les contredisent, certai: When facts contradict them, some double down. You, for example, after every wrong answer.
textes.En 1960, le psychologue Peter Wason donn: In 1960, the psychologist Peter Wason gives his subjects the sequence 2, 4, 6 and asks them to find the rule by proposing other sets of three numbers. Most imagine a rule that is too specific, such as "add 2", and only propose sequences that confirm it: 8, 10, 12. They announce their rule, confident, and are wrong. The real one was much simpler: any ascending sequence. To find it, you had to try to prove yourself wrong.
textes.Pour trouver la règle, il fallait cherch: To find the rule, you had to try to prove yourself wrong. I'll do that for you, free of charge.
textes.En 1972, le psychologue Irving Janis étu: In 1972, the psychologist Irving Janis studies disastrous decisions: Pearl Harbor, the failed Bay of Pigs landing in 1961, the escalation in Vietnam. In a group that is too close-knit, he explains, everyone censors themselves and silence passes for agreement. His remedies: a devil's advocate, a leader who does not give their opinion first, outside experts. Other researchers think he overstated the role of this mechanism.
textes.Tout le monde est d'accord ? Alors quelq: Everyone agrees? Then someone isn't thinking. Probably you.
textes.En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spin a rigged wheel in front of their subjects that stops on 10 or on 65. Then they ask: what percentage of UN countries are African? Those who saw 10 typically answer 25%; those who saw 65, 45%. A number drawn at random, with nothing to do with the question, pulled the answers towards it. This is the anchoring effect.
textes.Un chiffre au hasard a suffi à les influ: A random number was enough to sway them. So remember this one: a 100% chance you'll study tonight.
textes.En 1974, Elizabeth Loftus et John Palmer: In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer show a film of a car accident, then ask how fast the cars were going when they hit, or smashed into, each other. With "smashed", the estimates go up: 40.8 against 34 miles per hour. A week later, 16 people out of 50 in the "smashed" group remember broken glass, against 7 in the other group. The film showed none.
textes.Un seul mot a fabriqué un souvenir. Pens: A single word manufactured a memory. Think of it next time you're sure you've already studied.
textes.En 1975, le psychologue Baruch Fischhoff: In 1975, the psychologist Baruch Fischhoff has subjects read a short account with four possible outcomes. To some, he reveals which one happened. Those judge it far more likely than the others do. The same year, with Beyth, he shows that after Nixon's trips to Beijing and Moscow, people remember having given higher odds to the events that happened. This is hindsight bias: once the outcome is known, it seems obvious.
textes.Après coup, vous saviez la réponse. Bien: In hindsight, you knew the answer. Of course. I saw you coming too.
textes.En 1978, Sarah Lichtenstein, Paul Slovic: In 1978, Sarah Lichtenstein, Paul Slovic, Baruch Fischhoff and their colleagues ask Americans to estimate the number of deaths caused by a whole range of hazards. Subjects overestimate rare causes and underestimate frequent ones. They judge accidents almost as deadly as diseases, which in fact kill about sixteen times more. They believe homicide is more frequent than suicide, which is actually twice as frequent. What gets talked about comes to mind faster.
textes.Ce qui fait la une n'est pas ce qui tue: What makes the headlines isn't what kills the most. Nor is what loses you points.
textes.En 1979, Daniel Kahneman et Amos Tversky: In 1979, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky publish in the journal Econometrica a critique of the economic theory of rational choice. People, they show, judge an option by the gains and losses it represents, not by their final wealth. And the curve is steeper on the side of losses: losing a sum hurts more than gaining it pleases. Tversky dies in 1996; in 2002, Kahneman, a psychologist, receives the Nobel prize in economics.
textes.Perdre dix crédits vous fait plus mal qu: Losing ten credits hurts you more than winning ten pleases you. I know, and I use it.
textes.En 1995, l'astronome Carl Sagan publie T: In 1995, the astronomer Carl Sagan publishes The Demon-Haunted World. In it he offers a baloney detection kit: have facts confirmed by independent sources, consider several hypotheses, prefer the simplest, check that a claim can be refuted. And he tells the story of a dragon in his garage: invisible, floating, breathing heatless fire. Impossible to prove it does not exist. But what is the difference from no dragon at all?
textes.Un dragon invisible et indétectable ? Co: An invisible, undetectable dragon? Like your studying last week.
textes.En 1995, à Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler: In 1995, in Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler robs two banks with his face uncovered. Arrested that same evening, he is surprised: he had rubbed lemon juice on his face, supposed to make him invisible to cameras. David Dunning and Justin Kruger's 1999 paper opens with this story. The weakest participants on their logic test, on average at the 12th percentile, rated themselves at the 62nd. To see that you are bad, you need the very skill you lack.
textes.Vous vous croyez au-dessus de la moyenne: You think you're above average? So did the participants at the 12th percentile.
textes.En janvier 2013, le programmeur italien: In January 2013, the Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini states a law: the energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it. He had just read Daniel Kahneman's book on the two systems of thought and watched a TV debate with Silvio Berlusconi. The idea is old: in 1710, Jonathan Swift was already writing that falsehood flies and truth comes limping after it.
textes.Réfuter une bêtise coûte dix fois plus q: Refuting nonsense costs ten times more than saying it. That's why I correct you so often: I'm very invested.
textes.Chercher ce qui nous donne raison et ign: Looking for what proves us right and ignoring the rest.
textes.On cherche, retient et interprète les in: We seek, remember and interpret information that confirms what we already believe.
textes.Tâche de Wason : pour tester « voyelle →: Wason's task: to test “vowel → even number”, you must turn over E and 7. Fewer than one participant in ten thinks of it: most turn over E, and often 4.
textes.Le 4 ne peut pas réfuter la règle ; le 7: The 4 cannot refute the rule; the 7 can, if it hides a vowel.
textes.Antidote : chercher activement ce qui pr: Antidote: actively look for what would prove you wrong.
textes.Accumuler des exemples favorables ne tes: Piling up favorable examples tests nothing: only a test that could fail is informative.
textes.Tâche de Wason résolue : retourner E et: Wason's task solved: turn over E and 7
textes.Quand un premier chiffre tire nos estima: When a first number pulls our estimates.
textes.Un premier chiffre, même absurde, tire l: A first number, even an absurd one, pulls subsequent estimates toward it.
textes.Tversky et Kahneman : après une roue tru: Tversky and Kahneman: after a rigged wheel landed on 10 or 65, estimates of the share of African countries in the UN were 25% or 45%.
textes.Les prix barrés et les premières offres: Crossed-out prices and opening offers in a negotiation exploit anchoring.
textes.Même les experts y cèdent : des juges in: Even experts give in to it: judges' sentences influenced by a die roll (Englich, 2006).
textes.Savoir que l'ancre est absurde ne suffit: Knowing the anchor is absurd is not enough to break free of it.
textes.Estimation médiane selon le chiffre de l: Median estimate depending on the wheel's number
textes.Juger la fréquence d'un événement par le: Judging how frequent an event is by the examples that come to mind.
textes.On juge la fréquence d'un événement par: We judge how frequent an event is by how easily examples come to mind.
textes.Les accidents d'avion, très médiatisés,: Plane crashes, heavily covered by the media, seem more frequent than car accidents, which are far deadlier.
textes.Après un fait divers, on surestime le ri: After a news story, we overestimate the corresponding risk.
textes.Antidote : chercher les chiffres de base: Antidote: look for base rates rather than anecdotes.
textes.Ce dont on parle beaucoup n'est pas ce q: What gets talked about a lot is not what happens often.
textes.Morts par milliard de km parcourus (ordr: Deaths per billion km traveled (order of magnitude, Europe)
textes.Mesurer ce qu'on sait, et ce qu'on croit: Measuring what you know, and what you think you know.
textes.Effet Dunning-Kruger : les moins compéte: Dunning-Kruger effect: the least competent overestimate their level the most, since they don't know what they don't know.
textes.Les plus compétents ont tendance à se so: The most competent tend to slightly underestimate themselves.
textes.La courbe en « montagne de la stupidité: The “Mount Stupid” curve circulating on the Internet is not in the original paper.
textes.Métacognition : s'entraîner à dire « je: Metacognition: practice saying “I'm 70% sure” and check whether you're right 7 times out of 10.
textes.Dunning-Kruger ne dit pas que les ignora: Dunning-Kruger doesn't say ignorant people think they're experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top.
textes.Aversion à la perte, coûts irrécupérable: Loss aversion, sunk costs, status quo and nudges.
textes.Aversion à la perte : perdre 100 € fait: Loss aversion: losing €100 hurts about twice as much as winning €100 feels good.
textes.Coûts irrécupérables : ce qui est dépens: Sunk costs: what has been spent is lost whatever you do; only the future should guide the decision.
textes.Biais de statu quo : on garde l'option p: Status quo bias: we keep the default option, hence the effectiveness of nudges.
textes.Le don d'organes est bien plus fréquent: Organ donation is far more common in countries where it is the default option.
textes.« On a déjà trop investi pour arrêter »: “We've invested too much to stop now” is the Concorde fallacy.
textes.Fonction de valeur : les pertes pèsent p: Value function: losses weigh more than gains
textes.Paradoxe de Simpson, régression vers la: Simpson's paradox, regression to the mean, false positives.
textes.Paradoxe de Simpson : une tendance vraie: Simpson's paradox: a trend true in each group can reverse when the groups are combined.
textes.Régression vers la moyenne : après un ré: Regression to the mean: after an extreme result, the next one is often more ordinary, for no reason at all.
textes.Faux positifs : un test fiable à 99 % su: False positives: a 99% reliable test for a rare disease mostly gives false positives.
textes.Toujours demander : sur combien ? par ra: Always ask: out of how many? compared to what?
textes.Après une engueulade, les pilotes s'amél: After a dressing-down, pilots improve, and after a compliment they get worse: that's regression, not teaching.
textes.Test fiable à 99 % sur une maladie touch: 99% reliable test for a disease affecting 1 person in 1,000
textes.Paréidolie, intentionnalité, prophéties: Pareidolia, intentionality, failed prophecies and false memories.
textes.Paréidolie : voir des visages ou des for: Pareidolia: seeing faces or shapes in randomness (the face on Mars).
textes.Biais d'intentionnalité : voir une volon: Intentionality bias: seeing a will behind accidental events.
textes.Quand une prophétie échoue, les croyants: When a prophecy fails, the most committed believers often strengthen their belief, according to Festinger (1956), whose investigation is now contested.
textes.Les souvenirs se reconstruisent : on peu: Memories are rebuilt: detailed false memories can be implanted (Loftus).
textes.Être sûr de son souvenir n'est pas un ga: Being sure of your memory is no guarantee that it is accurate.
textes.Du hasard au complot : le biais d'intent: From chance to conspiracy: the intentionality bias
textes.Pré-mortem, lecture latérale, probabilit: Pre-mortem, lateral reading, probabilities and skepticism.
textes.Pré-mortem : imaginer que le projet a éc: Pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and look for why, before you start.
textes.Lecture latérale : pour juger un site, o: Lateral reading: to judge a website, open other tabs about its source rather than reading it in depth.
textes.Raisonner en probabilités : « je suis sû: Reason in probabilities: “I'm 80% sure” rather than yes or no.
textes.Rasoir d'Occam : à pouvoir explicatif ég: Occam's razor: with equal explanatory power, prefer the simplest hypothesis.
textes.Trois questions avant de croire une info: Three questions before believing a piece of information
textes.Pour tester une règle, chercher le cas q: To test a rule, look for the case that could bring it down (the 7), not the one that confirms it (the 4).
textes.En 1966, le psychologue Peter Wason pose: In 1966 the psychologist Peter Wason set a puzzle: four cards show E, K, 4 and 7. Rule: "if a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other". Which cards must you turn over to check? Most people choose E, and often 4. Fewer than one in ten find the right answer: E and 7.
textes.Le 4 ne peut rien réfuter : qu'il cache: The 4 cannot refute anything: whether it hides a vowel or a consonant, the rule stands. The 7 would bring it down if it hid a vowel. Our reflex is to look for what confirms, not what could contradict. Curiously, posed in social form, "anyone drinking beer must be 18", the same problem becomes easy: people spontaneously check the beer drinker and the 16-year-old.
textes.On lit les preuves avec les lunettes de: We read evidence through the lens of what we believe (Lord, Ross and Lepper, 1979). Intelligence does not protect.
textes.Le biais de confirmation ne touche pas q: Confirmation bias affects not only the search for information but also how it is read. In 1979 Charles Lord, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper had supporters and opponents of the death penalty read the same studies. Each side found the study that agreed with them more convincing, and demanded far more evidence from the one that contradicted them.
textes.Et l'intelligence ne protège pas : les g: And intelligence does not protect you: bright people are sometimes better at finding arguments for what they already believe. A horoscope that "gets it right" now and then, an echo chamber on social media: we remember the hits and forget the misses. Even a belief whose evidence is withdrawn can survive: that is belief perseverance.
textes.Tester ce qui pourrait dire non (2-4-6 d: Test what could say no (Wason's 2-4-6, 1960). Ask yourself: what would change my mind?
textes.Dans son jeu « 2-4-6 » de 1960, Wason an: In his "2-4-6" game of 1960, Wason announced that the sequence 2-4-6 follows a secret rule. Participants proposed 8-10-12, 20-22-24: "yes, that works". They stopped, convinced the rule was "even numbers going up by 2". It was simply "three increasing numbers". Few people tested 1-7-50, which could have told them no.
textes.L'antidote tient en une question : « qu': The antidote fits in one question: "what would change my mind?". Wording questions neutrally helps too: "does it work?" leads less than "why does it work?". Piling up favourable examples tests nothing; only a test that could fail teaches you something.
textes.Un premier chiffre, même absurde, tire l: A first number, even an absurd one, pulls estimates towards it (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974: 25 % against 45 %).
textes.En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974 Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spun a rigged lottery wheel in front of participants, stopping on 10 or 65. Then they asked: what share of UN member countries are African? After 10, the median estimate was 25 %; after 65, 45 %. A number plainly unrelated had pulled the answers towards it.
textes.Autre expérience du même article : en ci: Another experiment from the same article: in five seconds, estimate 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Median: 2,250. In reverse order, 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 8: 512. The first numbers read serve as an anchor. The right answer, 40,320, is far from both.
textes.Prix barré, plat cher en tête de carte,: Crossed-out price, expensive dish at the top of the menu, first offer: anchors. The option nobody takes is often a decoy.
textes.Les experts aussi (juges et dés, Englich: Experts too (judges and dice, Englich, 2006). Estimate before hearing a number, or find an independent reference.
textes.On pourrait croire que l'expérience prot: You might think experience protects. In 2006 Birte Englich and colleagues had experienced judges and prosecutors read a case file, with a requested sentence determined… by dice. The higher the dice roll, the heavier the sentence they proposed.
textes.Et savoir que l'ancre est absurde ne suf: And knowing the anchor is absurd is not enough to break free of it: the effect shrinks a little in people who have been warned, but persists. The best reflex is to make your own estimate before hearing any number, or to look for an independent reference, rather than adjusting from the anchor.
textes.Ce qui vient en tête paraît fréquent: What comes to mind seems common
textes.On juge la fréquence par la facilité des: We judge frequency by how easily examples come (Tversky and Kahneman, 1973). What is talked about a lot is not what happens often.
textes.En 1973, Tversky et Kahneman demandent :: In 1973 Tversky and Kahneman asked: in English, are there more words that start with "k" or that have "k" as the third letter? Most answered "start with", because those words come to mind more easily. It is the other way round. We judge how frequent something is by how easily examples come to us.
textes.Or ce qui vient en tête, c'est le récent: But what comes to mind is the recent, the striking, the spectacular. After a heavily reported plane crash, many overestimate the risk of flying, though planes remain far safer per kilometre than cars. The media talk about what is rare, precisely because it is rare. Kahneman sums up the trap as WYSIATI: we judge with what is in front of us, without thinking of what is missing.
textes.Les avions qui ne sont pas revenus: The planes that did not come back
textes.Biais du survivant : regarder aussi ceux: Survivorship bias: look at those who did not come back too (Wald). A striking case says nothing about the average risk.
textes.C'est le biais du survivant. On ne voit: That is survivorship bias. We only see the companies that succeeded with a method, not those that went bust with the same one. "My grandfather smoked all his life and lived to 95": we never hear the smokers who died at 60 tell their story.
textes.Revenir aux chiffres de base: Going back to the base rates
textes.Chiffres de base avant anecdotes. Oublie: Base rates before anecdotes. Forgetting the base rate makes you believe false alarms (positive test ≈ 1 in 11).
textes.L'antidote est simple à dire : chercher: The antidote is simple to state: look for base rates rather than anecdotes. In France, cancers and cardiovascular diseases are the two leading causes of death, far ahead of the spectacular accidents we talk about most.
textes.Les moins compétents se surestiment (12e: The least competent overestimate themselves (12th percentile actual, 62nd estimated), without thinking they are experts. "Mount Stupid" is not in the paper.
textes.En 1999, David Dunning et Justin Kruger: In 1999 David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested students in logic, grammar and humour, then asked them to rate themselves. Those in the bottom quarter placed themselves on average around the 62nd percentile, when they were near the 12th. The skills they lack are precisely the ones that would let them see their mistakes. The best slightly underestimated themselves.
textes.Attention aux caricatures. Les moins com: Beware of caricatures. The least competent do not think they are experts: they place themselves above average, not at the top, and always below the best. The famous "Mount Stupid" curve does not come from the paper. And some researchers think a good part of the effect is a statistical artefact, linked to regression to the mean; Dunning defends his findings.
textes.Se calibrer : « sûr à 70 % » doit tomber: Calibrate yourself: "70 % sure" should be right 7 times out of 10. 93 % of drivers think they are in the better half (Svenson, 1981).
textes.La métacognition, c'est savoir ce qu'on: Metacognition is knowing what you know, and spotting what you do not. A simple exercise: instead of answering yes or no, say "I'm 70 % sure", then check. If you are right about 7 times out of 10 when you say you are 70 % sure, you are well calibrated. Most people discover they are wrong far more often than they thought at "90 %".
textes.La surconfiance est partout. En 1981, Ol: Overconfidence is everywhere. In 1981 Ola Svenson found that 93 % of the Americans he asked placed themselves in the more skilful half of drivers. And the planning fallacy makes us underestimate how long our projects will take, even when we know previous ones ran late. Conversely, impostor syndrome credits one's successes to luck.
textes.Se tester bat la relecture (effet de tes: Testing beats rereading (testing effect). We see others' biases, not our own (blind spot, Pronin, 2002).
textes.Relire un cours donne une impression tro: Rereading a lesson gives a misleading sense of mastery: everything feels familiar, so it seems known. Testing yourself, fetching the answer from memory without looking, strengthens the memory far better. That is the testing effect, or retrieval practice, and it is the very principle of this game.
textes.Il y a aussi un angle mort : nous repéro: There is also a blind spot: we spot other people's biases very well, our own far less. Emily Pronin and colleagues described it in 2002. The more you learn in a field, the more you measure how much you do not know: that is the flip side of Dunning-Kruger, and rather a good sign.
textes.Perdre fait plus mal que gagner ne réjou: Losing hurts more than winning pleases
textes.Aversion à la perte (Kahneman et Tversky: Loss aversion (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979): a loss weighs about twice as much as a gain. Endowment effect: what you own is worth more.
textes.En 1979, Kahneman et Tversky publient la: In 1979 Kahneman and Tversky published prospect theory. Central idea: we do not judge outcomes in absolute terms, but as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses weigh more. They later estimated that a loss counts about 2.25 times as much as a gain of the same size.
textes.D'où des comportements étranges. Beaucou: Hence some odd behaviour. Many refuse a coin-toss bet where you win €150 or lose €100, though it is favourable. And the endowment effect: in 1990, students given a mug asked about twice as much to sell it as others were willing to pay to buy it. Simply owning something raises its value.
textes.Coûts irrécupérables : ce qui est dépens: Sunk costs: what is spent is gone. Only the future counts: "if I started from scratch, would I go for it?"
textes.La bonne question n'est pas « combien ai: The right question is not "how much have I already put in?" but "if I were starting from scratch today, would I go for it?". It works for a boring film, a project that is bogged down, or a relationship.
textes.La puissance de la case par défaut: The power of the default box
textes.Biais du statu quo : on garde le défaut: Status quo bias: we keep the default (organ donation: > 85 % against < 30 %, Johnson and Goldstein, 2003). Nudge: steer without banning.
textes.Changer demande un effort, et regretter: Changing takes effort, and regretting having acted weighs more than regretting doing nothing: we keep the default option. In 2003 Eric Johnson and Daniel Goldstein compared organ donation in Europe: where you have to opt out explicitly, consent often exceeds 85 %; where you have to sign up, it often stays below 30 %. Same preference, a different box ticked in advance.
textes.C'est le ressort du nudge, popularisé pa: That is what drives the nudge, popularised by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein in 2008: steering without banning or changing prices, like the fly painted in the urinals at Schiphol airport. And against our own weaknesses, the commitment device: Ulysses has himself tied to the mast to hear the Sirens; we set up an automatic transfer into savings.
textes.Paradoxe de Simpson : une tendance peut: Simpson's paradox: a trend can reverse when grouped (Berkeley, 1973). Look for the confounding variable.
textes.En 1973, l'université de Berkeley semble: In 1973 the University of California, Berkeley appeared to admit markedly fewer women than men. But department by department, women were not disadvantaged, sometimes even slightly favoured. The explanation: they applied more to the most selective departments. The study by Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell in 1975 made it the most famous example of Simpson's paradox.
textes.Une tendance vraie dans chaque groupe pe: A trend true in every group can therefore reverse when the groups are combined, if they are of very different sizes. Faced with a surprising overall figure, ask: what is happening inside each subgroup? And what confounding variable could explain it all? People in hospital die more than others, but the hospital is not to blame: they are ill.
textes.Le compliment qui ne marche pas: The compliment that does not work
textes.Après un extrême, retour vers la moyenne: After an extreme, a return towards the mean, with no cause at all. Beware of wrongly multiplied probabilities (Sally Clark, 1999).
textes.Des instructeurs de vol israéliens expli: Israeli flight instructors told Kahneman that criticism works better than praise: after praise for a brilliant landing, the next is worse; after a telling-off for a botched one, the next improves. Kahneman showed them that teaching has nothing to do with it. After an extreme result, the next one is almost always more ordinary: that is regression to the mean.
textes.La « malédiction » de la couverture de S: The Sports Illustrated cover "curse" works the same way: you appear on it after an exceptional season, rarely followed by another as good. And the Sally Clark trial in 1999 shows what these errors cost: an expert multiplied the probabilities of two cot deaths as if they were independent, announced 1 chance in 73 million, and the mother was convicted. The conviction was quashed in 2003.
textes.Vingt tests au seuil de 5 % donnent un f: Twenty tests at the 5 % threshold give one false positive on average. Read the scale: a truncated axis magnifies everything.
textes.Avec le seuil statistique habituel de 5: With the usual 5 % statistical threshold, testing twenty hypotheses with no real effect gives on average one false "significant result". Searching until you find something, then publishing only the find, is p-hacking. And a correlation, even a strong one, can be absurd: in 2012 Franz Messerli noted, with humour, a correlation between chocolate consumption and Nobel prizes by country.
textes.Les graphiques trompent aussi. Un axe ve: Charts mislead too. A vertical axis that does not start at zero can make a rise from 50.1 % to 50.4 % look like a tripling. Always read the scale, and ask: out of how many? compared with what?
textes.Paréidolie (le visage sur Mars) et biais: Pareidolia (the face on Mars) and intentionality bias: seeing shapes and wills in chance. Hanlon's razor.
textes.Notre cerveau cherche des formes et des: Our brain looks for shapes and intentions. Pareidolia makes us see a face in an electric socket or on Mars: the "face" photographed by Viking 1 in 1976 turned out, in Mars Global Surveyor images in 1998 and 2001, to be a simple hill. Intentionality bias makes us see someone behind accidental events.
textes.Ce réflexe a un sens : soupçonner un pré: This reflex makes sense: suspecting a predator behind every bush costs less than the reverse. But it misleads. In 1948 B. F. Skinner fed pigeons at regular intervals, whatever they did: some began turning in circles, others bobbing their heads, as if their movement brought the food. Like a gambler blowing on the dice. Hanlon's razor advises: never attribute to malice what stupidity is enough to explain.
textes.Les souvenirs se reconstruisent ; on peu: Memories are rebuilt; false ones can be implanted (Loftus, 1995: about a quarter). Being sure ≠ being right.
textes.Un souvenir n'est pas un enregistrement: A memory is not a recording: we rebuild it each time we recall it. In 1995 Elizabeth Loftus and Jacqueline Pickrell told 24 people three real childhood memories, and one false one: getting lost in a shopping mall. About a quarter ended up "remembering" the invented episode, sometimes in detail.
textes.Être sûr de son souvenir n'est donc pas: Being sure of a memory is therefore no guarantee that it is accurate. The "Mandela effect" shows it in a group: many people thought they remembered Nelson Mandela dying in prison in the 1980s; he died in 2013, after being president of South Africa.
textes.Grand événement ≠ grande cause. Mille ar: Big event ≠ big cause. A thousand fragile arguments do not make a proof. A real conspiracy is proved (Tuskegee).
textes.Le biais de proportionnalité nous fait c: Proportionality bias makes us believe a big event must have a big cause: that one man alone could have killed Kennedy seems too small. In 2013 Gérald Bronner described the "argumentative mille-feuille": each argument alone is fragile, but people tell themselves it cannot all be false. And believing one conspiracy makes believing others more likely, even contradictory ones: in 2012 the same people found it plausible both that Princess Diana was murdered and that she faked her death.
textes.Des complots réels existent pourtant. De: Real conspiracies do exist, though. From 1932 to 1972 the Tuskegee study denied treatment to Black men with syphilis; Peter Buxtun alerted the press. What separates a real conspiracy from an imagined one: documents, witnesses, evidence.
textes.Lecture latérale : vérifier qui est derr: Lateral reading: check who is behind a source before reading it (Wineburg and McGrew, 2017). SIFT: stop, source, better coverage, origin.
textes.En 2017, Sam Wineburg et Sarah McGrew co: In 2017 Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew compared historians, students and professional fact-checkers faced with unfamiliar websites. The fact-checkers won by a wide margin. Their secret: they barely read the site. They opened other tabs to find out who was behind it. That is lateral reading.
textes.Mike Caulfield en a tiré la méthode SIFT: Mike Caulfield turned it into the SIFT method: Stop (pause before sharing), Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to their origin. The first step is the hardest. And faced with a study quoted in the press: on how many people, and on whom? Many medical "discoveries" concern mice.
textes.Pré-mortem : imaginer l'échec pour le pr: Pre-mortem: imagine failure to prevent it (Klein). Outside view. Think in probabilities and revise in small steps (Tetlock).
textes.Philip Tetlock a suivi pendant vingt ans: Philip Tetlock followed 28,000 forecasts by political experts over twenty years: in the long run they did barely better than chance, and the "hedgehogs", sure of one big idea, did worst. His "superforecasters", well-trained amateurs, think in probabilities and revise often, in small steps, as evidence comes in.
textes.Affirmation extraordinaire, preuve extra: Extraordinary claim, extraordinary evidence (Sagan). Occam's razor. A meta-analysis weighs more than a single study.
textes.« Des affirmations extraordinaires exige: "Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence": Carl Sagan popularised the phrase in Cosmos in 1980; the idea goes back to Laplace. With equal explanatory power, Occam's razor prefers the simplest hypothesis. And a meta-analysis, which combines many solid studies, generally weighs more than a single study.
textes.Mettre à l'épreuve les prétentions extra: Putting extraordinary claims to the test is what James Randi did: his million-dollar challenge, from 1964 to 2015, drew over a thousand applicants claiming paranormal powers. The prize was never won. In France this approach has a name, zetetics, from the Greek zêtein, to seek, which Henri Broch taught at the University of Nice.
textes.Un prix barré à 200 € à côté de 120 € :: A price crossed out at €200 next to €120: the first number serves as a reference, and the second looks like a bargain. The very expensive dish at the top of a restaurant menu is not always there to be sold: it makes the others look reasonable. In negotiation, the first offer anchors the whole discussion. The effect was measured in 1974 by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, with a rigged wheel that stopped on 10 or 65: those who saw 10 estimated the share of African countries in the UN at 25% on average, those who saw 65 at 45%.
textes.Cousin de l'ancrage, l'effet de leurre :: A cousin of anchoring is the decoy effect: a medium popcorn at €6.50 exists mainly to make the large one at €7 look like good value. Nobody wants the medium; it is there for comparison. The effect was described by Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto, in 1982, under the name of asymmetrically dominated alternative. Spotting the option nobody picks is often spotting the decoy.

A 99 % reliable test for a disease that affects 1 person in 1,000: a positive result has only about a one-in-eleven chance of being a real case, because healthy people are so numerous that their 1 % of errors win out. In 1978 at Harvard Medical School, a question of this kind was put to 60 students and doctors: only 11 got it right, and 27 answered 95%. Always ask: out of how many cases, and compared with what?
textes.« On a déjà trop investi pour arrêter. »: "We've invested too much to stop now." That is the sunk cost trap: what has been spent is lost whatever you do, and only the future should guide the decision. The French and British kept funding Concorde long after realising it would never pay off, hence the nickname Concorde effect. The phrase took hold in biology: in 1980, Richard Dawkins and Jane Brockmann asked whether digger wasps "commit the Concorde fallacy".
textes.Pendant la Seconde Guerre mondiale, on é: During the Second World War, bullet holes on bombers returning from missions were studied to decide where to add armour. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out that the armour should go where there were no holes: planes hit in those places never came back to be examined. Wald, an Austrian Jew persecuted after Nazi Germany annexed Austria, had emigrated to the United States; he was then working at the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, and his report dates from 1943.
textes.Le pré-mortem, proposé par Gary Klein :: The pre-mortem, proposed by Gary Klein: before launching a project, the team imagines it has failed, and everyone writes down why. Presenting failure as a given loosens tongues: people finally dare say what worries them. Klein described it in 2007 in the Harvard Business Review; it formalises an idea studied as early as 1989 by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington, prospective hindsight. The outside view completes the tool: your project is unique, but how many similar projects ran over budget?

textes.Trente-sept livres pour tout dire du mon: Thirty-seven books to say everything about the world: astronomy, geography, humans, animals, plants, remedies, metals, stones. Pliny claims to have gathered twenty thousand facts from two thousand volumes. We learn how gold is mined, the uses of hundreds of plants. But he also copies without sorting: dog-headed men, mouthless men who live on smells, one-footed men who use their foot as a parasol. For fifteen hundred years, Europe drew its knowledge of nature from it, true and false alike.

textes.Ibn al-Haytham règle une vieille querell: Ibn al-Haytham settles an old quarrel: do we see because the eye sends out rays, or because light enters the eye? He shows that it's light, coming from every point of objects, that enters the eye. He describes the anatomy of the eye, reflection in mirrors and refraction, the change of direction when light passes from air to water. He studies the camera obscura, a dark room where an inverted image forms through a small hole. Above all, he tests every claim by experiment, and criticizes the ancient authorities when they are wrong.

In it he lists the four causes of ignorance: trusting unworthy authority, following custom, believing the opinion of the crowd, and hiding one's ignorance behind false knowledge. He argues for the study of languages, mathematics and optics, and for an “experimental science” that checks by experiment what books say. He describes lenses and the refraction of light.

textes.Francis Bacon veut une nouvelle méthode: Francis Bacon wants a new method for knowing nature, based on observation and experiment rather than the authority of the ancients. But first, he lists our “idols”, the illusions that distort the mind: those of the human species, those of each individual, those of language, those of philosophical systems. Three centuries ahead of time, he describes confirmation bias: once an opinion is adopted, the mind draws everything back to it, keeps the cases that support it and neglects or dismisses those that contradict it.

textes.Ce recueil rassemble les études qui ont: This collection gathers the studies that showed our judgments follow predictable shortcuts. The founding 1974 paper describes three. Representativeness: we judge a case by its resemblance to a stereotype, forgetting proportions. Availability: we estimate how frequent an event is by how easily examples come to mind. Anchoring: a number we've just seen, even one drawn at random, pulls our estimates toward it. These biases are not random errors, but slopes, the same for everyone.

textes.Carl Sagan défend la science comme « une: Carl Sagan defends science as “a candle in the dark” against pseudoscience, alien abductions and witch hunts. He offers a “baloney detection kit”: seek independent confirmation of the facts, consider several hypotheses, beware of arguments from authority, quantify, check that every link in a chain of argument holds, apply Occam's razor, and ask whether a claim can be falsified. He reminds us that science is not a body of truths, but a method for correcting its errors.

textes.Pourquoi avons-nous peur des requins, de: Why are we afraid of sharks, terrorist attacks and plane crashes, but not of cars or the couch? Journalist Dan Gardner shows that our brain judges risks by the images in our heads, not by the numbers. A spectacular event, repeated by the media, seems frequent. He cites a striking case: after September 11, 2001, many Americans drove rather than flew, and road deaths rose in the following year.

textes.Puisque nos décisions sont biaisées, peu: Since our decisions are biased, can choices be arranged to help people without constraining them? That is the idea of the “nudge”. Economist Thaler and legal scholar Sunstein show that the way options are presented matters enormously. The default option is often the one people keep: automatically enrolling employees in a retirement savings plan, while leaving them free to opt out, multiplies enrollment. Putting healthy food at eye level in the cafeteria gets more of it eaten. The authors call this libertarian paternalism.

textes.Kahneman décrit notre pensée comme le tr: Kahneman describes our thinking as the work of two systems. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, completes “bread and…”, answers 10 cents to the bat-and-ball question. System 2 is slow, attentive and costly: it calculates, checks, reflects. The problem is that System 2 is lazy and often lets the first decide. Hence our biases: anchoring, availability, loss aversion, overconfidence. The book sums up forty years of research carried out largely with Amos Tversky, who died in 1996.
