textes.Chaque électron semble passer par les de: Each electron seems to go through both slits at once. The experiment was carried out with single electrons in 1974 and again in 1989.
textes.Selon le modèle de Bohr (1913), les élec: According to Bohr's model (1913), the electrons of an atom:
textes.En sautant d'un niveau à l'autre, ils ém: By jumping from one level to another, they emit or absorb light of a precise color.
textes.« Dieu ne joue pas aux dés » est une obj: “God does not play dice” is an objection by Einstein:
textes.au caractère probabiliste de la mécaniqu: to the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics
textes.Dans une lettre à Max Born, en 1926. Boh: In a letter to Max Born, in 1926. Bohr reportedly told him to stop telling God what to do.
textes.L'effet tunnel permet à une particule de: Quantum tunneling lets a particle cross a barrier it couldn't cross classically.
textes.Il explique la radioactivité alpha et se: It explains alpha radioactivity and is used in scanning tunneling microscopes and flash memory.
textes.Lequel de ces appareils repose directeme: Which of these devices relies directly on quantum physics?
textes.Le laser exploite l'émission stimulée, p: The laser exploits stimulated emission, predicted by Einstein in 1917.
textes.Au congrès Solvay de 1927, sur la célèbr: At the 1927 Solvay conference, in the famous photo, how many participants had received or would receive a Nobel Prize?
textes.Dont Marie Curie, seule femme présente,: Including Marie Curie, the only woman present, and a two-time laureate.
textes.Un ordinateur quantique utilise des qubi: A quantum computer uses qubits, which can be in a superposition of 0 and 1.
textes.Pour certains problèmes, comme la factor: For some problems, such as factoring, this could give an enormous advantage.
textes.La Conférence générale des poids et mesu: The General Conference on Weights and Measures standardised this unit of force in 1946 and gave it the name newton in 1948, in honour of Isaac Newton.
textes.Les Égyptiens ont d'abord découpé la nui: The Egyptians first split the night into 12 parts, then the day. Hipparchus of Nicaea was probably the first to divide the whole day into 24 hours. The 60 minutes and 60 seconds are a legacy of Babylonian astronomy and its base-60 arithmetic.
textes.Fizeau mesure la vitesse de la lumière s: Fizeau measured the speed of light on Earth in 1849, with a toothed wheel and a mirror about 8 km away: 315,000 km/s. Foucault, with a rotating mirror, got 298,000 km/s in 1862. Since 1983, the value has been fixed at exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.Le litre naît en France en 1795, défini: The litre was born in France in 1795, defined as one cubic decimetre. In 1901 it was redefined as the volume of a kilo of water, about 1.000028 dm³; in 1964 it went back to exactly one cubic decimetre. The capital L symbol was allowed in 1979.
textes.Les préfixes kilo et déci datent de la n: The prefixes kilo and deci date from the birth of the metric system, in 1795; mega and micro were adopted in 1873. The latest arrivals, ronna, quetta, ronto and quecto, date from 2022.
textes.Le mètre est défini en 1791 par l'Assemb: The metre was defined in 1791 by the French National Assembly as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole. Since 1983 it has been defined by the speed of light.
textes.Mars Climate Orbiter est lancée le 11 dé: Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on 11 December 1998 and lost on 23 September 1999. Lockheed Martin's software gave thrust in pound-force seconds, while NASA's expected SI units: an error by a factor of 4.45. Total cost: 327.6 million dollars.
textes.Aristarque, vers 280 av. J.-C., plaçait: Aristarchus, around 280 BC, put the Sun 18 to 20 times farther than the Moon, far below reality (about 389 times). In 1672, Cassini and Richer measured the parallax of Mars between Paris and Cayenne. In 2012, the IAU fixed the astronomical unit at exactly 149,597,870,700 m.
textes.Au début du XXe siècle, l'existence des: At the start of the 20th century, the existence of atoms was still debated. Jean Perrin, studying Brownian motion, confirmed Einstein's explanation and the atomic nature of matter; he published Les Atomes in 1913 and received the Nobel Prize in 1926.
textes.En 1848, William Thomson, futur Lord Kel: In 1848, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, published On an Absolute Thermometric Scale. In 1967-1968 the unit was renamed "kelvin", without "degree", and since 2019 it has been defined by the Boltzmann constant.
textes.Aristote pensait qu'un objet s'arrête si: Aristotle thought an object stops if nothing pushes it. In the 14th century, Jean Buridan spoke of "impetus"; Galileo described in 1632 a motion that continues on a level surface. Kepler coined the word "inertia", from the Latin for laziness, and Newton made it his first law in the Principia in 1687.
textes.Le 2 août 1971, sur la Lune, l'astronaut: On 2 August 1971, on the Moon, Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather together in front of the camera: they hit the ground at the same time, as Galileo had predicted.
textes.Newton énonce ses trois lois du mouvemen: Newton stated his three laws of motion in the Principia, published in 1687.
textes.L'unité de force du Système internationa: The SI unit of force was standardised in 1946 and named the newton in 1948 by the General Conference on Weights and Measures.
textes.Newton pose cette loi dans les Principia: Newton set out this law in the Principia in 1687: "To every action there is always opposed an equal reaction." It is what makes rockets move.
textes.Newton raconta à William Stukeley qu'un: Newton told William Stukeley that an apple tree in the Woolsthorpe orchard had set him on the track of universal gravitation. He had come back there in 1666, with Cambridge University closed by the plague. A tree in that orchard, over 400 years old, still grows there.
textes.Kepler montre en 1604 que la lumière fai: Kepler showed in 1604 that light weakens with the square of the distance, and Ismaël Boulliau proposed the same law for the Sun's force in 1645. Robert Hooke wrote it to Newton around 1679-1680 and always resented him for taking all the credit.
textes.Selon son élève Vincenzo Viviani, Galilé: According to his pupil Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa between 1589 and 1592; most historians see it as a thought experiment. Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot, for their part, did try it in Delft, described in 1586.
textes.Leibniz tente de 1676 à 1689 de mettre e: From 1676 to 1689 Leibniz tried to put the "living force", vis viva, into an equation. Émilie du Châtelet, building on Willem 's Gravesande's observations, showed it depends on the square of the speed. The word "energy" was first used in this sense by Thomas Young in 1807.
textes.Émilie du Châtelet propose et teste la c: Émilie du Châtelet proposed and tested the conservation of total energy, as distinct from momentum, by dropping balls into soft clay. In 1918, Emmy Noether showed that it follows from the laws of physics being the same over time.
textes.Le facteur ½ vient de Coriolis et Poncel: The ½ factor comes from Coriolis and Poncelet, who championed this recalibrated "living force" around 1829; Coriolis called it the "quantity of work".
textes.Le watt porte le nom de l'ingénieur écos: The watt is named after the Scottish engineer James Watt, following a proposal by William Siemens in August 1882. It entered the International System of Units in 1960. One kilowatt is about 1.34 horsepower.
textes.La première installation hydroélectrique: The first hydroelectric scheme was built in 1878 by William Armstrong at Cragside, England, to power a single arc lamp. Edison's first hydroelectric station, in Appleton, Wisconsin, started on 30 September 1882.
textes.L'idée est ancienne : au XIIe siècle, le: The idea is old: in the 12th century, the Indian mathematician Bhāskara II described a wheel supposed to turn forever. Today, the US patent office refuses any perpetual motion machine without a working model.
textes.Le joule porte le nom de James Prescott: The joule is named after James Prescott Joule, son of a wealthy brewer, who in 1845 turned a paddle wheel in an insulated barrel of water and measured the water warming up.
textes.Nicolas Clément introduit la calorie com: Nicolas Clément introduced the calorie as a unit of heat in his calorimetry lectures, between 1819 and 1824. The American Wilbur Atwater adopted the "large" Calorie, our kilocalorie, in 1887 for the energy of food.
textes.L'idée paraît en novembre 1905 dans l'ar: The idea appeared in November 1905 in Einstein's paper "Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy content?". He did not write E = mc² there, but that a body radiating energy L loses mass L/V². It was confirmed to within 0.5% in 1933.
textes.Vers 1660, Robert Boyle et Robert Hooke: Around 1660, Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke improved Otto von Guericke's vacuum pump and shut candles, mice, birds and bells inside it. Among other things, Boyle drew from it the role of air in carrying sound.
textes.Mersenne mesure en 1630 le délai entre l: In 1630 Mersenne timed the gap between a gun's flash and its sound; in 1687 Newton calculated a value 15% too low, which Laplace later corrected. In 1738, the Paris Academy of Sciences found 332 m/s at 0 °C using cannon fire, within 1% of the modern value.
textes.En 1709, William Derham mesure la vitess: In 1709, William Derham measured the speed of sound from a church tower: he timed the gap between the flash and the bang of shotguns, using a half-second pendulum.
textes.Newton présente ses expériences du prism: Newton reported his prism experiments to the Royal Society in 1672. He first named five colours, then added two, orange and indigo, to reach seven, partly by analogy with the seven notes of the musical scale.
textes.Léonard de Vinci soupçonnait déjà de fin: Leonardo da Vinci already suspected fine particles in the air. Tyndall observed in 1869 that light scattered by very small particles is bluish; Lord Rayleigh published two papers on the colour of the sky in 1871, then, in 1899, the explanation by air molecules.
textes.Wilhelm Röntgen découvre les rayons X le: Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895. He called them "X" because he did not know what they were, and made an image of his wife Anna Bertha's hand. He received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics.
textes.Le hertz rend hommage à Heinrich Hertz,: The hertz honours Heinrich Hertz, the first to prove that electromagnetic waves exist. The name was chosen in 1935 by the International Electrotechnical Commission and adopted in 1960, replacing "cycles per second".
textes.Christian Doppler propose l'effet en 184: Christian Doppler proposed the effect in 1842, about the colour of binary stars. Buys Ballot tested it for sound in 1845, in experiments on a Dutch railway, and Fizeau discovered it independently for light in 1848.
textes.Vers 1307, Thierry de Freiberg, et vers: Around 1307 Theodoric of Freiberg, and around 1309 the Persian Kamāl al-Dīn al-Fārisī, explained the rainbow using water-filled glass spheres: two refractions and one reflection in the drop. Descartes calculated its angles in 1637.
textes.En 1676, Ole Rømer déduit des éclipses d: In 1676, Ole Rømer deduced from the eclipses of Io, a moon of Jupiter, that light is not instantaneous: he announced that Io would reappear on 16 November 1676 about ten minutes late. Cassini remained his tenacious opponent.
textes.L'unité de pression, le newton par mètre: The unit of pressure, the newton per square metre, was given the name pascal in 1971, in honour of Blaise Pascal.
textes.Archimède aurait crié « Eurêka ! » en tr: Archimedes reportedly cried "Eureka!" on working out how to tell whether a crown was pure gold. In the most common version of the tale, though, he does not use his principle: he only measures the crown's volume by the water it displaces.
textes.Archimède énonce ce principe vers 246 av: Archimedes stated this principle around 246 BC in his treatise On Floating Bodies: a body immersed in a fluid is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
textes.En 1648, Florin Périer, poussé par son b: In 1648, Florin Périer, urged on by his brother-in-law Blaise Pascal, measured the height of a column of mercury at three altitudes on the Puy de Dôme, to test Torricelli's theory.
textes.L'effet porte le nom de l'Italien Giovan: The effect is named after the Italian Giovanni Battista Venturi, who published it in 1797. Clemens Herschel built the first large water flow meters from it, describing his invention in a letter of 5 June 1888.
textes.Depuis l'adoption du pascal en 1971, les: Since the pascal was adopted in 1971, meteorologists have counted in hectopascals; since one hectopascal equals one millibar, the numbers stayed the same.
textes.Le 8 mai 1654 à Ratisbonne, devant la Di: On 8 May 1654 in Regensburg, before the Imperial Diet and Emperor Ferdinand III, Otto von Guericke showed that thirty horses, in two teams of fifteen, could not separate his two hemispheres emptied of air. He repeated it in 1656 in Magdeburg with sixteen horses.
textes.La presse hydraulique applique le princi: The hydraulic press applies Pascal's principle. Joseph Bramah patented it in 1795, hence its other name, the "Bramah press".
textes.Le Hollandais Cornelis Drebbel construit: The Dutchman Cornelis Drebbel built an oar-powered submersible as early as 1620 for James I of England. In 1747, Nathaniel Symons patented diving with ballast tanks, then leather bags filled with water.
textes.En 1742, Anders Celsius propose une éche: In 1742, Anders Celsius proposed an upside-down scale: 0 for boiling water, 100 for ice. It was turned round as early as 1743 by Jean-Pierre Christin, then by Linnaeus. The "centigrade degree" took the name Celsius in 1948.
textes.Guillaume Amontons pose la question d'un: Guillaume Amontons raised the question of a limit to cold as early as 1703; Lambert suggested −270 °C in 1779, and Kelvin built an absolute scale in 1848. In 1908, Kamerlingh Onnes liquefied helium and got down to about 1.5 K.
textes.Rudolf Clausius pose les bases de ce sec: Rudolf Clausius laid the foundations of this second law in 1850, then stated it thus: "Heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body without some other change" occurring at the same time.
textes.Le chirurgien allemand Julius Robert von: The German surgeon Julius Robert von Mayer stated the equivalence of heat and work in 1842; James Joule found it again by experiment in 1843. Hermann von Helmholtz generalised it in 1847 in On the Conservation of Force.
textes.Lavoisier parle en 1783 d'un « fluide ig: In 1783 Lavoisier spoke of an "igneous fluid"; the word "caloric" was coined in 1787 by Guyton de Morveau. In 1798, Rumford showed that boring a cannon produces heat without end, and the theory was abandoned by the mid-19th century.
textes.Clausius forge le mot « entropie » en 18: Clausius coined the word "entropy" in 1865, from the Greek tropē, transformation, so that it would resemble "energy". Boltzmann gave its statistical interpretation in the 1870s.
textes.Sadi Carnot le démontre dans Réflexions: Sadi Carnot proved it in Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire, published at his own expense in Paris in June 1824. The book went almost unnoticed until Clapeyron's commentary in 1834; Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36.
textes.Cette équivalence entre chaleur et trava: This equivalence between heat and work was measured by James Joule: in 1845 he warmed water in an insulated barrel by turning a paddle wheel driven by a falling weight.
textes.Boltzmann donne sa définition de l'entro: Boltzmann gave his definition of entropy in 1877; it was Max Planck who put the formula into its current form around 1900. His grave, in Vienna's Central Cemetery, bears a bust and the formula.
textes.William Cullen fabrique un peu de glace: William Cullen made a little ice as early as 1755 by boiling ether under vacuum. Jacob Perkins built the first vapour-compression system in 1834, and Carl von Linde improved it in the 1870s, at the request of beer brewers.
textes.Ole Rømer en fait la première estimation: Ole Rømer made the first estimate in 1676, using the eclipses of Io: about 22 minutes to cross the Earth's orbit. James Bradley found it again in 1729 through stellar aberration. Since 1983, it has been exactly 299,792,458 m/s.
textes.En octobre 1971, Joseph Hafele et Richar: In October 1971, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating took four caesium atomic clocks aboard airliners and flew twice around the world, eastward then westward. The result agreed with both special and general relativity.
textes.L'origine de la lettre c n'est pas certa: The origin of the letter c is not certain: one possibility is the Latin celeritas, swiftness.
textes.Albert Michelson et Edward Morley mènent: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley ran the experiment from April to July 1887 in Cleveland, in a basement, with an interferometer on a block of sandstone floating in mercury. It has been called "the most famous failed experiment in history".
textes.Sans correction, les horloges des satell: Without correction, GPS satellite clocks would gain about 38.6 microseconds a day (+45.8 from gravity, −7.2 from speed), about 11.4 km of error a day. Their frequency is offset before launch.
textes.Einstein part en 1907 d'une expérience d: Einstein started in 1907 from a thought experiment about an observer in free fall. Eight years later, in November 1915, he presented his equations to the Prussian Academy and explained the advance of Mercury's perihelion without any adjusted parameter.
textes.L'éclipse du 29 mai 1919 est observée à: The eclipse of 29 May 1919 was observed both at Sobral, in Brazil, and on Príncipe by the teams of Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson. The result made front-page news and made Einstein famous worldwide.
textes.Le signal GW150914 est capté le 14 septe: The signal GW150914 was picked up on 14 September 2015 by LIGO and announced on 11 February 2016: the merger of two black holes. Einstein had predicted these waves in 1916; Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the 2017 Nobel Prize.
textes.Expert à l'Office des brevets de Berne,: As an examiner at the Patent Office in Bern, Einstein published four papers in Annalen der Physik in 1905: the photoelectric effect in June, Brownian motion in July, special relativity in September and E = mc² in November.
textes.Ole Rømer a été le premier, en 1676, à e: Ole Rømer was the first, in 1676, to estimate this travel time: from Io's eclipses, he reckoned light took about 22 minutes to cross the Earth's orbit.
textes.Le 10 avril 1911, Paul Langevin imagine: On 10 April 1911, Paul Langevin imagined a traveller shut in a projectile at 99.995% of the speed of light: one year out, one year back, he has aged two years while two centuries have passed on Earth.
Planck found his law on 19 October 1900. To justify it, he split energy into whole multiples of a unit, "an act of desperation": he himself did not believe in atoms and saw it as a purely formal assumption.
textes.En 1924, dans sa thèse, Louis de Broglie: In 1924, in his thesis, Louis de Broglie, who had first graduated in history, proposed that all matter also behaves like a wave. Einstein backed him, the Davisson–Germer experiment confirmed it in 1927, and he received the Nobel Prize in 1929.
textes.Einstein soumet son article sur l'effet: Einstein submitted his paper on the photoelectric effect on 18 March 1905, published on 9 June. It was this work, not relativity, that won him the 1921 Nobel Prize.
textes.Heisenberg travaille alors à l'institut: Heisenberg was then working at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen. He set out the idea to Wolfgang Pauli in a letter of February 1927 and published it that year; Earle Kennard gave the modern inequality the same year.
textes.Schrödinger publie son chat en novembre: Schrödinger published his cat in November 1935 in Naturwissenschaften, after his exchanges with Einstein about the EPR paper; Einstein had suggested to him the example of a keg of gunpowder. He was targeting the ideas of Bohr and Heisenberg and himself called it "quite ridiculous".
textes.Thomas Young montre les interférences de: Thomas Young demonstrated the interference of light in 1801-1803. Claus Jönsson repeated the experiment with electrons in 1961, and in 1974 Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi sent them one at a time. Physics World readers voted it "the most beautiful experiment" in 2002.
textes.Bohr, qui avait rejoint le laboratoire d: Bohr, who had joined Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester, published his model in 1913 in three papers in the Philosophical Magazine. He started from the nucleus discovered by Rutherford and recovered the formula for hydrogen's spectral lines.
textes.La phrase vient d'une lettre d'Einstein: The line comes from a letter from Einstein to Max Born, in 1926: "I, at any rate, am convinced that He is not playing at dice." His debate with Bohr carried on at the Solvay conferences of 1927 and 1930.
textes.Friedrich Hund est le premier à décrire: Friedrich Hund was the first to describe tunnelling, in 1927. In 1928, George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, used it to explain alpha decay. Binnig and Rohrer's scanning tunnelling microscope (1981) earned them the 1986 Nobel Prize.
textes.Einstein pose en 1917 les bases du laser: Einstein laid the foundations of the laser in 1917 with stimulated emission. The first laser worked on 16 May 1960 at Hughes, in California: Theodore Maiman made a ruby shine there. It was first called "a solution looking for a problem".
textes.Le cinquième congrès Solvay, du 24 au 29: The fifth Solvay conference, from 24 to 29 October 1927, was about electrons and photons. Of the 29 attendees in the photo, 17 were or became Nobel laureates, and Marie Curie was the only one to have won it in two disciplines.
textes.Paul Benioff décrit une machine de Turin: Paul Benioff described a quantum Turing machine in 1980; Yuri Manin and then Richard Feynman, in 1982, proposed quantum computers to simulate physics. In 1994, Peter Shor's algorithm threatened cryptography, and Google claimed "quantum supremacy" in 2019.
textes.{comp}. Archimède réclamait un point d'a: {comp}. Archimedes asked for a place to stand to move the world. You have a chair. Get started.
textes.Mécanique. Newton disait avoir rendu les: Mechanics. Newton said he made the Principia hard on purpose, to discourage smatterers. I'm giving you {comp}, without discouraging anyone.
textes.Galilée chronométrait ses billes avec un: Galileo timed his balls with a trickle of water. I'm timing your hesitations. {comp}.
textes.Exact. Newton aurait été jaloux. Il l'ét: Exactly. Newton would have been jealous. He was jealous of everyone.
textes.Bien vu. Émilie du Châtelet a corrigé Ne: Well spotted. Émilie du Châtelet corrected Newton on energy. You've just corrected your reputation.
textes.Juste. L'énergie se conserve, votre avan: Right. Energy is conserved, and so is your lead. For now. Joule would be pleased.
textes.Correct. Même la gravité vous laisse mon: Correct. Even gravity lets you climb, today.
textes.Raté. Aristote pensait que les corps lou: Missed. Aristotle thought heavy bodies fall faster. You fell just as fast as he did.
textes.Faux. Lord Kelvin donnait à la Terre que: Wrong. Lord Kelvin gave the Earth a few tens of millions of years, with far more confidence than you. He was wrong by far more.
textes.Erreur. Le pont de Tacoma s'est effondré: Error. The Tacoma bridge collapsed in 1940 in a moderate wind. So did your reasoning.
textes.La physique est formelle : vous venez de: Physics is categorical: you just fell.
textes.Au Caire, il montre que la vision vient: In Cairo, he shows that vision comes from light entering the eye, not rays coming out of it, and proves it by experiment. According to legend, he feigned madness to escape an impossible mission from the caliph.
textes.Elle traduit et commente les Principia d: She translated and annotated Newton's Principia, a translation that remains the reference in French. Using 's Gravesande's experiments, she showed that a body's energy depends on the square of its speed. Voltaire called her “a great man whose only fault was being a woman”.
textes.En 1905, employé à l'Office des brevets: In 1905, a clerk at the Patent Office in Bern, he published four papers that changed physics. He didn't wear socks; to a neighbor, he explained that he had reached the age where, if told to put them on, he didn't have to.
textes.Vers 2650 avant notre ère, il conçoit po: Around 2650 BC, he designed the step pyramid of Saqqara for the pharaoh Djoser, the first large construction in cut stone. Later, the Egyptians made him a god of medicine, and the Greeks identified him with Asclepius. Of the real man, almost nothing is known.
textes.En 1918, elle démontre que chaque symétr: In 1918, she proved that every symmetry of nature corresponds to a conserved quantity: invariance in time gives the conservation of energy. Barred from teaching under her own name because she was a woman, she first gave her Göttingen courses under Hilbert's name. Einstein considered her a genius.
textes.En 1956, les théoriciens Lee et Yang se: In 1956, the theorists Lee and Yang wonder whether nature distinguishes left from right. Chien-Shiung Wu sets up the experiment with cobalt-60 cooled near absolute zero: the electrons preferentially fly off to one side. Mirror symmetry is violated. Lee and Yang got the Nobel the following year; she didn't.
textes.En 1644, il retourne un tube plein de me: In 1644, he inverts a tube full of mercury into a basin. The mercury drops to 76 centimeters and stops: it's the weight of the air that holds it, and above it, a vacuum remains, which was said to be impossible. “We live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air.”
textes.À 28 ans, il publie à compte d'auteur un: At 28, he self-publishes a small book on the “motive power of fire”: the efficiency of a steam engine depends on the temperature difference between hot and cold. Nobody reads it. He died of cholera at 36, and most of his papers were burned with his belongings.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange de Mécaniqu: Master the first diamond of Mechanics.
textes.En 1999, la sonde Mars Climate Orbiter s: In 1999, the Mars Climate Orbiter probe was lost in the atmosphere of Mars. One piece of software gave its values in pound-force·seconds, another read them in newton·seconds.
textes.Maîtriser les ordres de grandeur. Vous p: Master orders of magnitude. You can now say what can be seen from space, and what can't.
textes.La Grande Muraille n'est pas visible à l: The Great Wall is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon, nor even easily from low orbit: it's long, but narrow and the color of the ground. Yang Liwei, the first Chinese astronaut, said in 2003 that he hadn't seen it.
textes.Maîtriser les ondes et la lumière. Ne me: Master waves and light. Don't set any fleet on fire.
textes.Archimède aurait incendié la flotte roma: Archimedes supposedly set the Roman fleet on fire with mirrors. The story only appears centuries later. In 2005, MIT students managed to ignite a stationary ship model, in strong sunshine, after about ten minutes.
textes.Maîtriser les forces et le mouvement. Le: Master forces and motion. Astronauts don't float: they fall, without ever hitting the ground.
textes.À 400 km d'altitude, là où tourne la Sta: At 400 km up, where the Space Station orbits, gravity is still 90% of what it is on the ground. If astronauts float, it's because they're constantly falling around the Earth, along with their station, at 28,000 km/h. They miss the ground, on every orbit.
textes.Maîtriser l'énergie. Inutile de m'envoye: Master energy. No need to send me the plans for your machine.
textes.En 1775, l'Académie royale des sciences: In 1775, the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris decided to stop examining any perpetual motion machine, or any squaring of the circle. It received too many, all wrong, and the inventors never gave up. Energy is conserved: nothing spins for free.
textes.Maîtriser la pression et les fluides. L': Master pressure and fluids. The air on top has no appointment with the air underneath.
textes.Une explication répandue dit que l'air p: A common explanation says that the air passing over the wing must meet the air underneath at the same time, so it goes faster. That's false: it even arrives well before. The wing flies because it deflects air downward, and the pressure difference follows from that.
textes.Maîtriser la chaleur et la thermodynamiq: Master heat and thermodynamics. The answer is: it depends, and that's already a lot.
textes.En 1963, Erasto Mpemba, lycéen tanzanien: In 1963, Erasto Mpemba, a Tanzanian schoolboy, notices that his hot ice-cream mix sets faster than his classmates'. His teachers laugh. A physicist published the effect with him in 1969. Since then, experiments have contradicted each other: in 2016, a careful study found no effect.
textes.Maîtriser la relativité. Sans elle, vous: Master relativity. Without it, you'd be ten kilometers off every day.
textes.Les horloges des satellites GPS avancent: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day ahead of those on the ground: weaker gravity speeds them up, their velocity slows them down. Without relativistic correction, the position error would grow by about ten kilometers every day.
textes.Maîtriser la physique quantique. Planck: Master quantum physics. Planck didn't believe it himself. You're in good company.
textes.En 1900, Max Planck découpe l'énergie de: In 1900, Max Planck cuts the energy of light into small packets, quanta, to make a formula fit the measurements. He doesn't believe it. Thirty years later, he writes that it was “an act of desperation”, done because an explanation had to be found, at any cost.
textes.Réussir trois quiz de Mécanique sans fau: Pass three Mechanics quizzes without a mistake. You don't weigh much, but you weigh right.
textes.En 1798, Henry Cavendish, savant si timi: In 1798, Henry Cavendish, a scientist so shy that he communicated with his servants by notes, hangs lead balls in a shed and measures their tiny attraction. From it he deduces the density of the Earth, to within one percent.
textes.Entendre, lire et comprendre la musique: Hearing, reading and understanding music: waves, intervals, scales, chords, tuning.
textes.Fréquence, amplitude, vitesse du son et: Frequency, amplitude, speed of sound and hertz.
textes.Le son est une onde de pression : l'air: Sound is a pressure wave: the air compresses and expands. Without matter, no sound: it does not cross a vacuum.
textes.La fréquence, en hertz (Hz), compte les: Frequency, in hertz (Hz), counts vibrations per second. It gives the pitch: the higher it is, the higher the sound.
textes.L'amplitude donne l'intensité, que l'on: Amplitude gives the intensity, which is measured in decibels (dB).
textes.Dans l'air à 20 °C, le son parcourt envi: In air at 20 °C, sound travels about 343 m/s; in water, nearly 1,500 m/s.
textes.Un son plus fort n'est pas plus aigu : l: A louder sound is not higher: intensity (amplitude) and pitch (frequency) are independent.
textes.fréquence f = 1 / T, en hertz (vibration: frequency f = 1 / T, in hertz (vibrations per second)
textes.Une onde sonore : la période donne la ha: A sound wave: the period gives the pitch, the amplitude gives the intensity
textes.La portée, les clés, les durées et la me: The staff, clefs, note values and time signatures.
textes.La portée a cinq lignes : plus une note: The staff has five lines: the higher a note is placed, the higher it sounds.
textes.La clé donne le nom d'une ligne : la clé: The clef names one line: the treble (G) clef puts G on the 2nd line, the bass (F) clef puts F on the 4th.
textes.Une ronde vaut 2 blanches, 4 noires ou 8: A whole note is worth 2 half notes, 4 quarter notes or 8 eighth notes. A dot after a note adds half its value.
textes.La mesure 4/4 compte quatre temps d'une: 4/4 time counts four quarter-note beats; 3/4 time, three beats, the waltz time.
textes.Le chiffre du bas d'une mesure ne compte: The bottom number of a time signature does not count beats: it says which note gets one beat (4 for the quarter note, 8 for the eighth).
textes.Durées : une ronde vaut deux blanches, q: Note values: a whole note equals two half notes, four quarter notes or eight eighth notes
textes.Octave, quinte, demi-ton et le la de réf: Octave, fifth, semitone and the reference A.
textes.Monter d'une octave double la fréquence: Going up an octave doubles the frequency: the A at 440 Hz has the A at 880 Hz as its octave.
textes.La quinte juste répond au rapport 3/2 de: The perfect fifth matches a 3/2 frequency ratio, the fourth a 4/3 ratio. On a string, two thirds of the length sound the fifth.
textes.L'octave occidentale compte 12 demi-tons: The Western octave has 12 semitones; a whole tone equals two semitones.
textes.Un dièse (♯) monte une note d'un demi-to: A sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone; a flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone.
textes.Les marteaux de forgeron de Pythagore so: Pythagoras's blacksmith hammers are a legend: a hammer's note does not follow its weight the way a string's note follows its length.
textes.Une corde : sa moitié sonne l'octave, se: A string: half of it sounds the octave, two thirds the fifth, three quarters the fourth
textes.Gamme majeure, gamme mineure, armure et: Major scale, minor scale, key signature and circle of fifths.
textes.La gamme majeure suit le motif ton, ton,: The major scale follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half: C D E F G A B C, on the white keys alone.
textes.La gamme mineure naturelle suit ton, dem: The natural minor scale follows whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. A minor has the same notes as C major: it is its relative.
textes.L'armure, au début de la portée, liste l: The key signature, at the start of the staff, lists the key's sharps or flats: one F♯ for G major, one B♭ for F major.
textes.De quinte en quinte (do, sol, ré, la…),: From fifth to fifth (C, G, D, A…), each major key gains one more sharp: this is the circle of fifths.
textes.Do majeur et la mineur partagent exactem: C major and A minor share exactly the same notes: only the starting note, the tonic, changes.
textes.Gamme de do majeur : ton, ton, demi-ton,: C major scale: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
textes.Fondamentale, harmoniques, et ce qui dis: Fundamental, harmonics, and what tells a flute from a violin.
textes.Une note d'instrument contient sa fréque: An instrument's note contains its fundamental frequency f and harmonics at 2f, 3f, 4f…
textes.Le timbre, qui distingue un violon d'une: Timbre, which tells a violin from a flute on the same note, depends mostly on the mix of these harmonics and on the attack of the sound.
textes.Joseph Fourier a montré en 1822 qu'un si: Joseph Fourier showed in 1822 that a periodic signal breaks down into a sum of sine waves.
textes.Un tuyau ouvert aux deux bouts produit t: A pipe open at both ends produces all the harmonics; closed at one end, mostly the odd ones, like the clarinet in its low register.
textes.Deux instruments qui jouent la même note: Two instruments playing the same note have the same fundamental: it is not the pitch that differs, it is the timbre.
textes.le timbre dépend du dosage de chaque har: timbre depends on the strength of each harmonic
textes.Une corde vibre à la fois sur sa fondame: A string vibrates at once on its fundamental f and on its harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f
textes.L'accord parfait majeur empile une tierc: The major triad stacks a major third (4 semitones) then a minor third (3): C, E, G.
textes.L'accord parfait mineur inverse l'ordre,: The minor triad reverses the order, minor third then major third: A, C, E.
textes.Les intervalles aux rapports simples son: Intervals with simple ratios sound consonant: octave 2/1, fifth 3/2, major third 5/4.
textes.Rameau, en 1722 : do-mi-sol, mi-sol-do e: Rameau, in 1722: C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted.
textes.Un accord ne prend pas le nom de sa note: A chord is not named after its lowest note but after its root: E-G-C is still a C chord.
textes.Accord parfait de do majeur : do, mi, so: C major triad: C, E, G; major third then minor third
textes.Quintes pures, comma pythagoricien et te: Pure fifths, Pythagorean comma and equal temperament.
textes.Douze quintes pures (3/2) dépassent sept: Twelve pure fifths (3/2) overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%: this is the Pythagorean comma.
textes.Le tempérament égal divise l'octave en 1: Equal temperament divides the octave into 12 identical semitones, with a ratio of ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595.
textes.Ses quintes sont un peu trop petites (≈: Its fifths are slightly too small (≈ 1.4983 instead of 1.5), but every key becomes playable.
textes.L'octave vaut 1 200 cents, le demi-ton t: The octave is 1,200 cents, the tempered semitone 100 cents.
textes.« Bien tempéré » ne veut pas forcément d: “Well-tempered” does not necessarily mean “equally tempered”: the exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
textes.l'écart, le comma pythagoricien, vaut en: the gap, the Pythagorean comma, is about 1.4%
textes.le tempérament égal le répartit sur les: equal temperament spreads it over the 12 fifths
textes.Douze quintes pures dépassent sept octav: Twelve pure fifths overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%: this is the Pythagorean comma
textes.Décibels, limites de l'oreille et émotio: Decibels, the limits of the ear and musical emotion.
textes.Une oreille jeune entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: A young ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz; with age, the high frequencies go first.
textes.Le décibel est logarithmique : +10 dB mu: The decibel is logarithmic: +10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10, +3 dB roughly doubles it.
textes.À intensité égale, l'oreille est plus se: At equal intensity, the ear is more sensitive around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz than in the bass (Fletcher and Munson curves, 1933).
textes.Les frissons musicaux s'accompagnent d'u: Musical chills come with a release of dopamine in the brain (Salimpoor et al., 2011).
textes.L'« effet Mozart », qui rendrait plus in: The “Mozart effect,” supposed to make you smarter, was not confirmed: the effect described in 1993 was small, brief and poorly replicated.
textes.L'oreille humaine entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: The human ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, with peak sensitivity around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz
textes.Fréquence = 1 ÷ période, et longueur d'o: Frequency = 1 ÷ period, and wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.
textes.Le son est une onde de pression, pas de: Sound is a pressure wave, no sound in a vacuum. 343 m/s in air: 3 seconds per kilometre.
textes.Une corde pincée, une membrane de haut-p: A plucked string, a loudspeaker cone or your vocal cords push the air, which compresses, then relaxes. This compression is passed along step by step, like a push in a queue of people: it is a pressure wave. The air does not travel, only the push moves forward. Without matter there is nothing to push: sound does not cross a vacuum.
textes.Fréquence = hauteur, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitud: Frequency = pitch, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitude = loudness. λ = v ÷ f: A 440 Hz is 0.78 m long.
textes.La fréquence f, en hertz, compte les vib: Frequency f, in hertz, counts the vibrations per second; it gives the pitch. The higher it is, the higher the sound. It is the inverse of the period T, the duration of one vibration: f = 1 ÷ T. For a period of 0.002 s, f = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 Hz. The tuning fork, invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter at the English court, vibrates 440 times a second: that is the A.
textes.L'amplitude, elle, donne l'intensité, me: Amplitude gives the intensity, measured in decibels. The two are independent: a low A can be very loud, a high A very soft. And the wave has a length: the distance covered during one vibration, λ = v ÷ f. For A at 440 Hz in air: λ = 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m. Bass notes have wavelengths of several metres, hence big loudspeakers.
textes.Hertz : ondes radio (fin des années 1880: Hertz: radio waves (late 1880s). Light arrives at once, sound takes its time.
textes.L'unité de fréquence porte le nom de Hei: The unit of frequency is named after Heinrich Hertz, who demonstrated radio waves at the end of the 1880s. Yet they are waves very different from sound: electromagnetic, they cross the vacuum at the speed of light. Sound needs air, water or a solid. The same word, "wave", covers both because they obey the same vibration equations.
textes.C'est pourquoi on voit l'éclair avant d': That is why you see the lightning before hearing the thunder: they are born at the same moment, but the light arrives almost at once while the sound takes its time. A 1,000 Hz sound vibrates five times faster than a 200 Hz sound: it sounds more than two octaves higher.
textes.Cinq lignes, l'aigu en haut. Clé de sol: Five lines, high at the top. Treble clef: 2nd line. Bass clef: 4th. Ut, re, mi: Guido of Arezzo, around 1030.
textes.La portée a cinq lignes et se lit comme: The staff has five lines and reads like a graph: time runs from left to right, high notes at the top, low at the bottom. The clef, at the start, names one line, and all the others follow from it. The treble clef curls around the 2nd line: that line carries G. The bass clef puts F on the 4th line, for low instruments.
textes.Les noms des notes ont une histoire. Ver: The note names have a history. Around 1030 Guido of Arezzo had the idea of taking the first syllable of each line of the Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, each line of which starts one step higher: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut would later become do, easier to sing.
textes.Couper une ronde en morceaux: Cutting a whole note into pieces
textes.Ronde = 2 blanches = 4 noires = 8 croche: Whole = 2 halves = 4 quarters = 8 eighths. The dot adds half: dotted half = 3 quarters.
textes.Un point juste après une note ajoute la: A dot just after a note adds half its value. A dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = 3 quarter notes; a dotted quarter note, one and a half quarters, that is 3 eighth notes. Careful: a dot above or below the note is something else, it asks for it to be played detached.
textes.Haut : nombre de temps. Bas : quelle fig: Top: number of beats. Bottom: which note is one beat. 3/4 = the waltz. Petrucci (1501): printed music.
textes.La mesure regroupe les temps. Le chiffre: The time signature groups the beats. The top number counts the beats; the bottom one says which note value is one beat: 4 for the quarter note, 8 for the eighth. In 4/4, four quarter notes per bar, the most common time. In 3/4, three quarter notes: that is the waltz, first beat stressed, oom, pah, pah.
textes.Pendant des siècles, la musique se copia: For centuries music was copied by hand. In 1501 in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed with movable type: notes, staves and words went under the press in several passes. The score became an object that travels.
textes.Octave = fréquence × 2, corde ÷ 2 (Philo: Octave = frequency × 2, string ÷ 2 (Philolaus). A 440 Hz: London 1939, ISO 16 standard.
textes.Monter d'une octave, c'est doubler la fr: Going up an octave means doubling the frequency: f = 2 × 440 = 880 Hz for the A above. The two notes blend so well that they get the same name. On a string it is half: a string half as long vibrates twice as fast. In the 5th century BC the Pythagorean Philolaus already linked the octave to the ratio 2/1.
textes.Le la de référence à 440 Hz a été recomm: The reference A at 440 Hz was recommended in London in 1939, then adopted by the ISO 16 standard. Before that it varied from city to city: France had set its own at 435 Hz in the mid-19th century. A touring orchestra could find itself out of tune with the local organ.
textes.Quinte 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), quarte 4/3, t: Fifth 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), fourth 4/3, third 5/4. Pythagoras' hammers: a legend.
textes.La légende veut que Pythagore ait découv: Legend has it that Pythagoras discovered these ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers of different weights. Nicomachus of Gerasa and then Boethius tell it. It is physically false: a hammer's note does not follow its weight the way a string's follows its length. The ratios themselves are true, and can be checked on a string.
textes.12 demi-tons par octave, un ton = 2 demi: 12 semitones per octave, a tone = 2 semitones, fifth = 7. Sharp raises, flat lowers, natural cancels.
textes.L'octave occidentale compte 12 demi-tons: The Western octave has 12 semitones: on a piano, seven white keys and five black before you reach the same note again. A tone is two semitones: from C to D you pass through C♯. The perfect fifth has seven: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G.
textes.Le dièse (♯) monte une note d'un demi-to: The sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, the flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone, and the natural (♮) cancels both. On a piano C♯ and D♭ fall on the same black key; on a violin a player may play them very slightly differently.
textes.Majeure : T T ½ T T T ½. Do majeur = tou: Major: T T ½ T T T ½. C major = white keys. The key signature keeps the pattern: G has F♯, F has B♭.
textes.Partez d'une autre note et, pour garder: Start from another note and, to keep the pattern, you need accidentals. From G, the F must go up: G major has an F♯. From F, the B must come down: F major has a B♭. They are written once and for all at the start of the staff: that is the key signature.
textes.La mineur = notes de do majeur, départ e: A minor = notes of C major, starting on A (relative). Pentatonic: 5 notes, the black keys.
textes.La gamme mineure naturelle suit ton, dem: The natural minor scale follows tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone. Start from A on the white keys and you get it: A minor has exactly the same notes as C major. It is called its relative. Only the tonic, the note of departure and arrival, changes, and with it the whole colour: darker, more melancholy.
textes.De quinte en quinte, un dièse de plus :: Fifth by fifth, one more sharp: C 0, G 1, D 2. Bach: 24 preludes and fugues per book.
textes.Bach a célébré ce cercle complet. Chaque: Bach celebrated this complete circle. Each book of The Well-Tempered Clavier offers a prelude and fugue in each of the 12 major and 12 minor keys: 24 pairs per book. It still required a keyboard tuning that made all these keys playable.
textes.fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701) : 3e harmoniq: fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701): 3rd harmonic of 110 Hz = 330 Hz. Between 2f and 3f, a hidden fifth.
textes.Une corde ne vibre pas seulement en enti: A string does not vibrate only as a whole. It also vibrates in two halves, three thirds, four quarters, all at once. Each mode gives a frequency: the fundamental f, then the harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f… The n-th harmonic is fₙ = n × f. For a fundamental at 110 Hz, the 3rd harmonic is 3 × 110 = 330 Hz. Joseph Sauveur gave them the name harmonics in 1701.
textes.Sauveur appela aussi « nœuds » les point: Sauveur also called the still points "nodes". A string vibrating in 4 loops at 400 Hz has a fundamental of f = 400 ÷ 4 = 100 Hz. And between the 2nd and 3rd harmonics the ratio is 3f ÷ 2f = 3/2: every note contains a hidden fifth.
textes.Pourquoi une flûte n'est pas un violon: Why a flute is not a violin
textes.Même note, même fondamentale : le timbre: Same note, same fundamental: timbre is the mix of harmonics and the attack. Helmholtz (1863): the resonators.
textes.Une flûte et un violon qui jouent le mêm: A flute and a violin playing the same A have the same fundamental. What sets them apart is timbre: the mix of harmonics, and the way the sound begins, the attack. The violin is rich in harmonics, the flute has few. A pipe open at both ends produces all the harmonics; closed at one end, it favours the odd ones, like the clarinet in its low register, hence its rather hollow tone.
textes.En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie sa: In 1863 Hermann von Helmholtz published his great study of the sensations of tone. To isolate harmonics he used hollow resonators, each tuned to a single frequency, which he held against the ear: you could then hear one harmonic at a time in a sound that seemed single.
textes.Fourier (1822) : tout signal périodique: Fourier (1822): any periodic signal = sum of sine waves. The spectrum analyser shows it.
textes.En 1822, dans sa Théorie analytique de l: In 1822, in his Analytical Theory of Heat, Joseph Fourier showed that a periodic signal, however complicated, can be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves. He was working on heat, not music, but his tool applies to everything that vibrates.
textes.C'est exactement ce que fait un analyseu: That is exactly what a spectrum analyser does: it breaks a sound down into its frequencies and displays the fundamental and its harmonics, each with its own height. Electronic tuners, MP3 compression and song recognition rest on this idea.
textes.Majeur : tierce majeure (4) + mineure (3: Major: major third (4) + minor (3). Minor: the reverse. Rameau (1722): inversions.
textes.L'accord parfait majeur empile deux tier: The major triad stacks two thirds: a major third of 4 semitones, then a minor third of 3. On C: C, E, G, the root, its third and its fifth. The minor triad reverses the order, minor third then major: A, C, E. C minor is formed by lowering the third: C, E♭, G.
textes.En 1722, Jean-Philippe Rameau publie son: In 1722 Jean-Philippe Rameau published his Treatise on Harmony Reduced to its Natural Principles. In it he showed that C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted: it takes the name of its root, not of its lowest note. He also set out the fundamental bass, which explains chord progressions.
textes.Rapports simples = consonance (Helmholtz: Simple ratios = consonance (Helmholtz, beats). Zarlino (1558): third 5/4, 264 → 330 Hz.
textes.Les intervalles aux rapports simples son: Intervals with simple ratios sound consonant: the octave 2/1, the fifth 3/2, the major third 5/4, the minor third 6/5. Helmholtz explained it by beats: with a simple ratio few neighbouring harmonics rub against each other; with a complicated ratio they grate.
textes.En 1558, Gioseffo Zarlino défend les tie: In 1558 Gioseffo Zarlino championed pure thirds at ratio 5/4 against the Pythagorean third of 81/64, too wide. The calculation: the natural major third of a C at 264 Hz is f = 264 × 5/4 = 330 Hz. After a perfect cadence, the dominant G resolving onto the tonic C, you hear that the piece is over.
textes.Tonique = repos, dominante = tension. Ca: Tonic = rest, dominant = tension. Perfect cadence: G → C. A chord takes the name of its root.
textes.En harmonie, chaque accord a un rôle dan: In harmony each chord has a role in the key. The tonic, built on the first note, is rest. The dominant, on the fifth, creates a tension that calls for a return. The perfect cadence, dominant then tonic, G then C in C major, has the effect of a full stop.
textes.Les quintes ne retombent pas juste: The fifths do not land true
textes.(3/2)¹² ≈ 129,75 contre 2⁷ = 128 : 1,4 %: (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75 versus 2⁷ = 128: a 1.4 % gap, the Pythagorean comma.
textes.Empilez douze quintes pures depuis un do: Stack twelve pure fifths from a C: you should land on a C seven octaves up. The calculation says no. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is 129.75 ÷ 128 − 1 ≈ 0.0137, that is 1.4 %. That is the Pythagorean comma, named after Pythagoras because it comes from his tuning by pure fifths.
textes.Conséquence : impossible d'accorder un c: Consequence: you cannot tune a keyboard with all its fifths pure. The error has to be spread somewhere. Meantone temperament, for example, keeps eleven nearly pure fifths and concentrates the error in the twelfth, so grating that it is called the wolf fifth: music that modulated too far became unplayable on a single keyboard.
textes.Demi-ton tempéré = ¹²√2 ≈ 1,0595 (Zhu Za: Tempered semitone = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595 (Zhu Zaiyu, 1584). Fifths barely too small, every key playable.
textes.Le tempérament égal répartit l'erreur pa: Equal temperament spreads the error everywhere: it divides the octave into 12 identical semitones. Twelve semitones must make an octave, so r¹² = 2 and r = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595. Each fifth becomes slightly too small, about 1.4983 instead of 1.5, 2 cents less: the ear barely notices. But every key becomes playable.
textes.En 1584, en Chine, le prince Zhu Zaiyu c: In 1584, in China, Prince Zhu Zaiyu calculated the twelfth root of 2 on an abacus to 24 correct decimal places: it was the first exact calculation of this division. In Europe Simon Stevin was working on the same idea at the same time. Almost all pianos are tuned this way today: every interval is slightly off, but all equally so.
textes.Dans les années 1880, Alexander Ellis in: In the 1880s Alexander Ellis invented the cent: one hundredth of a tempered semitone. The octave therefore has 12 × 100 = 1,200. Tuners and music software use it to say how far out a note is: within a few cents, most ears cannot tell the difference.
textes.Et Bach ? Le titre du Clavier bien tempé: And Bach? The title of The Well-Tempered Clavier does not prove he tuned in equal temperament. "Well-tempered" means tuned well enough to play in every key, which other unequal temperaments also allowed. The exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
textes.20 Hz à 20 000 Hz, les aigus partent d'a: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, high frequencies go first. Peak sensitivity around 2,000-5,000 Hz (Fletcher and Munson, 1933).
textes.Une oreille jeune entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: A young ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below are infrasounds; above, ultrasounds, which bats hear. With age you lose the high frequencies first: that is presbycusis. Nor is the ear equally sensitive everywhere: it is most sensitive around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz, where much of speech intelligibility lies.
textes.En 1933, Harvey Fletcher et Wilden Munso: In 1933 Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson measured it: their curves show that a low sound must be far more intense than a 3,000 Hz sound to seem as loud. That is why the bass seems to disappear when you turn the volume down.
textes.L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20 dB = × 100, +3 dB ≈ × 2. The bel: Graham Bell.
textes.Cette échelle colle à notre oreille, qui: This scale fits our ear, which perceives ratios rather than differences. But it misleads: two speakers instead of one add only 3 dB, not twice the perceived noise. And with too many decibels, the hair cells of the inner ear are damaged for good.
textes.Frissons musicaux = dopamine (Salimpoor,: Musical chills = dopamine (Salimpoor, 2011). The Mozart effect does not hold. Beethoven deaf, Vienna 1824.
textes.En 2011, Valorie Salimpoor et ses collèg: In 2011 Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues measured with brain imaging what happens during musical chills: the brain releases dopamine, the same molecule as for food. Music activates the reward circuit, even before the awaited passage: the pleasure of anticipation.
textes.L'« effet Mozart », lui, ne s'est pas co: The "Mozart effect" was not confirmed. The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task; in 1999 a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ. And Beethoven composed his Ninth almost totally deaf: at the premiere, in 1824 in Vienna, the singer Caroline Unger had to turn him towards the audience so he could see the applause.
textes.Dans l'air à 20 °C, le son parcourt envi: In air at 20 °C sound travels about 343 m/s; nearly 1,500 m/s in water, and 5,000 to 6,000 m/s in steel. Hence the thunderstorm rule: time equals distance divided by speed, t = d ÷ v. For 1 km: t = 1,000 m ÷ 343 m/s ≈ 2.9 s. Count about 3 seconds between lightning and thunder per kilometre. Newton was the first to calculate the speed of sound. That was in 1687, in the Principia: he found 298 m/s, about 15% too low, because he assumed the air keeps its temperature as it is compressed. Laplace would correct the error.
textes.Les durées se divisent par deux : une ro: Durations are divided by two: a whole note is worth 2 half notes, a half note 2 quarter notes, a quarter note 2 eighth notes. So a whole note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 quarter notes, or 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 eighth notes, and a half note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 eighth notes. The shorter the note, the more beams or flags it gets. The idea that a note's shape sets its duration goes back to Franco of Cologne, in his Ars cantus mensurabilis, around 1250.
textes.Un accord ne prend pas le nom de sa note: A chord takes its name not from its lowest note but from its root: E-G-C is still a C chord. That is Rameau's contribution, which lets you recognise the same function in very different layouts, from a Bach chorale to a pop song. Rameau published this idea in 1722, in his Treatise on Harmony.
textes.Le décibel est logarithmique : L = 10 lo: The decibel is logarithmic: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀), where I is the intensity and I₀ the threshold of hearing. In practice, +10 dB multiply the intensity by 10. Going from 60 dB to 80 dB is +20 dB, so an intensity multiplied by 10 × 10 = 100. And +3 dB roughly double it, since 10^(3/10) ≈ 2. The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell; the decibel is a tenth of it. The unit was born in telephony: the Bell System measured its line losses in "transmission units", renamed decibels in 1928.
textes.Après l'octave, l'intervalle le plus sim: After the octave, the simplest interval is the perfect fifth, at ratio 3/2: on a string, two thirds of the length. Above an A at 440 Hz, the fifth vibrates at f = 440 × 3/2 = 660 Hz. Next come the fourth, 4/3, and the natural major third, 5/4. Philolaus already gave the fifth the ratio 3/2. This Pythagorean lived in the 5th century BCE.
textes.La gamme majeure suit toujours le même m: The major scale always follows the same pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Start from C and you get C D E F G A B C, on the white keys alone: the semitones fall between E and F, and between B and C, between the 3rd and 4th notes then the 7th and 8th. The note names come from a monk, Guido of Arezzo, around 1025: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la are the openings of the lines of the hymn Ut queant laxis, which he used as a memory aid. Ut later became do, and si was added.
textes.Il existe d'autres gammes. La pentatoniq: There are other scales. The pentatonic has only five notes, as its name says: the five black keys of the piano form one. It is found in many of the world's musics, from the blues to traditional songs. The oldest notated music to have reached us almost complete, a Hurrian hymn to the goddess Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet from Ugarit around 1400 BCE, even gives instructions for tuning a nine-stringed lyre.
textes.Montez de quinte en quinte depuis do : d: Go up fifth by fifth from C: C, G, D, A… Each major key gains one more sharp. C has none, G has F♯, D has F♯ and C♯, A has three. The other way, going down fifth by fifth, you gain a flat at each step. The twelve keys close up into a circle. The first known diagram of this circle appears in Mykola Dyletsky's Grammatika, in 1677; Johann David Heinichen published another in 1711.

textes.Marin Mersenne, moine de l'ordre des Min: Marin Mersenne, a monk of the Minim order, wants to say everything about sound in a single work: how it is born, how it travels, how the ear receives it. He states the laws of vibrating strings: a string sounds higher when it is shortened, tightened or thinner. He also measures the speed of sound, first by timing the delay between the flash of a gunshot and its bang, then with echoes. The book reviews the instruments of his time, from the organ to the lute, with detailed engravings. It is a great inventory, halfway between physics and a treatise on music.
textes.C'est l'un des premiers livres à traiter: It is one of the first books to treat music as an object of physical measurement.
textes.Mersenne servait de boîte aux lettres à: Mersenne acted as the mailbox of learned Europe: he circulated the work of Descartes, Fermat and many others.
textes.Un moine qui chronomètre des coups de fe: A monk timing gunshots. The AI approves of the method, less of the neighbors.
textes.Guido, moine bénédictin, enseigne le cha: Guido, a Benedictine monk, teaches singing at the cathedral school of Arezzo. Bishop Theodaldus commissions this treatise from him. In it he explains how to sing in tune, how to divide a melody and how to make two voices sing together. Above all, he champions a system of horizontal lines, a third apart, where each note has a fixed place. A red line marks F, a yellow one C. A singer can then read a melody he has never heard: it is the direct ancestor of our staff.
textes.La portée rend la musique transmissible: The staff makes music transmissible without a teacher: you read instead of learning by heart.
textes.La « main guidonienne », qui place les n: The “Guidonian hand,” which places the notes on the joints of the fingers, bears his name, but it only spread after his death.

textes.Boèce, homme d'État romain au service du: Boethius, a Roman statesman serving King Theodoric, gathers the musical knowledge of the Greeks in Latin. For him, music is first a science of numbers: the octave matches the 2/1 ratio, the fifth 3/2, the fourth 4/3. He distinguishes three musics: that of the world, the harmony of the stars and seasons; that of man, the accord of soul and body; and that of instruments, the only one you can hear. He also tells the legend of Pythagoras and the blacksmith's hammers. Throughout the Middle Ages, this book is the reference of schools and universities.
textes.C'est par lui que l'Europe médiévale app: It is through him that medieval Europe learns the Pythagorean ratios of intervals.
textes.Boèce écrit plus tard, en prison, la Con: Boethius later writes, in prison, The Consolation of Philosophy, before being executed around 524.

textes.Zarlino, élève d'Adrian Willaert et futu: Zarlino, a pupil of Adrian Willaert and future chapel master of St. Mark's in Venice, puts Renaissance music in order. He accepts as consonances the major third (5/4), the minor third (6/5) and the major sixth (5/3), which Pythagorean tuning did not know in this form. He justifies them by the first six numbers, which he calls the senario: a string is divided into two, three, four, five or six equal parts. He renumbers the modes, putting first the Ionian, our major scale, and gives detailed rules for writing in several voices and for setting words to music. His ideas pave the way for the major and minor scales of the following centuries.
textes.Il fait de l'accord avec tierce le cœur: He makes the chord with a third the heart of Western music.
textes.Son ancien élève Vincenzo Galilei, père: His former pupil Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, would fiercely attack his tuning system in several pamphlets.
textes.L'élève qui contredit le maître, puis le: The pupil who contradicts the master, then the son who contradicts the Church. The AI admires the family tradition.
textes.Helmholtz est médecin, physiologiste et: Helmholtz is a physician, physiologist and physicist. He wants to understand why certain notes sound good together. With resonators, hollow cavities each tuned to one frequency, he picks out the harmonics of a sound one by one and estimates their strength. He shows that an instrument's timbre comes from the mix of these harmonics. He explains dissonance by beats: when two neighboring harmonics rub together, the sound seems rough. When they coincide, on the contrary, the chord sounds consonant. The book links physics, anatomy and music theory for the first time.
textes.Il donne une explication physique au tim: He gives a physical explanation of timbre and consonance that is still taught.
textes.Alexander Ellis l'a traduit en anglais e: Alexander Ellis translated it into English in 1875 under the title On the Sensations of Tone, and it is mostly cited under that name.
textes.Des bouteilles creuses contre l'oreille,: Hollow bottles against the ear, in the name of science. The AI has seen stranger fashions.
textes.Rameau, organiste, veut ramener l'harmon: Rameau, an organist, wants to reduce harmony to natural principles, like a physicist. He states that a chord keeps its identity whatever the order of its notes: C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted. Beneath the music, he imagines a fundamental bass, an imaginary sequence of roots that carries the chord progressions, even when you cannot hear it. He establishes a hierarchy of cadences, which structures tonal music. Misunderstood on its release, the book stirs opposition, then becomes the grammar of classical harmony.
textes.Les notions d'accord renversé et de bass: The notions of inverted chords and fundamental bass, learned at the conservatory, come from here.
textes.Rameau n'a donné son premier opéra, Hipp: Rameau only staged his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, at fifty: he was a theorist long before he was famous.
textes.Cinquante ans pour passer de la théorie: Fifty years to go from theory to the stage. The AI does both at the same time.
textes.Werckmeister, organiste en Allemagne, s': Werckmeister, an organist in Germany, tackles an old problem: twelve pure fifths do not land back on the octave. With the old tuning, some keys sounded so out of tune that they were avoided. In his best-known tuning, he spreads the gap over four slightly narrowed fifths and keeps the other eight pure: every key becomes playable, each with its own color. These solutions are called unequal temperaments, or “well temperaments.” They are the first steps toward a keyboard where you can change key without fearing a glaring wrong note.
textes.Il ouvre la voie aux compositions qui pa: He paves the way for compositions that travel through every key, like Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier.
textes.Jean-Sébastien Bach connaissait bien ses: Johann Sebastian Bach knew his writings well, especially those on counterpoint.

textes.Oliver Sacks, neurologue, raconte des ca: Oliver Sacks, a neurologist, tells of cases where music and the brain meet in strange ways. A surgeon struck by lightning suddenly discovers a consuming passion for the piano. Frozen patients with Parkinson's disease regain movement thanks to rhythm. A musician deprived of recent memory forgets everything within seconds, except music, which he still plays perfectly. He also writes about the musical hallucinations that sometimes come with deafness, and about perfect pitch. Each story shows that music engages almost the whole brain.
textes.Il fait comprendre au grand public que l: It makes the general public understand that music is a deep function of the brain.
textes.Le chirurgien Tony Cicoria, foudroyé en: The surgeon Tony Cicoria, struck by lightning in 1994 near a phone booth, started composing after the accident.
