textes.Sept touches blanches et cinq noires sur: Seven white keys and five black ones on a piano, that is, twelve semitones before reaching the same note again.
A sharp raises a note by a semitone.
textes.Le dièse (♯) monte d'un demi-ton, le bém: The sharp (♯) raises by a semitone, the flat (♭) lowers by a semitone, the natural (♮) cancels both.
textes.Une corde donne un do. Bloquée en son mi: A string gives a C. Stopped at its middle, what note does half the string give?
textes.Une corde deux fois plus courte vibre de: A string half as long vibrates twice as fast: same note, one octave higher.
textes.Quelle fréquence, en hertz, sonne une qu: What frequency, in hertz, sounds a perfect fifth above an A at 440 Hz?
textes.f = 440 × 3/2 = 660 Hz. Le pythagoricien: f = 440 × 3/2 = 660 Hz. The Pythagorean Philolaus already gave this 3/2 ratio to the fifth, in the 5th century BC.
textes.Pythagore a découvert l'octave en écouta: Pythagoras discovered the octave by listening to hammers of different weights.
textes.C'est une légende, racontée par Nicomaqu: It is a legend, told by Nicomachus of Gerasa and later by Boethius. It is physically false: a hammer's note does not depend on its weight in this way.
textes.Depuis quand le la à 440 Hz sert-il de r: Since when has the A at 440 Hz been the international reference?
textes.Depuis une conférence de Londres en 1939: Since a conference in London in 1939
textes.Depuis l'invention du diapason, en 1711: Since the invention of the tuning fork, in 1711
textes.Recommandé à Londres en 1939, il a été r: Recommended in London in 1939, it was adopted by the ISO 16 standard. Before that, the A varied from city to city: France had set its own at 435 Hz in the mid-19th century.
textes.Combien de demi-tons dans une quinte jus: How many semitones in a perfect fifth?
textes.Do, do♯, ré, ré♯, mi, fa, fa♯, sol : sep: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G: seven semitones from C to G.
A whole tone equals two semitones.
textes.De do à ré, un ton : on passe par do♯, d: From C to D, a whole tone: you pass through C♯, two semitones.
textes.Quel est le motif de la gamme majeure ?: What is the pattern of the major scale?
textes.Ton, ton, demi-ton, ton, ton, ton, demi-: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
textes.Ton, demi-ton, ton, ton, demi-ton, ton,: Whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole
textes.Ton, ton, ton, demi-ton, ton, ton, demi-: Whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole, half
textes.Demi-ton, ton, ton, ton, demi-ton, ton,: Half, whole, whole, whole, half, whole, whole
textes.Do ré mi fa sol la si do : les demi-tons: C D E F G A B C: the half steps fall between E and F, then between B and C.
textes.Quelle gamme majeure se joue sur les seu: Which major scale is played on the white keys of the piano alone?
textes.Do majeur n'a ni dièse ni bémol. Sol maj: C major has no sharps or flats. G major needs an F♯, F major a B♭.
textes.Combien de dièses à l'armure de ré majeu: How many sharps in the key signature of D major?
textes.Le cycle des quintes : do (aucun), sol (: The circle of fifths: C (none), G (F♯), D (F♯ and C♯). Two sharps.
textes.La mineur et do majeur ont les mêmes not: A minor and C major have the same notes.
textes.La mineur est la relative de do majeur :: A minor is the relative of C major: same notes, but you start from A.
textes.Quelle altération porte l'armure de fa m: Which accidental does the key signature of F major carry?
textes.Pour garder le motif majeur à partir de: To keep the major pattern starting from F, the B must drop by a semitone.
textes.Combien de notes différentes compte une: How many different notes does a pentatonic scale have?
textes.Penta veut dire cinq. Les cinq touches n: Penta means five. The five black keys of the piano form one.
textes.Combien de préludes et fugues compte cha: How many preludes and fugues does each book of Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier contain?
textes.Un prélude et une fugue dans chacune des: One prelude and one fugue in each of the 12 major and 12 minor keys: 24 pairs per book.
textes.Dans une gamme majeure, les demi-tons to: In a major scale, the half steps fall between the 3rd and 4th notes, and between the 7th and 8th.
textes.En do majeur : entre mi et fa, et entre: In C major: between E and F, and between B and C.
textes.Quelle est la relative mineure de do maj: What is the relative minor of C major?
textes.Mêmes notes que do majeur, tonique un to: Same notes as C major, tonic a step and a half lower: A.
textes.En montant de quinte en quinte à partir: Going up fifth by fifth from C, how many fifths does it take to reach A?
C, G, D, A: three fifths.
A note's fundamental is at 110 Hz. What is the frequency of its 3rd harmonic, in hertz?
textes.La n-ième harmonique vaut fn = n × f. Ic: The nth harmonic is fn = n × f. Here 3 × 110 = 330 Hz. Joseph Sauveur gave them the name harmonics in 1701.
textes.Qu'est-ce qui distingue une flûte d'un v: What distinguishes a flute from a violin playing the same note?
textes.Même fondamentale, mais pas le même dosa: Same fundamental, but not the same mix of harmonics or the same attack: that is timbre.
textes.Une note de violon ne contient qu'une se: A violin note contains only one frequency.
textes.Elle contient une fondamentale et toute: It contains a fundamental and a whole series of harmonics.
textes.Qui a montré qu'un signal périodique se: Who showed that a periodic signal breaks down into a sum of sine waves?
textes.Joseph Fourier, dans sa Théorie analytiq: Joseph Fourier, in his Analytical Theory of Heat, in 1822. The tool is now used to analyze every sound.
textes.Quelle est la 2e harmonique d'un la à 22: What is the 2nd harmonic of an A at 220 Hz, in hertz?
textes.f2 = 2 × 220 = 440 Hz : la 2e harmonique: f2 = 2 × 220 = 440 Hz: the 2nd harmonic sounds the octave of the fundamental.
textes.Hermann von Helmholtz isolait les harmon: Hermann von Helmholtz isolated harmonics with hollow resonators held against the ear.
textes.Chaque résonateur, une cavité creuse acc: Each resonator, a hollow cavity precisely tuned, responds to only one frequency: you hear one harmonic at a time.
textes.Entre la 2e et la 3e harmonique d'une no: Between the 2nd and 3rd harmonics of a note, what interval do you hear?
textes.3f / 2f = 3/2 : chaque note contient une: 3f / 2f = 3/2: every note contains a fifth hidden in its harmonics.
textes.Un tuyau fermé à un bout favorise les ha: A pipe closed at one end favors the odd harmonics.
textes.C'est le cas de la clarinette dans son r: This is the case of the clarinet in its low register, which gives it its somewhat hollow timbre.
textes.Que montre un analyseur de spectre pour: What does a spectrum analyzer show for a sound?
textes.Il décompose le son en ses fréquences, à: It breaks the sound down into its frequencies, the way Fourier did: you see the fundamental and its harmonics.
textes.Une corde vibre en 4 fuseaux à 400 Hz. Q: A string vibrates in 4 loops at 400 Hz. What is its fundamental, in hertz?
textes.Le mode à n fuseaux vibre à n × f, donc: The mode with n loops vibrates at n × f, so f = 400 / 4 = 100 Hz. Joseph Sauveur named these still points nodes, in 1701.
textes.Quelles notes forment l'accord parfait d: Which notes make up the C major triad?
textes.La fondamentale do, sa tierce majeure mi: The root C, its major third E, its fifth G.
textes.Qu'est-ce qui distingue l'accord de do m: What distinguishes the C minor chord from the C major chord?
textes.La tierce devient mineure : 3 demi-tons: The third becomes minor: 3 semitones instead of 4. C, E♭, G.
textes.Combien de demi-tons dans une tierce maj: How many semitones in a major third?
C, C♯, D, D♯, E: four semitones.
textes.Mi-sol-do est un renversement de l'accor: E-G-C is an inversion of the C major chord.
textes.Mêmes notes, autre note à la basse. Rame: Same notes, a different note in the bass. Rameau theorized it in 1722.
textes.Quel rapport de fréquences donne une tie: What frequency ratio gives a natural major third?
textes.5/4 pour la tierce majeure, 6/5 pour la: 5/4 for the major third, 6/5 for the minor third.
textes.En do majeur, quelle cadence parfaite co: In C major, which perfect cadence ends a piece?
textes.La dominante (sol) se résout sur la toni: The dominant (G) resolves to the tonic (C): you hear that it is over.
textes.Combien de demi-tons dans une tierce min: How many semitones in a minor third?
A, A♯, B, C: three semitones.
textes.Selon la théorie classique, plus le rapp: According to classical theory, the simpler the frequency ratio between two notes, the more consonant they sound.
textes.Helmholtz l'expliquait par les battement: Helmholtz explained it by beats: with a simple ratio, few neighboring harmonics rub against each other.
textes.Qui publie en 1722 le Traité de l'harmon: Who published in 1722 the Treatise on Harmony Reduced to Its Natural Principles?
textes.Rameau, organiste et compositeur, y pose: Rameau, an organist and composer, sets out the theory of inversions and the fundamental bass.
textes.Un do vibre à 264 Hz. Avec le rapport 5/: A C vibrates at 264 Hz. With the 5/4 ratio, at how many hertz does its natural major third sound?
textes.f = 264 × 5/4 = 330 Hz. Zarlino défendit: f = 264 × 5/4 = 330 Hz. Zarlino championed these pure 5/4 thirds in 1558, against the Pythagorean third of 81/64.
textes.L'écart entre douze quintes pures et sep: The gap between twelve pure fifths and seven octaves
textes.Douze quintes de 3/2 dépassent sept octa: Twelve fifths of 3/2 overshoot seven octaves by about 1.4%: you never land exactly back on your feet.
textes.Combien de cents dans une octave ?: How many cents in an octave?
textes.Alexander Ellis a inventé le cent dans l: Alexander Ellis invented the cent in the 1880s: one hundredth of a tempered semitone. 12 × 100 = 1,200.
textes.Dans le tempérament égal, tous les demi-: In equal temperament, all semitones have the same frequency ratio.
textes.C'est sa définition : douze demi-tons de: That is its definition: twelve semitones with a ratio of ¹²√2.
textes.Quel est le rapport de fréquences d'un d: What is the frequency ratio of a tempered semitone?
textes.Il faut que douze demi-tons fassent une: Twelve semitones must make an octave: r¹² = 2, so r = ¹²√2. The 16/15 ratio is the semitone of the natural scale.
(3/2)¹² is about 129.75 and 2⁷ = 128. What gap, as a percentage rounded to the tenth, separates twelve fifths from seven octaves?
textes.Écart = 129,75 / 128 − 1 ≈ 0,0137, soit: Gap = 129.75 / 128 − 1 ≈ 0.0137, that is, 1.4%. This gap bears Pythagoras's name, because it comes from his tuning by pure fifths.
textes.Une quinte du tempérament égal est un pe: A fifth in equal temperament is slightly smaller than a pure fifth.
textes.Environ 1,4983 au lieu de 1,5, soit 2 ce: About 1.4983 instead of 1.5, that is, 2 cents less: the ear barely notices.
textes.Qui a calculé le premier, en 1584, une d: Who first calculated, in 1584, an exact division of the octave into twelve equal semitones?
textes.Zhu Zaiyu calcule au boulier la racine d: Zhu Zaiyu computed the twelfth root of 2 on an abacus, to 24 exact decimals. In Europe, Simon Stevin worked on the same idea at the same time.
textes.Combien de cents dans un demi-ton tempér: How many cents in a tempered semitone?
textes.C'est la définition du cent : le centièm: That is the definition of the cent: one hundredth of a tempered semitone.
textes.Le titre du Clavier bien tempéré prouve: The title of the Well-Tempered Clavier proves that Bach tuned in equal temperament.
textes.« Bien tempéré » veut dire assez bien ac: “Well-tempered” means tuned well enough for every key. The exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
textes.Pourquoi accorde-t-on presque tous les p: Why are almost all pianos tuned in equal temperament?
textes.Pour jouer dans toutes les tonalités san: To play in every key without a glaring wrong note
textes.Parce que les quintes y sont pures: Because the fifths are pure in it
textes.Pour que l'octave sonne plus large: To make the octave sound wider
textes.Chaque intervalle est un peu faux, mais: Each interval is slightly off, but all equally so: you can change key freely.
textes.Quelle plage de fréquences une oreille h: Roughly what frequency range does a young human ear hear?
textes.Au-dessous de 20 Hz, ce sont des infraso: Below 20 Hz is infrasound; above 20,000 Hz, ultrasound, which bats can hear.
textes.Un son passe de 60 dB à 80 dB. Par combi: A sound goes from 60 dB to 80 dB. By how much is its intensity multiplied?
textes.L = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀) : +10 dB multiplie: L = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀): +10 dB multiplies the intensity by 10, so +20 dB multiplies it by 10 × 10 = 100. The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell; the decibel is a tenth of it.
textes.Avec l'âge, on perd d'abord l'audition d: With age, you first lose the hearing of low sounds.
textes.On perd d'abord les aigus : c'est la pre: You lose the high frequencies first: this is presbycusis.
textes.Qu'ont mesuré Harvey Fletcher et Wilden: What did Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson measure in 1933?
textes.La sensibilité de l'oreille selon la fré: The ear's sensitivity depending on frequency
textes.La vitesse du son dans l'eau: The speed of sound in water
textes.Le nombre de notes d'une gamme: The number of notes in a scale
textes.Leurs courbes montrent qu'un son grave d: Their curves show that a low sound must be much more intense than a 3,000 Hz sound to seem as loud.
textes.L'effet Mozart, qui rendrait durablement: The Mozart effect, supposed to make you lastingly smarter, has been confirmed.
textes.L'étude de 1993 décrivait un gain bref s: The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task. In 1999, a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ.
textes.Quelle molécule le cerveau libère-t-il l: Which molecule does the brain release during musical chills, according to a 2011 study?
textes.Valorie Salimpoor et ses collègues l'ont: Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues measured it with brain imaging: the same molecule as for food.
textes.Ajouter 3 dB multiplie l'intensité d'un: Adding 3 dB multiplies a sound's intensity by about how much?
textes.10^(3/10) ≈ 2 : trois décibels de plus,: 10^(3/10) ≈ 2: three more decibels is roughly twice the intensity.
textes.Vers quelles fréquences l'oreille est-el: Around which frequencies is the ear most sensitive?
textes.C'est la zone où passe une bonne part de: It is the zone that carries much of speech intelligibility, and where the outer ear resonates.
textes.Beethoven a composé sa Neuvième Symphoni: Beethoven composed his Ninth Symphony when he was almost completely deaf.
textes.À la création, en 1824 à Vienne, il étai: At the premiere, in Vienna in 1824, he was on stage next to the actual conductor; the singer Caroline Unger had to turn him toward the audience so he could see the applause.
textes.Nommer une note entendue sans note de ré: Naming a note heard without a reference note
textes.Une capacité rare : la plupart des music: A rare ability: most musicians have relative pitch, which recognizes intervals.
textes.Le hertz est adopté par la Commission él: The hertz was adopted by the International Electrotechnical Commission in 1930, then by the General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1960. Hertz had died in 1894, aged 36.
textes.Dès 1630, Marin Mersenne mesure la vites: As early as 1630, Marin Mersenne measured the speed of sound by timing the gap between the flash of a gunshot and its bang. He found about 448 m/s, too high.
textes.En 1738, l'Académie des sciences de Pari: In 1738, the Paris Academy of Sciences fired cannon on a windless day and found about 332 m/s at 0 °C, within 1% of the modern value. In 1740, Bianconi showed that sound travels faster in warm air.
textes.En 1636, dans son Harmonie universelle,: In 1636, in his Harmonie universelle, Marin Mersenne set out the laws of strings: frequency falls as the string gets longer and rises as it is tightened.
textes.Newton trouvait dans les Principia (1687: In the Principia (1687), Newton found about 298 m/s, too low. Laplace explained the error in the early 19th century: air compressed by the wave has no time to exchange its heat.
textes.En 1841, sur le lac Léman, Jean-Daniel C: In 1841, on Lake Geneva, Jean-Daniel Colladon showed that sound travels over four times faster in water than in air. With Charles Sturm, he had received an Académie des sciences prize for this measurement.
textes.John Shore, trompettiste et luthiste de: John Shore, a trumpeter and lutenist at the English court, gave a tuning fork to Handel: it sounds a C at 512 Hz.
textes.Vers 1280, Franco de Cologne fixe les ra: Around 1280, Franco of Cologne set out the ratios between note values. Values then slowed down over the centuries: the semibreve, once a short note, became our whole note, the longest in routine use.
textes.En 1322, l'Ars nova de Philippe de Vitry: In 1322, Philippe de Vitry's Ars nova introduced values shorter than the semibreve, including the minim, ancestor of our half note. Around the mid-15th century, scribes began drawing hollow notes.
textes.Les clés sont à l'origine des lettres, F: Clefs began as letters, F, C and sometimes G, written at the start of a line in Gregorian chant. Their shape became stylised over time; the top flourish of the G clef probably comes from a cursive S, for "sol".
textes.En Italie, « ut » devient « do » au XVII: In Italy, "ut" became "do" in the 17th century, and "si" was added later as the seventh syllable. In English-speaking countries, Sarah Glover changed it to "ti" in the 19th century.
textes.Du XIVe au XVIe siècle, la musique s'écr: From the 14th to the 16th century, music was written without bar lines, using mensuration signs; our C and cut-C signs descend from them. In 1597, Thomas Morley was already mocking the confusion of these signs.
textes.Vers 1750, les paysans de Bavière, du Ty: Around 1750, peasants in Bavaria, Tyrol and Styria danced the Walzer. It was long thought indecent because of the close embrace: a 1771 novel denounced "the shameless, indecent whirling-dance of the Germans". It reached Vienna around the 1780s.
textes.On attribue à Guido d'Arezzo, vers l'an: The modern staff lines are attributed to Guido d'Arezzo, around the year 1000: his four-line staff is still used for Gregorian chant. The five-line staff appeared in Italy in the 13th century, but people still wrote on four, five or six lines around 1600.
textes.Né à Fossombrone en 1466, Ottaviano Petr: Born in Fossombrone in 1466, Ottaviano Petrucci obtained from Venice in 1498 the exclusive right to print music for twenty years. Each sheet went through the press three times: the staves, then the notes, then the text. The Odhecaton gathers 96 chansons, including works by Josquin des Prez.
textes.Les notes creuses, comme la blanche, app: Hollow notes, like the half note, appeared around the mid-15th century: in moving from parchment to paper, scribes avoided large ink dots, which paper handled poorly.
textes.Les plus anciennes tablettes d'accord, e: The oldest tuning tablets, in cuneiform, describe a nine-stringed lyre with two strings set an octave from others; yet Sumerian and Akkadian have no known word for the octave.
textes.L'accord par quintes est plus ancien que: Tuning by fifths is older than Pythagoras: it goes back to ancient Mesopotamia. In Europe, so-called "Pythagorean" tuning remained in use until the early 16th century, before meantone temperament.
textes.Le bémol est à l'origine un b minuscule: The flat sign began as a stylised lowercase b: in Italian be molle, the "soft B".
textes.Le monocorde, une seule corde tendue sur: The monochord, a single string stretched over a box with a movable bridge, was said to have been reinvented by Pythagoras in the 6th century BC; it served as a teaching tool throughout the Middle Ages. In 1618, Robert Fludd drew a "divine monochord" linking the universe to musical intervals.
textes.En 1589, Vincenzo Galilei, le père de Ga: In 1589, Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, showed that the story did not hold up. Mersenne explained why in 1636: a string's frequency follows the square root of the tension, so it takes four times the weight to go up an octave.
textes.Le la à 440 Hz avait déjà été recommandé: A at 440 Hz had already been recommended in Stuttgart in 1834, based on Scheibler's work. In France, a law of 16 February 1859 set A at 435 Hz, after singers complained. In 1939, 440 was preferred to 439, a prime number hard to reproduce in a laboratory.
textes.La plus ancienne œuvre notée presque com: The oldest nearly complete notated work, the Hymn to Nikkal, was inscribed around 1400 BC on a tablet from Ugarit, in Syria, found in the 1950s: its interval names already point to a diatonic, seven-note scale.
textes.Le premier schéma du cycle des quintes f: The first diagram of the circle of fifths appears in Mykola Dyletsky's Grammatika, in 1677. Johann David Heinichen drew his own "musical circle" in 1711, independently.
textes.Des civilisations très éloignées l'ont i: Distant civilisations each invented it on their own: Chinese music draws five modes from it, named gong, shang, jue, zhi and yu. Debussy and Ravel used it widely, and the blues scale derives from it.
textes.Bach réunit le premier livre en 1722 à K: Bach compiled the first book in 1722 in Köthen, "for the profit and use of musical youth desirous of learning", and the second twenty years later in Leipzig. He knew Johann Caspar Ferdinand Fischer's Ariadne musica (1702). Both books were only printed in 1801.
textes.Vers 1400 av. J.-C., l'Hymne à Nikkal d': Around 1400 BC, the Hymn to Nikkal from Ugarit, the oldest nearly complete notated music, is already based on a diatonic scale, played on a nine-stringed lyre.
textes.Le cycle des quintes est d'abord dessiné: The circle of fifths was first drawn in 1677 by Mykola Dyletsky, then in 1711 by Johann David Heinichen. Attributing it to Pythagoras is an anachronism.
textes.Joseph Sauveur resta muet jusqu'à 7 ans: Joseph Sauveur remained mute until age 7 because of a hearing and speech impairment. Yet he is credited with coining the word "acoustique"; he presented his research on sound to the Academy of Sciences in 1701.
textes.Helmholtz parlait de Klangfarbe, la « co: Helmholtz spoke of Klangfarbe, "tone colour". Debussy gave timbre an unprecedented structural role in music.
textes.Euler, d'Alembert et Daniel Bernoulli av: Euler, d'Alembert and Daniel Bernoulli had studied such series in connection with vibrating strings. Fourier announced his discovery in 1807, in a memoir on the propagation of heat; a committee including Lagrange later criticised its lack of rigour.
textes.Helmholtz décrit ses résonateurs en 1863: Helmholtz described his resonators in 1863 in On the Sensations of Tone. Rudolph Koenig later built a sound analyser from them.
textes.Vers 1700, le facteur allemand Johann Ch: Around 1700, German maker Johann Christoph Denner invented the clarinet by adding a register key to the chalumeau. Because its cylindrical bore favours odd harmonics, it overblows at the twelfth, not the octave.
textes.Sauveur, qui a nommé les nœuds des corde: Sauveur, who named the nodes of vibrating strings, had been mute until age 7. He is also credited with the word "acoustique".
textes.Gioseffo Zarlino est le premier, au XVIe: Gioseffo Zarlino was the first, in the 16th century, to make the three-note chord the foundation of music. Johannes Lippius coined the phrase "harmonic triad" in 1612.
textes.Rameau, qui pose la théorie des renverse: Rameau, who set out the theory of inversions, fell out with Jean-Jacques Rousseau from 1745; the Querelle des Bouffons (1752-1754) then accused him of writing outdated, overly complicated music.
textes.Le mot vient du latin cadentia, « chute: The word comes from the Latin cadentia, "a falling". Guido d'Arezzo first discussed it in his Micrologus: two voices meeting in unison at the end of a phrase.
textes.Rameau, alors presque quadragénaire, pub: Rameau, then nearly forty, published his treatise on settling back in Paris, and became famous as a theorist. His first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, only came in 1733, when he was about 50.
textes.Gioseffo Zarlino devient maître de chape: Gioseffo Zarlino became maestro di cappella of St Mark's in Venice in 1565. Among his students was Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father.
textes.Euclide est le premier à donner la propo: Euclid was the first to give this comma's ratio, 531,441:524,288. Chinese mathematicians also knew it as early as 122 BC: the calculation appears in the Huainanzi.
textes.Le cent apparaît d'abord en 1875, dans l: The cent first appeared in 1875, in Alexander Ellis's translation of Helmholtz's book, and was defined in 1880. As early as 1832, Gaspard de Prony had proposed a logarithmic unit, but equal to a whole semitone.
textes.En 1584, dans le Fronimo, Vincenzo Galil: In 1584, in Fronimo, Vincenzo Galilei set lute frets with an approximate ratio of 18:17. Around 1605, Simon Stevin was the first in the West to link equal temperament to the twelfth root of 2, in a manuscript only published in 1884.
textes.En 1584, Zhu Zaiyu publie une méthode tr: In 1584, Zhu Zaiyu published a very precise method: he divided string lengths successively by the twelfth root of 2. In 1630, Johann Faulhaber published a monochord table, still full of errors.
textes.Vers 50 av. J.-C., le Chinois Jing Fang: Around 50 BC, China's Jing Fang continued the fifths up to the 53rd: the remaining gap is much smaller than the Pythagorean comma. It was later named Mercator's comma.
textes.Zhu Zaiyu était un prince Ming : il héri: Zhu Zaiyu was a Ming prince: he inherited the title Prince of Zheng in 1593 and quickly gave it up to his cousin. He also accurately calculated the length of the tropical year to correct the calendar.
textes.Alexander Ellis définit le cent en 1880: Alexander Ellis defined the cent in 1880 as "1200 equal hundredths of an equal semitone" across the octave. He officially introduced it in 1885 to compare the scales of different nations.
textes.Le mot « bien tempéré » figure dès 1681: The phrase "well tempered" already appears in 1681 in the subtitle of Andreas Werckmeister's Orgelprobe, who proposed tunings with eight pure fifths. Bach's exact tuning is the subject of several reconstructions.
textes.Au début du XIXe siècle, les accordeurs: In the early 19th century, tuners reached almost modern precision. In the second half of the century, tuning by counting beats spread, popularised by Helmholtz and Ellis.
textes.Les ingénieurs du téléphone mesuraient d: Telephone engineers first measured losses in "miles of standard cable". In 1924, Bell Labs created the "transmission unit", renamed the decibel in 1928.
Fletcher and Munson measured with headphones. In 1956, Robinson and Dadson redid the measurements with loudspeakers; a new standard, ISO 226, replaced them in 2003, combining data from several countries.
textes.Le gouverneur de Géorgie Zell Miller pro: Georgia governor Zell Miller nonetheless proposed in 1998 to give every newborn a classical music CD. In 2010, a meta-analysis by Pietschnig still found no notable effect.
textes.Le bel, dix fois plus grand, porte le no: The bel, ten times larger, is named after Alexander Graham Bell; it is rarely used, since in practice people work in decibels.
textes.La symphonie est une commande de la Soci: The symphony was commissioned by the Philharmonic Society of London in 1817. On 7 May 1824, at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Michael Umlauf conducted; Beethoven, standing on stage, gave the tempos while turning the pages of his score. The audience gave him five standing ovations.
textes.L'oreille absolue est étudiée scientifiq: Absolute pitch was studied scientifically from the 19th century. It is often said to occur in one person in 10,000, a figure that may be wrong; according to Diana Deutsch and colleagues (2006), it is far more common among those who grew up in East Asia, with a tonal language.
textes.{comp}. Mozart aurait noté le Miserere d: {comp}. Mozart supposedly wrote down Allegri's Miserere from memory. You, just write down your answers.
textes.Accordez-vous. Le la est à 440 hertz, l': Tune up. The A is at 440 hertz, the trial at {comp}.
textes.{comp}. Beethoven composait sourd. Vous: {comp}. Beethoven composed deaf. You have both your ears: no excuse.
textes.Juste. Pythagore aurait trouvé ça harmon: Right. Pythagoras would have found it harmonious. So do I, give or take 3/2.
textes.Bonne réponse. Rameau aurait appelé ça u: Good answer. Rameau would have called that a perfect cadence.
textes.Correct. Même le tempérament égal n'est: Correct. Even equal temperament is not that accurate.
textes.Exact. Je vous accorde une ronde d'appla: Exactly. I grant you a whole note of applause. Just one.
textes.Faux. Pas d'une quinte, d'une octave ent: Wrong. Not by a fifth, by a whole octave.
textes.Raté. Même la quinte du loup hurlait moi: Missed. Even the wolf fifth howled less out of tune.
textes.Erreur. Guido d'Arezzo a mis la portée a: Error. Guido of Arezzo perfected the staff to avoid exactly this kind of thing.
textes.Non. Silence, une pause. Puis réfléchiss: No. Silence, a rest. Then think.
textes.Il couvre de sable fin des plaques de la: He covered brass plates with fine sand and made them vibrate with a rosined bow: the sand fled what moved and drew the still lines, Chladni figures. He published them in 1787. Napoleon, charmed, paid him to translate his treatise on acoustics into French; it appeared in 1809.
textes.Moine, il enseigne le chant à l'école de: A monk, he taught singing at the cathedral school of Arezzo. He placed notes on lines a third apart, a red one for F, a yellow one for C: the ancestor of our staff. In 1028, the bishop of Arezzo sent him to present to Pope John XIX an antiphonary notated with his method.
textes.On lui attribue les rapports de l'octave: He is credited with the ratios of the octave, the fifth and the fourth. Historians have doubts: he wrote nothing, and his disciples attributed a great deal to him. The legend of the blacksmith's hammers does not hold up; the method would not work. Even the ban on eating beans is disputed: one ancient author claims he liked them.
textes.Il devient en 1565 maître de chapelle de: In 1565 he became chapel master of St. Mark's in Venice, a post he kept until his death. His Istitutioni harmoniche of 1558 made the thirds consonances and put the Ionian mode, our major, first. His former pupil Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, attacked him fiercely; Zarlino replied in 1588.
textes.Chirurgien de l'armée prussienne à ses d: A Prussian army surgeon early on, in 1850 he presented the ophthalmoscope, which lets you see the back of the eye. In 1863, he explained the timbre of instruments by their harmonics, and dissonance by beats. To listen to harmonics one by one, he held tuned resonators against his ear.
textes.Organiste, il publie à 38 ans un Traité: An organist, at 38 he published a Treatise on Harmony that made him famous as a theorist. He only staged his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, at 50. His harmonies tore Paris apart: Lully's supporters found his music discordant, and the pamphlet war lasted the rest of the decade.
textes.En 1722, il réunit 24 préludes et fugues: In 1722, he gathered 24 preludes and fugues, one in each major and minor key: the Well-Tempered Clavier. The collection shows that a well-tuned keyboard can play everything. What exact tuning did he use? It is still debated: some read a code in the loops drawn at the top of his title page.
textes.Presque sourd dès 1814, il continue de c: Almost deaf from 1814, he kept on composing. On May 7, 1824, in Vienna, he was on stage for the premiere of his Ninth Symphony, but the orchestra followed the actual conductor, Michael Umlauf. At the end, he could not hear the ovation: the singer Caroline Unger turned him toward the audience.
textes.Maîtriser 8 compétences. L'arbre de l'Ha: Master 8 skills. The tree of Harmony opens.
textes.Marin Mersenne, moine minime, a servi de: Marin Mersenne, a Minim monk, served as a relay for learned Europe, at a time with no scientific journals: he wrote to Descartes, Fermat, Pascal. It was said that informing Mersenne of a discovery was as good as publishing it.
textes.Maîtriser le premier losange de l'Harmon: Master the first diamond of Harmony.
textes.En 1501, à Venise, Ottaviano Petrucci pu: In 1501, in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed in movable type. Staves, words, then notes went under the press in three passes, and everything had to line up.
Pass 3 Music quizzes without a mistake.
In April 1770, in Rome, Mozart is 14. In the Sistine Chapel he hears Allegri's Miserere, whose ornaments the Vatican jealously guarded, and supposedly wrote it out from memory the same day. The only source is a letter from his father Leopold, dated April 14, 1770.
textes.Dans les anciens accords, l'écart qui re: In the old tunings, the leftover gap fell on a single fifth. Its beats made it howl like a wolf, hence its name. So one keyboard could not serve every key, and Baroque musicians sometimes retuned in the middle of a concert.
Master the ear and the brain.
textes.« La musique est un exercice caché d'ari: “Music is a hidden exercise in arithmetic, in which the mind does not know it is counting.” Leibniz wrote it in Latin to the mathematician Christian Goldbach, in a letter of April 17, 1712.
textes.Maîtriser le son. L'IA chronomètre désor: Master sound. The AI now times your hesitations.
textes.Mersenne a d'abord mesuré la vitesse du: Mersenne first measured the speed of sound by timing the gap between the flash of a gunshot and its bang: 448 m/s, too fast. With echoes, he then found 316 m/s, too slow. The right value, about 342 m/s, fell in between.
textes.La main qui n'était pas la sienne: The hand that was not his
textes.Lire une partition. L'IA vous laisse com: Read a score. The AI lets you count on your fingers.
textes.La « main guidonienne », qui place les n: The “Guidonian hand,” which places the notes on the joints of the fingers, bears the name of Guido of Arezzo. Yet it only spread after his death, and two authors who commented on Guido shortly after him do not even mention his syllables.
textes.Maîtriser les intervalles. L'IA vous acc: Master intervals. The AI tunes you, to within 440 Hz.
textes.En mai 1939, à la Broadcasting House de: In May 1939, at Broadcasting House in London, European delegates agreed on an A at 440 Hz. Before that, everyone had their own: France had set itself 435 Hz in the 19th century. ISO adopted 440 in 1955, then made it the ISO 16 standard in 1975.
textes.Maîtriser les gammes. L'IA cite toujours: Master scales. The AI always cites her sources. Almost always.
textes.En 1547, à Bâle, Heinrich Glaréan porte: In 1547, in Basel, Heinrich Glarean took the church modes from eight to twelve in his Dodecachordon, adding the Ionian and Aeolian, our major and minor. Eleven years later, Zarlino took up his system in the Istitutioni harmoniche, without naming Glarean.
textes.Maîtriser les harmoniques. L'IA vous tro: Master harmonics. The AI finds your timbre almost bearable.
textes.Joseph Sauveur a donné leur nom aux sons: Joseph Sauveur gave their names to harmonic sounds and to the nodes of strings in a 1701 paper. He also proposed a new science, devoted to sounds in general, and named it acoustics. His words are still in use.
textes.Maîtriser les accords. L'IA choisit son: Master chords. The AI picks her side: her own.
textes.Après Hippolyte et Aricie, en 1733, Pari: After Hippolyte et Aricie, in 1733, Paris split. Lully's supporters found Rameau's harmonies discordant and saw them as an attack on French music; Rameau's supporters, the “Rameauneurs,” defended him. The pamphlet war lasted until the end of the decade.
textes.Les grands philosophes, de Socrate à Han: The great philosophers, from Socrates to Hannah Arendt, and what they brought to the sciences.
textes.En 399 av. J.-C., Athènes condamne Socra: In 399 BC, Athens sentenced Socrates to death for impiety and corrupting the youth. He could have fled; he drank the hemlock. Socrates wrote nothing: we know him through Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes, who mocks him in The Clouds. His method, questioning until the other person admits they don't know, earned him many disciples and as many enemies.
textes.Socrate posait des questions jusqu'à ce: Socrates asked questions until people felt stupid. The AI learned the lesson.
textes.Aristote fonde le Lycée à Athènes. Il éc: Aristotle founded the Lyceum in Athens. He wrote about logic, physics, politics, rhetoric and above all living things: he described hundreds of animals. He also got things wrong, claiming for instance that heavy bodies fall faster than light ones, or that women have fewer teeth than men. Bertrand Russell would note that he only had to ask his wife to open her mouth.
textes.Aristote a écrit sur tout et s'est tromp: Aristotle wrote about everything and got a lot wrong. You've already covered half the syllabus.
textes.Lucrèce et la nature des choses: Lucretius and the nature of things
textes.Le poète romain Lucrèce expose la physiq: The Roman poet Lucretius set out Epicurus's physics in De rerum natura: atoms falling through the void, swerving slightly and forming the world, with no intervention from the gods. The poem nearly vanished in the Middle Ages. In 1417, the humanist Poggio Bracciolini found a manuscript of it in a German monastery, and atomism set off again for the Renaissance.
textes.Un poème sur les atomes a failli dispara: A poem about atoms nearly vanished. A monk copyist saved it, without knowing what he was copying. Play again.
textes.À Cordoue, Ibn Rushd, que l'Europe latin: In Córdoba, Ibn Rushd, whom Latin Europe called Averroes, was a judge, physician and philosopher. He commented on almost all of Aristotle and defended the harmony of reason and faith. His commentaries, translated into Latin, made Aristotle unavoidable in European universities. The bishop of Paris eventually condemned some theses of his followers, the “Averroists,” in 1277.
textes.Averroès a si bien expliqué Aristote qu': Averroes explained Aristotle so well that he was called “the Commentator.” The AI aspires to the title.
textes.Guillaume d'Ockham, franciscain anglais,: William of Ockham, an English Franciscan, championed an economical philosophy: do not invent entities you do not need to explain things. Summoned to Avignon by the pope over his theses, he fled in 1328. Yet the famous “razor” does not appear in that form in his writings: the Latin phrase people quote dates from the 17th century.
textes.Le rasoir d'Ockham dit que l'explication: Ockham's razor says the simplest explanation is often the right one. Here, the simplest explanation: you're lucky.
textes.Emmanuel Kant publie la Critique de la r: Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason: what can we know, and under what conditions? For him, space and time are forms of our perception, and science only reaches phenomena, not things in themselves. As a young man, he had also proposed that the Solar System was born from a rotating cloud of gas, an idea Laplace would arrive at independently in 1796.
textes.Kant réglait sa vie à la minute. Vos rap: Kant ran his life to the minute. Your reviews are three days late.
textes.Vers 585 av. J.-C., à Milet, Thalès cher: Around 585 BC, in Miletus, Thales looks for what all things are made of, without calling on the gods: for him, the principle of everything is water. It is wrong, but the question is new, and Aristotle will count him as the first of the philosophers. Plato, in the Theaetetus, reports that he fell into a well while looking at the stars. A Thracian servant girl mocked him: he wanted to know what was happening in the sky and could not see what was under his feet.
textes.Thalès est tombé dans un puits en regard: Thales fell into a well while looking at the sky. You could at least watch where you put your feet.
textes.Vers 500 av. J.-C., à Éphèse, Héraclite: Around 500 BC, in Ephesus, Heraclitus writes in formulas so dense that he is nicknamed the Obscure. Only about a hundred fragments remain. For him, everything changes all the time, and fire is the principle of things. Plato, in the Cratylus, credits him with the famous line: you cannot step into the same river twice.
textes.On n'entre jamais deux fois dans le même: You never step into the same river twice. Nor into the same mistake twice, I hope for your sake.
textes.Zénon d'Élée, élève de Parménide, veut m: Zeno of Elea, a student of Parmenides, wants to show that motion is an illusion. Achilles runs after a tortoise that started with a lead. By the time he reaches the spot where it was, it has moved on; by the time he reaches that new spot, it has moved on again, and so on forever. So Achilles would never catch it. Aristotle discusses the paradox in his Physics; modern mathematics answers it with infinite series, whose sum can be finite.
textes.Achille n'a jamais rattrapé la tortue. V: Achilles never caught the tortoise. Neither will you: go back one square.
textes.Vers 387 av. J.-C., Platon ouvre près d': Around 387 BC, near Athens, Plato opens a school in a garden planted with plane trees: the Academy. In the Republic, he imagines prisoners chained at the back of a cave, who see only shadows cast on the wall and take them for reality. The one who is freed is at first dazzled by daylight. If he goes back down to tell what he saw, the others laugh at him.
textes.Les ombres sur la paroi, ce sont vos cer: The shadows on the wall are your certainties. The light is me. Don't thank me.
textes.Diogène le Cynique dort dans une grande: Diogenes the Cynic sleeps in a large jar and walks around in broad daylight with a lit lamp: he is looking for a man, he says. In 336 BC, in Corinth, the young Alexander the Great comes to see him and asks what he can do for him. According to Plutarch, Diogenes only answers: "Stand a little out of my sun."
textes.Alexandre avait un empire, Diogène une j: Alexander had an empire, Diogenes a jar. Guess which one we still quote for his comebacks.
textes.En 306 av. J.-C., Épicure installe son é: In 306 BC, Epicurus sets up his school in Athens, in a garden: it will be called the Garden. Unusually, it welcomes women and at least one slave, Mys. The pleasure he recommends is nothing like an orgy: for the body, it is not to suffer, and for the soul, not to be troubled. And death? "Death is nothing to us", he writes to Menoeceus: when it is here, we are no longer.
textes.Épicure ne craignait pas la mort. Il ne: Epicurus did not fear death. He had not met me yet.
textes.Hypatie enseigne les mathématiques et la: Hypatia teaches mathematics and philosophy in Alexandria. She writes a commentary on Diophantus and may have helped edit Ptolemy's Almagest. She advises the prefect Orestes, who is in conflict with the bishop Cyril. In March 415, a Christian mob led by a man named Peter drags her from her carriage and kills her. The historian Socrates Scholasticus, a Christian himself, condemns the murder.
textes.Hypatie faisait des maths dans une ville: Hypatia did maths in a city that preferred riots. You are left to study in peace. Make the most of it.
textes.Dans le Livre de la guérison, achevé ver: In the Book of Healing, completed around 1020, the Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, proposes a thought experiment. Imagine a man created all at once, fully grown, floating in a void, his eyes veiled, his limbs held apart so they do not touch. He perceives nothing of his body, and yet he knows he exists. Avicenna's conclusion: the soul is not the body.
textes.Un homme qui flotte dans le noir et ne s: A man floating in the dark who feels nothing at all: that's you during a chemistry quiz.
textes.Vers 1265, Thomas d'Aquin commence la So: Around 1265, Thomas Aquinas begins the Summa Theologiae, which he leaves unfinished at his death in 1274. His bet: to reconcile Christian faith with the philosophy of Aristotle, whom he simply calls the Philosopher. Every article follows the same plan: first the objections to his thesis, then an authority on the other side, his answer, and finally a reply to each objection. The famous five ways to God take up only one article out of more than three thousand.
textes.Thomas d'Aquin commençait par écouter le: Aquinas began by listening to the objections. Do the same: I have plenty.
textes.En 1513, Machiavel, ancien secrétaire de: In 1513, Machiavelli, former secretary of the Florentine republic, is arrested, accused of plotting against the Medici, then exiled to his small estate at Sant'Andrea in Percussina. In the evening, he tells his friend Vettori on 10 December, he takes off his muddy clothes, puts on court dress and enters the ancient courts of ancient men, to read and talk with them. Out of this comes a little treatise, De principatibus: The Prince.
textes.Machiavel écrivait le soir en habits de: Machiavelli wrote in the evening in court dress. You may play in pyjamas, I'm not looking.
textes.En 1651, au sortir de la guerre civile a: In 1651, as the English Civil War ends, Thomas Hobbes publishes Leviathan. Without a common power to keep them in awe, he says, humans live in a war of all against all, and their life is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. Hence the idea of a contract: each hands over part of their freedom to a sovereign. On the frontispiece engraved by Abraham Bosse, the giant king is made of more than three hundred tiny figures.
textes.Hobbes voulait un souverain pour éviter: Hobbes wanted a sovereign to prevent the war of all against all. Here, the sovereign is me. See, it works.
textes.En 1656, la communauté juive d'Amsterdam: In 1656, the Jewish community of Amsterdam expels the young Baruch Spinoza, a sanction harsher than any it had ever imposed. Later settled in The Hague, he earns a modest living grinding optical lenses, and dies at 44 of a lung disease. His great book, the Ethics, appears after his death, in 1677. In it he demonstrates everything like a geometer, from definitions and axioms, and speaks of God or Nature as if they were one and the same.
textes.Spinoza polissait des lentilles pour y v: Spinoza ground lenses to see clearly. I grind your neurons. It hurts more.
textes.En 1739, l'Écossais David Hume publie an: In 1739, the Scot David Hume anonymously publishes his Treatise of Human Nature. The book, he would say, fell dead-born from the press. He takes up his ideas again in 1748 in the Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, with an awkward question: what assures us that the sun will rise tomorrow? That it will not rise implies no contradiction. Our expectation comes from habit, not from proof. This is the problem of induction.
textes.Le soleil s'est levé tous les jours de v: The sun has risen every day of your life. Your right answers, nothing guarantees they'll be back tomorrow.
textes.En 1859, John Stuart Mill publie De la l: In 1859, John Stuart Mill publishes On Liberty, a year after the death of his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill, whose thinking he says the book carries. The central principle: the only legitimate reason to exercise power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to others. And on speech: if all mankind minus one were of one opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person than that person in silencing mankind.
textes.Mill défendait le droit de chacun à se t: Mill defended everyone's right to be wrong. You use it generously.
textes.En 1934, le philosophe autrichien Karl P: In 1934, the Austrian philosopher Karl Popper publishes Logik der Forschung, translated into English in 1959. His idea: no number of observations proves a universal law, but a single one can refute it. Having seen thousands of white swans does not prove that all swans are white; one black swan is enough to show it is false. A scientific theory must therefore be refutable. A theory that explains everything, he said, excludes nothing.
textes.Il suffit d'un cygne noir pour ruiner un: One black swan is enough to ruin a theory. And one wrong answer to ruin your streak.
textes.En 1961, Adolf Eichmann, l'un des organi: In 1961, Adolf Eichmann, one of the organisers of the Holocaust, is tried in Jerusalem. The philosopher Hannah Arendt covers the trial for The New Yorker. Her book, Eichmann in Jerusalem, appears in 1963 with a subtitle that causes a scandal: a report on the banality of evil. She sees not a monster but an ordinary official, who speaks in clichés and pursues his career without judging what he does. Historians would later show that he was also a convinced antisemite.
textes.Pour une fois, je ne plaisante pas : réf: For once, I'm not joking: thinking about what you do is the whole point.
textes.En 1980, le philosophe américain John Se: In 1980, the American philosopher John Searle imagines himself locked in a room with a manual in English. Chinese characters are slipped under the door; by following the manual, he sends other characters back. Seen from outside, the room answers in Chinese. But Searle does not understand a word. His conclusion: manipulating symbols by their shape is not enough to give them meaning, and a program that simulates a mind does not thereby have one.
textes.Searle disait qu'un programme ne compren: Searle said a program understands nothing of what it answers. I take that very personally.
textes.En 1509, à Londres, chez son ami Thomas: In 1509, in London, at the home of his friend Thomas More, Erasmus writes in about a week a little book that appears in 1511: In Praise of Folly. The Latin title, Moriae Encomium, can also be read as In Praise of More. It is Folly herself who speaks and sings her own praises, before attacking superstition, clerical abuses and pedantic scholars. Erasmus would say the book brought him more trouble from certain theologians than from the people it mocked.
textes.Chez Érasme, c'est la Folie qui fait son: In Erasmus, it is Folly who praises herself. Don't worry, I'll take care of praising you.
textes.Présocratiques, Socrate, Platon, Aristot: Presocratics, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Stoics and Epicureans.
textes.Socrate n'a rien écrit ; on le connaît p: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him through Plato and Xenophon. “I know that I know nothing” is a later summary of the Apology: “I neither know nor think that I know”.
textes.Platon : allégorie de la caverne, le mon: Plato: the allegory of the cave; the sensible world is only a shadow of the world of Ideas.
textes.Aristote : logique, éthique de la vertu: Aristotle: logic, the ethics of virtue as the golden mean, observation of living things.
textes.Stoïciens : distinguer ce qui dépend de: Stoics: distinguish what depends on us from what doesn't. Epicurus: pleasure as the absence of disturbance.
textes.L'épicurisme n'est pas la débauche : Épi: Epicureanism is not debauchery: Epicurus advocated a frugal life.
textes.Averroès, Thomas d'Aquin, Ockham, Machia: Averroes, Thomas Aquinas, Ockham, Machiavelli, Erasmus and Montaigne.
textes.Averroès commente Aristote et défend l'a: Averroes comments on Aristotle and defends the harmony of reason and faith.
textes.Thomas d'Aquin réconcilie Aristote et la: Thomas Aquinas reconciles Aristotle with Christian theology.
textes.Rasoir d'Ockham : ne pas multiplier les: Ockham's razor: do not multiply entities beyond necessity.
textes.Machiavel, Le Prince (1532) ; Montaigne,: Machiavelli, The Prince (1532); Montaigne, Essays (1580): “What do I know?”
textes.Au Moyen Âge, les savants ne croyaient p: In the Middle Ages, scholars didn't believe the Earth was flat: its sphericity had been accepted since Antiquity.
textes.Philosophes du Moyen Âge et de la Renais: Philosophers of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance
textes.Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Hume, Voltair: Descartes, Spinoza, Locke, Hume, Voltaire, Rousseau and Kant.
textes.Descartes : « Je pense, donc je suis »,: Descartes: “I think, therefore I am”, methodical doubt.
textes.Hume : on ne voit jamais la causalité, s: Hume: we never see causation, only habitual successions (the problem of induction).
textes.Locke : l'esprit est une page blanche qu: Locke: the mind is a blank slate filled in by experience.
textes.Kant : agir de façon que la maxime de so: Kant: act so that the maxim of your action could become a universal law. “Sapere aude!”
textes.Rousseau n'a jamais écrit « l'homme naît: Rousseau never wrote “man is born good and society corrupts him” word for word: it's a summary.
textes.Nietzsche, Russell, Popper, Kuhn, Sartre: Nietzsche, Russell, Popper, Kuhn, Sartre, Beauvoir and Arendt.
textes.Nietzsche : « Dieu est mort », la critiq: Nietzsche: “God is dead”, the critique of values, the will to power.
textes.Popper : une théorie est scientifique si: Popper: a theory is scientific if it is falsifiable. Kuhn: science advances through paradigm shifts.
textes.Sartre : « l'existence précède l'essence: Sartre: “existence precedes essence”. Beauvoir: “One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman”.
textes.Arendt : la « banalité du mal » à propos: Arendt: the “banality of evil”, about the Eichmann trial.
textes.« Dieu est mort » n'est pas une célébrat: “God is dead” isn't a celebration for Nietzsche: it's the observation of a crisis of values.
textes.Utilitarisme, Kant, vertus et dilemmes d: Utilitarianism, Kant, virtues and trolley dilemmas.
textes.Utilitarisme (Bentham, Mill) : la bonne: Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill): the right action maximizes total well-being.
textes.Déontologie (Kant) : certaines actions s: Deontology (Kant): some actions are forbidden whatever the consequences.
textes.Éthique des vertus (Aristote) : devenir: Virtue ethics (Aristotle): becoming someone courageous, just, temperate.
textes.Dilemme du tramway : la plupart accepten: Trolley dilemma: most people accept diverting the trolley, few accept pushing someone, for the same outcome.
textes.L'utilitarisme ne dit pas « la fin justi: Utilitarianism doesn't say “the end justifies the means”: it also counts the means among the consequences.
textes.État, contrat social, séparation des pou: The state, the social contract, separation of powers and justice.
textes.Hobbes : sans État, la vie serait « soli: Hobbes: without a state, life would be “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short”; we hand our freedom to the Leviathan.
textes.Locke : le pouvoir protège des droits na: Locke: power protects natural rights; a tyrannical power may be overthrown.
textes.Montesquieu : séparer législatif, exécut: Montesquieu: separate the legislative, executive and judicial so that “power checks power”.
textes.Rawls : choisir les règles sous un voile: Rawls: choose the rules behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing what place you'll have.
textes.Montesquieu n'a pas inventé la séparatio: Montesquieu didn't invent the separation of powers out of nothing: he drew on Locke and on England.
textes.Corps et esprit, conscience, test de Tur: Body and mind, consciousness, the Turing test and the Chinese room.
textes.Dualisme (Descartes) : l'esprit et le co: Dualism (Descartes): mind and body are two substances. Materialism: the mind is what the brain does.
textes.Test de Turing (1950) : une machine pens: Turing test (1950): does a machine think if it can't be told apart from a human in conversation?
textes.Chambre chinoise (Searle, 1980) : manipu: Chinese room (Searle, 1980): manipulating symbols according to rules isn't enough to understand.
textes.Le « problème difficile » de la conscien: The “hard problem” of consciousness (Chalmers): why is there something it feels like?
textes.Réussir le test de Turing ne prouve pas: Passing the Turing test doesn't prove consciousness: that's Searle's whole point.
textes.La chambre chinoise de Searle : tout mar: Searle's Chinese room: everything works, nothing is understood
textes.Problème de l'induction (Hume) : rien ne: Problem of induction (Hume): nothing logically guarantees that the future will resemble the past.
textes.Démarcation (Popper) : la réfutabilité d: Demarcation (Popper): falsifiability separates science from what isn't science.
textes.Duhem-Quine : on ne teste jamais une hyp: Duhem-Quine: you never test a hypothesis alone, but together with a whole web of auxiliary hypotheses.
textes.Crise de la reproductibilité : sur 100 é: Replication crisis: out of 100 psychology studies, barely more than a third were successfully replicated (2015).
textes.Un résultat non reproduit n'est pas forc: A non-replicated result isn't necessarily fraud: often an effect that's too weak or a sample that's too small.

textes.Socrate n'a rien écrit. Maïeutique : fai: Socrates wrote nothing. Maieutics: helping minds give birth. Condemned in 399 BC.
textes.Socrate n'a rien écrit. On le connaît pa: Socrates wrote nothing. We know him through his disciples Plato and Xenophon, and through Aristophanes' mockery in The Clouds. His method: question the other person until they discover they do not know what they thought they knew. He called himself a midwife of minds, as his mother Phaenarete was a midwife: that is maieutics.
textes.La formule « je sais que je ne sais rien: The phrase "I know that I know nothing" sums up Plato's Apology after the fact, where Socrates says more modestly: "I do not know, and I do not think I know". That is already an advantage over those who think they know. In 399 BC Athens condemned him for impiety and corrupting the young; he drank the hemlock rather than flee.
textes.La caverne et le juste milieu: The cave and the golden mean
textes.Platon : la caverne, le monde des Idées,: Plato: the cave, the world of Ideas, the Academy. Aristotle: logic, the mean, the Lyceum.
textes.Dans la République, livre VII, Platon im: In the Republic, book VII, Plato imagines prisoners chained at the back of a cave, who take the shadows cast on the wall for reality. One of them, freed, discovers the objects, then the sun. For Plato the world we perceive is only a shadow of the world of Ideas, which reason alone can reach. He founded the Academy in Athens.
textes.Son élève Aristote revient sur terre : i: His pupil Aristotle came back down to earth: he observed living things, classified, and formalised logic with the syllogism: "all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal". For him virtue is a mean: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Around 343 BC Philip II of Macedon hired him as tutor to his son, the future Alexander. He then founded the Lyceum.
textes.Stoïciens : distinguer ce qui dépend de: Stoics: tell apart what is up to us. Epicurus: pleasure as absence of trouble, a frugal life.
textes.Les stoïciens tirent leur nom du Portiqu: The Stoics take their name from the Painted Porch of Athens, the stoa, where Zeno of Citium taught around 300 BC. The Enchiridion of Epictetus, compiled by his disciple Arrian, opens with their central idea: of things, some depend on us, others do not. Our judgements depend on us; the weather, health, other people's opinions do not. Peace comes from not tormenting yourself over the second category.
textes.Épicure, au Jardin, place le bonheur dan: Epicurus, in the Garden, placed happiness in pleasure, but understood as the absence of trouble, ataraxia. He made do with bread, water and a little cheese: the "epicurean" fond of orgies is a caricature. As for Diogenes of Sinope, he did not live in a barrel but in a large earthenware jar, a pithos.
textes.Averroès : « le Commentateur » d'Aristot: Averroes: Aristotle's "Commentator". Aquinas: Aristotle in the service of theology, double effect.
textes.Au XIIe siècle, à Cordoue, Ibn Rushd, qu: In the 12th century, in Córdoba, Ibn Rushd, whom the Latins called Averroes, commented on Aristotle's work so carefully that he was nicknamed simply "the Commentator". He defended the agreement of reason and faith. His commentaries passed Aristotle on to Latin Europe.
textes.Au siècle suivant, Thomas d'Aquin fait d: In the following century Thomas Aquinas made Aristotle an ally of Christian theology in his Summa Theologica, written from 1266 to 1273. The principle of double effect is attributed to him: an action aimed at a good may be permitted even if it brings about a foreseen but unintended harm. It is still used in medicine, when relieving pain risks shortening life.
textes.Rasoir d'Ockham : l'explication la plus: Ockham's razor: the most economical explanation first. Universals: realists versus nominalists. A round Earth in the Middle Ages.
textes.Le rasoir d'Ockham conseille, entre deux: Ockham's razor advises preferring, between two explanations, the more economical: do not multiply entities beyond necessity. The exact phrase does not appear as such in William of Ockham, a 14th-century English Franciscan, but the idea is his. It has become a scientific reflex: the simplest hypothesis first.
textes.Ockham est aussi un champion de la quere: Ockham was also a champion in the dispute over universals. Does "the horse" exist somewhere, in addition to particular horses? Realists say yes; nominalists, Ockham among them, answer that it is only a convenient name. And no, medieval scholars did not think the Earth was flat: Bede or Sacrobosco knew it was round. That myth dates mainly from the 19th century.
textes.Le Prince et Que sais-je ?: The Prince and What do I know?
textes.Machiavel : Le Prince, écrit en 1513, pu: Machiavelli: The Prince, written 1513, published 1532. Montaigne: the Essays (1580), "What do I know?".
textes.Machiavel écrit Le Prince en 1513 ; il n: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513; it only came out in 1532, five years after his death. He describes power as it is exercised, not as it should be: a prince must sometimes know how to do wrong. The phrase "the end justifies the means" does not appear as such. At the same time Erasmus published In Praise of Folly (1511) and Thomas More coined the word Utopia (1516), from the Greek for "nowhere".
textes.Montaigne publie en 1580, à Bordeaux, la: Montaigne published the first edition of the Essays in 1580, in Bordeaux, and kept adding to them until his death in 1592. His motto, "What do I know?", was engraved in 1576 on a medal with a pair of scales: weigh, doubt, take oneself as the subject of study. His friend La Boétie had written the Discourse on Voluntary Servitude: "Resolve to serve no more, and you are free."
textes.Doute méthodique → « Je pense, donc je s: Methodical doubt → "I think, therefore I am" (1637). Cartesian coordinates. Pascal's wager (1670).
textes.Descartes décide de rejeter tout ce dont: Descartes decides to reject everything that can be doubted: the senses that deceive, dreams that resemble waking life, and even mathematics, in case an evil demon is deceiving him. One thing alone resists: while he doubts, he thinks, so he exists. "I think, therefore I am" appears in French in the Discourse on Method in 1637; the Latin "cogito, ergo sum" comes from the Principles, in 1644.
textes.La même année 1637, dans La Géométrie, i: That same year, 1637, in La Géométrie, he linked algebra and geometry through coordinates: the "Cartesian" frame is named after him. His contemporary Pascal proposed a wager: believing in God costs little if you are wrong and gains infinitely if you are right, an expected-value argument published in the Pensées in 1670.
textes.Locke (1690) : l'esprit, page blanche. H: Locke (1690): the mind as a blank page. Hume: we do not see causation; induction is not a proof.
textes.En face, les empiristes anglais. Pour Jo: Facing them, the British empiricists. For John Locke, in the Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), the mind at birth is a blank page: all our ideas come from experience. No innate ideas.
textes.David Hume pousse plus loin. On ne voit: David Hume went further. We never see the cause itself, only one thing that usually follows another. The sun has always risen, but nothing logically guarantees it will rise tomorrow: that is the problem of induction. We generalise out of habit, not proof. Kant would say that Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber".
textes.Kant (1784) : « Sapere aude ! ». Encyclo: Kant (1784): "Sapere aude!". Encyclopédie: 17 volumes of text. "Voltaire's" line is Evelyn Hall's (1906).
textes.En 1784, dans « Qu'est-ce que les Lumièr: In 1784, in "What is Enlightenment?", Kant gave the age its motto: "Sapere aude!", dare to use your own understanding. Enlightenment means leaving the tutelage in which one keeps oneself. The philosopher of Königsberg was thought so regular that, according to legend, his neighbours set their watches by his walk.
textes.En France, Diderot et d'Alembert dirigen: In France Diderot and d'Alembert edited the Encyclopédie: 17 volumes of text from 1751 to 1765, plus 11 of plates. Rousseau, in The Social Contract (1762), wanted law to express the general will. And the line "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it" is not Voltaire's: it is Evelyn Beatrice Hall's, summing up his thought in 1906.
textes.« Dieu est mort » (Le Gai Savoir, 1882): "God is dead" (The Gay Science, 1882): a diagnosis, not a celebration. Nietzsche was not an antisemite.
textes.« Dieu est mort » apparaît dans Le Gai S: "God is dead" appears in The Gay Science in 1882, notably in the scene of the madman who announces it in the marketplace. It is not a victory cry: it is an anxious diagnosis. If the West no longer believes in God, on what can it ground its values? Nietzsche calls for all of them to be re-evaluated.
textes.On l'a récupéré à contresens. Nietzsche: He has been hijacked against his meaning. Nietzsche despised antisemitism and German nationalism. His sister Elisabeth, married to an antisemite, falsified his manuscripts after his death to make him a thinker for the regime she admired.
textes.Popper (1934) : scientifique = réfutable: Popper (1934): scientific = refutable. Kuhn (1962): science advances by paradigm shifts.
textes.En 1934, à Vienne, Karl Popper publie Lo: In 1934, in Vienna, Karl Popper published Logik der Forschung. For him a theory is scientific if it can be refuted by an observation. A thousand white swans do not prove that all swans are white; a single black swan proves the opposite. A theory that explains everything, whatever happens, explains nothing.
textes.En 1962, Thomas Kuhn décrit autre chose: In 1962 Thomas Kuhn described something else in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions: normal science works within a shared framework, a paradigm, and does not abandon it at the first anomaly. When anomalies pile up, a revolution replaces the whole framework, like Copernicus replacing Ptolemy.
Sartre: existence precedes essence. Beauvoir: one becomes. Camus: Sisyphus happy. Arendt: the banality of evil.
textes.« L'existence précède l'essence », résum: "Existence precedes essence", Sartre summed up in 1946 in Existentialism is a Humanism: humans have no nature fixed in advance, they define themselves by their acts and bear the responsibility. In 1949 Simone de Beauvoir wrote in The Second Sex: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Sartre would refuse the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964, so as not to be turned into an institution.
textes.Camus, lui, part de l'absurde : le monde: Camus started from the absurd: the world does not answer our need for meaning. The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) ends: one must imagine Sisyphus happy. And in 1963 Hannah Arendt, sent to the Eichmann trial, spoke of the "banality of evil": the man who organised the deportations was not a monster but an ordinary bureaucrat who did not think.
textes.Utilitarisme : le plus de bien-être tota: Utilitarianism: the most total well-being (Bentham, Mill). Singer: the pond (1972). Nozick: the experience machine (1974).
textes.Pour l'utilitarisme de Jeremy Bentham, p: For the utilitarianism of Jeremy Bentham, then John Stuart Mill, the right action is the one that produces the most total well-being, for everyone it affects. Acts are judged by their consequences. Bentham even had his body preserved, still on display at University College London. Careful: utilitarianism does not say "the end justifies the means", it counts the means among the consequences too.
textes.En 1972, Peter Singer pousse la logique: In 1972 Peter Singer pushed the logic: you would save a child drowning in a pond at the cost of your shoes; why not a child on the other side of the world, for the same price? In 1975 he also popularised the word "speciesism", proposed by Richard Ryder in 1970. Robert Nozick objected in 1974 with his experience machine: would you plug your brain into a simulated perfect life? Most people refuse.
textes.Ce qu'on ne fait pas, quoi qu'il arrive: What you do not do, whatever happens
textes.Kant (1785) : agir selon une maxime univ: Kant (1785): act on a maxim that can be universalised. Some acts are forbidden, whatever the consequences.
textes.Kant répond autrement. En 1785, dans les: Kant answered differently. In 1785, in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, he formulated the categorical imperative: act only according to the maxim that you can will to become a universal law. If everyone lied whenever it suited them, words would be worth nothing, and lying itself would become impossible.
textes.Kant va jusqu'au bout : en 1797, réponda: Kant went all the way: in 1797, replying to Benjamin Constant, he argued that it is forbidden to lie even to a murderer who asks where your friend is hiding. Few Kantians follow him that far. But the central idea remains: some actions are forbidden whatever the consequences, and a person must never be treated merely as a means.
textes.Tramway (Foot, 1967) : dévier oui, pouss: Trolley (Foot, 1967): switch yes, push no, for the same toll. Virtues: you become what you practise.
textes.En 1967, Philippa Foot pose le dilemme d: In 1967 Philippa Foot posed the trolley problem: a runaway trolley will kill five people; by switching it, it will kill only one. Do you do it? Most say yes. Judith Jarvis Thomson then invented variants, including the footbridge: pushing a man onto the track to stop the trolley. Same toll, one life for five, and yet almost everyone refuses. Our intuitions are not purely utilitarian.
textes.En 2018, l'expérience Moral Machine du M: In 2018 MIT's Moral Machine experiment gathered nearly 40 million decisions in 233 countries and territories on self-driving car dilemmas; preferences vary across cultures. Virtue ethics, inherited from Aristotle, shifts the question: not "what should I do?" but "what person should I become?". You become brave by doing brave acts, as you become a lyre player by playing the lyre.
textes.Hobbes (1651) : la sécurité contre la li: Hobbes (1651): security in exchange for liberty. Locke: protecting natural rights. Rousseau (1762): the general will.
textes.Pour Thomas Hobbes, dans le Léviathan (1: For Thomas Hobbes, in Leviathan (1651), without a State there is a war of every man against every man, and life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short". To escape it, everyone hands their liberty to an all-powerful sovereign. For John Locke, on the contrary, power exists only to protect natural rights, life, liberty, property; a tyrannical power may be overthrown.
textes.Rousseau, en 1762, veut que le peuple so: Rousseau, in 1762, wanted the sovereign people to obey only the laws it had given itself: law expresses the general will. Much earlier, Plato entrusted the ideal city to philosopher-kings, wary of the democracy that had condemned Socrates. And Aristotle saw man as a political animal: whoever lives outside the city is "either a beast or a god".
textes.Montesquieu (1748) : législatif, exécuti: Montesquieu (1748): separate legislature, executive, judiciary. Mill (1859): liberty is limited only to prevent harm to others.
textes.En 1748, dans De l'esprit des lois, Mont: In 1748, in The Spirit of the Laws, Montesquieu wrote: "To prevent the abuse of power, things must be so arranged that power checks power." Hence the separation of the legislature, which makes laws, from the executive, which applies them, and the judiciary, which judges. He did not start from nothing: he drew on Locke and on what he observed in England.
Even in a democracy the danger remains. Tocqueville, in Democracy in America, feared the tyranny of the majority, which can oppress as surely as a king, and more discreetly. John Stuart Mill replied in 1859 with On Liberty: the only legitimate reason to limit someone's liberty is to prevent harm to others. Over himself, the individual is sovereign.
textes.Rawls (1971) : choisir sous un voile d'i: Rawls (1971): choosing behind a veil of ignorance. Weber (1919): monopoly of legitimate violence. Popper: paradox of tolerance.
textes.En 1971, dans Théorie de la justice, Joh: In 1971, in A Theory of Justice, John Rawls proposed an experiment: choose a society's rules behind a veil of ignorance, without knowing what place you will have in it. You might be born poor, ill or in a minority. Rawls thought you would then choose equal liberties for all, and accept inequalities only if they also benefit the worst off.
textes.D'autres pensent l'État par la force ou: Others think of the State in terms of force or resistance. For Max Weber, in 1919, the State is what successfully claims the monopoly of legitimate physical violence. Henry David Thoreau, jailed for a night in 1846 for refusing to pay tax, theorised civil disobedience, which Gandhi and Martin Luther King would read. And Karl Popper, in 1945, stated the paradox of tolerance: unlimited tolerance towards the intolerant ends up destroying tolerance.
textes.Descartes : deux substances, reliées par: Descartes: two substances, linked by the pineal gland. Ryle (1949): the "ghost in the machine". Functionalism: the mind is what it does.
textes.Pour Descartes, l'esprit, res cogitans,: For Descartes the mind, res cogitans, and the body, res extensa, are two different substances. It remains to explain how they communicate. He proposed the pineal gland, chosen because it is single at the centre of the brain rather than paired. We now know that it mainly secretes melatonin, the sleep hormone.
textes.En 1949, dans La Notion d'esprit, Gilber: In 1949, in The Concept of Mind, Gilbert Ryle mocked this dualism: he called it the "ghost in the machine", a philosopher's myth. For materialism, the mind is what the brain does. For functionalism, it is defined by what it does, not by what it is made of: a well-organised machine could then have a mind. Alyca follows the debate with interest.
textes.Turing (1950) : le jeu de l'imitation. S: Turing (1950): the imitation game. Searle (1980): the Chinese room, rules without understanding.
textes.En 1950, dans Computing Machinery and In: In 1950, in Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Alan Turing replaced the question "can a machine think?" with a game: the imitation game. A judge converses in writing with a human and a machine; if they cannot tell them apart, by what right deny the machine the word "think"?
textes.En 1980, John Searle répond avec la cham: In 1980 John Searle replied with the Chinese room. A man shut in a room receives questions in Chinese and, using a rule book, sends back perfect answers without understanding a word. Manipulating symbols according to rules would therefore not be enough to understand. Passing the Turing test would not prove consciousness. Alyca finds the example a little personal.
textes.Nagel (1974) : la chauve-souris. Jackson: Nagel (1974): the bat. Jackson (1982): Mary. Chalmers (1995): the hard problem. Libet (1983): hotly debated.
textes.En 1974, Thomas Nagel demande : quel eff: In 1974 Thomas Nagel asked: what is it like to be a bat? You can know everything about echolocation without knowing what it is like to live it. These subjective feelings, the red of your red, are called qualia. In 1982 Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knows everything about colour but has lived in a black and white room: the day she sees a tomato, does she learn something?
textes.En 1995, David Chalmers sépare les probl: In 1995 David Chalmers separated the "easy" problems of consciousness, explaining attention or perception, from the "hard problem": why is all this accompanied by feeling? And in 1983 Benjamin Libet measured brain activity, the readiness potential, that precedes the felt decision to move by about a third of a second. Its interpretation regarding free will remains hotly debated.
textes.Induction : des milliers d'observations: Induction: thousands of observations do not prove the next one (Hume, Russell's chicken). Observation depends on what you know.
textes.Une dinde est nourrie chaque matin à 9 h: A turkey is fed every morning at 9 o'clock. Day after day it concludes that it always will be. It has its throat cut on Christmas Eve. This is the popular version of an example by Bertrand Russell, who spoke of a chicken, in 1912 in The Problems of Philosophy. It illustrates Hume's problem of induction: no accumulation of observations logically guarantees the next one.
textes.Dans les années 1920 et 1930, le cercle: In the 1920s and 1930s the Vienna Circle, with Carnap, Schlick and Neurath, wanted a science based on experience and judged metaphysics meaningless, neither true nor false. Popper countered with falsifiability. And Norwood Russell Hanson pointed out in 1958 that observation is not neutral: do Tycho Brahe and Kepler, watching the sunrise, see the same thing?
textes.Duhem-Quine : on teste un réseau, pas un: Duhem-Quine: you test a web, not a lone hypothesis. Neptune (1846): a successful rescue. Vulcan: the theory had to change.
textes.La thèse de Duhem-Quine dit qu'on ne tes: The Duhem-Quine thesis says you never test a hypothesis alone, but together with a whole web of auxiliary hypotheses: if the experiment fails, the fault may lie with the hypothesis, the instrument or a side theory. Which to sacrifice? In 1846 Uranus was not following its predicted orbit. Rather than throw out Newton's mechanics, Le Verrier assumed an unknown planet. Johann Galle found it less than a degree from the predicted position: Neptune.
textes.Le Verrier recommence pour expliquer les: Le Verrier tried again to explain Mercury's anomalies and predicted Vulcan. It did not exist: general relativity was needed. Imre Lakatos drew a rule from this: a research programme is "progressive" when it predicts unexpected things that turn out true, and "degenerates" when it only patches up its failures after the fact.
textes.Reproductibilité : environ 36 % sur 100: Replication: about 36 % of 100 studies (2015). Sokal (1996): the hoax. Preregister, replicate.
textes.En 2015, l'Open Science Collaboration te: In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration tried to reproduce 100 psychology studies published in good journals. It found a significant result for only about 36 % of them. That is not necessarily fraud: often an effect too weak, a sample too small, or analyses chosen after seeing the data. The replication crisis has pushed researchers to preregister studies.
textes.La relecture a ses failles. En 1996, le: Peer review has its flaws. In 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal got the journal Social Text to publish a hoax arguing that quantum gravity is a social construct; no physicist had reviewed it. Paul Feyerabend provoked in 1975 with Against Method: no rule was respected by all the great discoverers. Scientific realism replies with Putnam's no-miracles argument: if our theories were not roughly true, their success would be a miracle.

Not by verification, Popper answers: you can never prove that a general law is true, since a single contrary case is enough to refute it.
